documents.title: ACR guideline for screening treatment and management of lupus nephritis

chunks.content: Rheumatology key messages Previous studies have identified prognostic clinical factors for achieving complete renal response (CRR) when treating patients with LN. The Lupus Cruces Nephritis (LCN) protocol has been proven superior to standard of care (SOC) for achieving CRR at 12 months. The LCN protocol is more effective than SOC across different prognostic clinical groups and clusters. Introduction LN is the most frequent visceral involvement in SLE, with important prognostic implications [ ]. The rapid achievement of complete renal response (CRR) mitigates its long-term impact [ ]. The Lupus-Cruces Nephritis (LCN) protocol, based on the repeated administration of one pulse of methyl-prednisolone (MP) with each 2-weekly i.v. dose of 500 mg of CYC, plus reduced initial doses of prednisone and a fixed tapering time of 12 weeks to 5 mg/day, has recently been shown to increase CRR rates and to improve long-term renal prognosis compared with CYC- or MMF-based standard of care (SOC) [ ]. However, these effects have not been assessed in subgroups of different severity. In this study, we aim to further analyse the efficacy of the LCN protocol vs SOC in achieving CRR among subpopulations according to the presence of known prognostic response factors for LN. Patients and methods Study design and patients This is an extended analysis of the recently published observational comparative study on the long-term effects of the LCN ( vs SOC) protocol, thus comprising the same cohort of 147 patients previously described [ ]. Patients with biopsy-proven LN from the longitudinal Lupus-Cruces (Cruces-EAS, n = 62) and Lupus-Bordeaux (BDX, n = 43) cohorts and from the historic Lupus-Cruces cohort (Cruces-historic, n = 42) were included. All eligible participants fulfilled the ACR/ SLICC criteria for the classification of SLE [ , ], had class III, IV or V LN confirmed by renal biopsy and a follow-up of at least 12 months. Treatment protocols As detailed in our previous study, the LCN protocol has been routinely administered in the combined renal clinic of the Autoimmune Diseases Unit at Hospital Universitario Cruces since 2006 [ ]. The therapeutic assignment of the specific form of SOC depended on the site and the form of presentation of LN, including clinical and histologic features [ ]. The LCN and the MMF or CYC-based SOC protocols are presented in detail in the . In brief, patients receiving the LCN protocol were treated with three initial MP 250–500 mg/day, then with oral prednisone at 20–30 mg/day, with a fixed rapid tapering to 5 mg/day in ≤12 weeks. All patients received i.v. CYC 500 mg/2 weeks, for an initial total number of six doses (up to nine doses according to clinical response), with one MP 125–250 mg given just before each dose of CYC. Clinical monitoring by the same team of one internist (G.R.-I.) and one nephrologist (A.O.), including the evaluation of the urine protein/creatinine ratio (Pr/Cr), is booked biweekly at the day hospital before the administration of each CYC-MP dose. After the induction phase was completed, maintenance therapy was started with either AZA or MMF. All patients received baseline therapy with HCQ 200 mg/day. Under certain circumstances, rituximab, belimumab and/or calcineurin inhibitors could be also used. The different schemes for the SOC included MMF at a maximum dose of 1000 mg/12 h, the Eurolupus regime with i.v. CYC 500 mg/2 weeks or a high-dose CYC-based scheme with monthly i.v. CYC (1 g/m 2 ) for 6 months [ ]. MP 250–1000 mg/day ×3 was given depending on the specific site protocol and disease severity. Seven patients in the Cruces-historic cohort received induction therapy with glucocorticoids and AZA, and one with glucocorticoids only. Prednisone starting doses and tapering schemes depended on the site. HCQ was not used in all patients. Maintenance therapy included AZA or MMF. Outcome measure The outcome of this study was the achievement of CRR, as defined in the 2024 Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines [ ]: reduction in the urine Pr/Cr <0.5 g/g and stabilization or improvement in kidney function, ±10–15% of baseline, at 12 months after the initiation of induction therapy. Prognostic variables for subgroup analyses For the analysis by subgroups, a number of baseline variables with prognostic value for achieving CRR in LN were identified from previous publications. These included: gender [ ]; age <25 years [ ]; anti-dsDNA positivity [ , ]; anti-RNP positivity [ ]; low C4 levels [ ]; low C3 levels [ ]; first episode ( vs relapsing) LN [ ]; glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 [ , ]; Pr/Cr ≥1.5 g/g [ , , , ] or ≥2 g/g [ ]; and LN class [ , ]. Regarding the latter, we followed the KDIGO guidelines scheme [ ], thus classifying as class V only those patients with pure membranous LN; any combinations of class V with classes III or

identified from previous publications. These included: gender [ ]; age <25 years [ ]; anti-dsDNA positivity [ , ]; anti-RNP positivity [ ]; low C4 levels [ ]; low C3 levels [ ]; first episode ( vs relapsing) LN [ ]; glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 [ , ]; Pr/Cr ≥1.5 g/g [ , , , ] or ≥2 g/g [ ]; and LN class [ , ]. Regarding the latter, we followed the KDIGO guidelines scheme [ ], thus classifying as class V only those patients with pure membranous LN; any combinations of class V with classes III or IV were classified according to the proliferative pattern. Clustering We aimed to identify different clusters based on combinations of the mentioned prognostic variables, and then to compare the efficacy of both protocols within each cluster. Given the categorical nature of the prognostic variables, we applied a two-way clustering analysis: we first performed a multiple correspondence analysis (MCA), and, by using the dimension factors obtained, we subsequently applied the k-means algorithm [ ]. We used the Calinski–Harabascz pseudo-F test to evaluate the optimal number of clusters. Statistical analysis Descriptive data were generated using percentages, means and s . d . In all the subgroup analyses, both univariant and multivariant, patients treated with the LCN vs SOC protocols were compared regarding the achievement of CRR, separately among patients with or without each of the identified prognostic factors and also within each of the different clusters. For the univariant analysis, the proportions of patients achieving CRR at 12 months in each treatment group were compared by χ 2 test. For the multivariant analysis, a propensity score (PS) adjustment was performed, using the same PS calculated in our previous study with the same population [ ]. The individual probability of being treated with the LCN protocol was estimated by using a logistic regression model, in which age at the time of diagnosis of LN, gender, subcohort (BDX, Cruces-EAS, Cruces-historic), race (White vs non-White), LN class, first episode of LN vs relapse, baseline serum Cr and Pr/Cr levels, dose of HCQ and use of antiproteinuric dugs during the first year were the independent predictors. The PS was then used as an adjustment covariate in all the multivariant models: for the outcome CRR at 12 months, we used binary logistic regression models; for the time-to-CRR analysis, we used Cox proportional hazards models. The statistical analysis was performed using STATA/MP 18 for Mac (StataCorp LP, TX, USA). Ethics approval The study protocol was approved by the Comité Etico de Investigación Clínica de Euskadi (CEIC-E), study code PI2014054, and patients provided informed consent. Results A total of 147 patients were included in this study: 47 in the LCN and 100 in the SOC group. The mean follow-up time was 341 vs 347 weeks, respectively ( P = 0.84). The distribution of the different prognostic factors at baseline was similar in both the LCN and SOC groups, with a significant lower proportion of White patients in the LCN group ( ). No significant differences were found regarding other clinical variables [ ]. The detailed therapeutic variables during the first year are shown in . Overall, 119 patients (81%) eventually achieved CRR, at a median time of 34 weeks. Patients receiving the LCN protocol achieved CRR at higher rates and earlier than SOC patients (85% vs 44% at 12 months, P < 0.001; median time to CRR 21 vs 48 weeks, P < 0.001). The use of additional therapy was similar in both groups and did not influence the results, as shown in our previous study [ ]. LCN patients achieved CRR more frequently than SOC in all subpopulations ( ), with statistically significant differences except for patients with positive anti-RNP antibodies and with normal baseline C3 values, probably a result of low sample size. CRR rates in the LCN group were >80% in all subgroups, except for those with positive anti-RNP antibodies (75%), with normal baseline C3 (71%) and in non-White patients (73%). The PS-adjusted logistic regression models confirmed an increased odds of achieving CRR at 12 months with the LCN protocol in all subgroups; however, the statistical significance was not reached in the subsets of patients with positive anti-RNP ( n = 36, P = 0.37), with normal C3 levels ( n = 34, P = 0.2), non-White ( n = 30, P = 0.053) and male ( n = 29, P = 0.08). The logistic regression was not possible to complete in patients with class V LN, since 100% of those treated with the LCN protocol achieved CRR at 12 months. Of note, all odds ratios (Ors) exceeded 5 except for the subgroups of patients anti-RNP-positive (OR 2.1) or with normal C3 levels (OR 3.7). Cluster analysis The results of the MCA and K-means analyses are shown

anti-RNP ( n = 36, P = 0.37), with normal C3 levels ( n = 34, P = 0.2), non-White ( n = 30, P = 0.053) and male ( n = 29, P = 0.08). The logistic regression was not possible to complete in patients with class V LN, since 100% of those treated with the LCN protocol achieved CRR at 12 months. Of note, all odds ratios (Ors) exceeded 5 except for the subgroups of patients anti-RNP-positive (OR 2.1) or with normal C3 levels (OR 3.7). Cluster analysis The results of the MCA and K-means analyses are shown in detail in the and in . After clustering, patients were divided into three subgroups ( ): cluster 1 (C1), mainly composed of patients with membranous LN, negative anti-DNA antibodies, normal complement levels, normal GFR and nephrotic proteinuria; cluster 2 (C2), including patients with proliferative LN with the highest proportion of class III LN, serologically active, normal GFR and sub-nephrotic proteinuria; and cluster 3 (C3), grouping those patients with the most severe forms of LN, mostly class IV, serologically active, with reduced GFR and the highest levels of proteinuria. There were no significant differences among clusters regarding sex, race, age or first episode ( vs relapsing) LN. The univariant and PS-adjusted logistic regression analyses showed that the LCN protocol was statistically superior to the SOC across all three clusters ( ), although the model was not able to run in the C1 group due to the 100% CRR achieved with the LCN protocol in this subgroup. Likewise, the PS-adjusted Cox regression analysis confirmed the higher likelihood of eventually achieving CRR of patients in the LCN group in the three clusters ( ): C1, PS-adjusted hazard ratio (HR) 10.7 ( P = 0.013); C2, PS-adjusted HR 2.2 ( P = 0.016); and C3, PS-adjusted HR 6.1 ( P < 0.001). Cluster analysis excluding the Cruces-historic subcohort Given the relative heterogeneity derived from the inclusion of historic patients, who apart from the differences in general clinical care caused by changes in the management of lupus over the time were the only ones receiving the high-dose CYC scheme, we repeated the cluster analysis after excluding such patients, as we did in our previous study [ ]. The full results, shown in , were very much alike in showing the superiority of the LCN scheme in the three clusters. However, the reduced sample size widened CIs, and although the magnitudes of the differences for CRR achievement between LCN and SOC were similar than in the analysis of the whole cohort, they did not marginally reach the statistically significant level in cluster C2: CRR rates 80% vs 54%, ( P = 0.059); OR 3.3 ( P = 0.09); HR 1.81 ( P = 0.053). Discussion This expanded analysis of the joined Lupus-Cruces and Lupus-Bordeaux cohort confirms the higher efficacy of the LCN protocol over SOC across different subgroups according to the presence or not of prognostic factors, and also within each of the three clusters, reflecting well-defined clinical subsets of LN. These findings reinforce the idea that the addition of MP before each dose of CYC plays an important role in inducing remission in LN. Although the differences between the LCN and SOC schemes were less apparent among patients with milder forms of proliferative LN (patients included in cluster C2), the LCN protocol was also superior in this group. Indeed, patients with the most severe forms of LN, those included in cluster C3, achieved CRR rates >85% at 1 year. The results in patients with pure class V LN, although limited by the low number of patients (four treated with the LCN scheme), also open a door for further research regarding the role of CYC (plus MP) in this subclass [ ]. Although recent data also support the efficacy of CYC in idiopathic membranous nephropathy [ ], a direct inference with class V LN cannot be yet made. CYC (plus glucocorticoids and HCQ) has almost disappeared from the first-line induction therapy options for LN. Among the three major recently updated guidelines, both the ACR [ ] and EULAR [ ] recommendations aim for initial triple therapy, adding either belimumab (to MMF or to CYC) or a calcineurin inhibitor (to MMF, not to CYC); the 2024 KDIGO guidelines are the only ones still considering CYC plus glucocorticoids and HCQ as an initial therapy for induction [ ]. Our results support that the Eurolupus CYC protocol, modified by adding repeated MP with each CYC dose (the LCN regime), obtains CRR rates much higher than those reported in the pivotal randomized controlled trials with combination therapy including belimumab [ ], voclosporin [ ] or obinutuzumab [ ]. Indeed, many studies in real-life settings reported higher CRR rates than randomized controlled trials, which could help us put into context

a calcineurin inhibitor (to MMF, not to CYC); the 2024 KDIGO guidelines are the only ones still considering CYC plus glucocorticoids and HCQ as an initial therapy for induction [ ]. Our results support that the Eurolupus CYC protocol, modified by adding repeated MP with each CYC dose (the LCN regime), obtains CRR rates much higher than those reported in the pivotal randomized controlled trials with combination therapy including belimumab [ ], voclosporin [ ] or obinutuzumab [ ]. Indeed, many studies in real-life settings reported higher CRR rates than randomized controlled trials, which could help us put into context the generalizability of those results; however, CRR rates >80% at 12 months have been rarely reported even in observational studies [ ]. Whilst our recent study confirming the long-term efficacy of the LCN protocol [ ] supported a wider use of this scheme as a general therapeutic approach to LN, this extended analysis of the same cohort confirms its efficacy in all the range of patients with class III, IV and V LN. The main limitation of this study is its observational design. However, the real-world setting, the strict protocol followed in the LCN group (constituting a pattern of global care rather than a mere therapeutic scheme) and the PS-adjusted analysis make the results more robust. In addition, the clustering analysis aids understanding of the effects of both protocols (LCN and SOC) in easily identifiable subgroups of patients. Although the group receiving the LCN protocol comprised a relatively low number of 47 patients, the magnitude of the differences resulted in highly significant comparisons between groups. As stated, the low representation of some subpopulations, such as non-White patients or those with pure class V LN, makes the conclusions in these subgroups less robust. Lastly, in-ward admission is needed is some centres for the administration of i.v. medication (CYC and MP) [ ], however the availability of day hospital settings simplifies the use of protocols like the LCN, while also assuring adherence. Indeed, frequent in-person visits with a combined team of internists/rheumatologists and nephrologists before each drug infusion, as marked by our clinical protocol, reinforces the doctor–patient relationship and allows a close monitoring of clinical and renal responses or possible complications of therapy, thus contributing to the achievement of CRR [ ]. In summary, this study supports the more extensive use of the LCN protocol and its possible inclusion in future guidelines for the management of class III, IV and V LN, including cases with severe proteinuria and impaired renal function. Future studies should eventually confirm the performance of this schedule in different settings and more diverse groups of patients. Supplementary Material keag214_Supplementary_Data

documents.title: 2021 ACR VF guideline for the management of ANCA-associated vasculitis

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION The anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitides (AAV) are comprised of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss). These diseases affect small- and medium-sized vessels and are characterized by multisystem organ involvement. GPA is characterized histologically by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in addition to vasculitis. Common clinical manifestations include destructive sino-nasal lesions, pulmonary nodules, and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. GPA is most commonly associated with cytoplasmic-staining ANCA and antibodies to proteinase 3. Among European populations, the prevalence ranges from 24 to 157 per million, with the highest prevalence reported in Sweden and the UK.[ ] MPA is characterized histologically by vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation. Common clinical manifestations include rapidly progressive pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and alveolar hemorrhage. MPA is most commonly associated with perinuclear staining ANCA and antibodies to myeloperoxidase. The prevalence of MPA ranges from 0 to 66 cases per million among European countries and 86 cases per million in Japan.[ , ] EGPA is characterized histologically by eosinophilic tissue infiltration in addition to vasculitis. Common clinical manifestations include asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, and peripheral neuropathy. Only 40% of patients produce detectable ANCA. The overall prevalence of EGPA in European populations has been estimated to range from 2 to 38 cases per million.[ , ] Prior to the use of alkylating agents, survival with these diseases was quite poor (e.g., median survival of patients with GPA at ~5 months).[ ] Current treatment regimens have reversed this poor prognosis, but treatments are still associated with toxicity. Recent clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and toxicity of both biologic and non-biologic immunosuppressive agents for the treatment of AAV. Observational studies have provided additional insight regarding management strategies for these diseases. Therefore, this guideline was developed to provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment and management of adults and children with GPA, MPA, and EGPA. Although this guideline may inform an international audience, these recommendations are developed for health care providers within the United States. METHODS This guideline follows the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guideline development process ( https://www.rheumatology.org/Practice-Quality/Clinical-Support/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines ) using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology to rate the quality of evidence and develop recommendations[ , ]. ACR policy guided the management of conflicts of interest and disclosures ( https://www.rheumatology.org/Practice-Quality/Clinical-Support/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/Vasculitis ). presents a detailed description of the methods. Briefly, the Literature Review team undertook systematic literature reviews for pre-specified questions addressing specific clinical populations, interventions, comparators, and outcomes (PICO). An in-person Patient Panel of 11 individuals with different types of vasculitis, moderated by a member of the Literature Review team, reviewed the evidence report (along with a summary and interpretation by the moderator) and provided patient perspectives and preferences. The patient panel included 4 patients with GPA, 1 patient with MPA, and 2 patients with EGPA. The Voting Panel, comprised of 14 physicians and 2 patients, reviewed the Literature Review team’s evidence summaries and, bearing in mind the Patient Panel’s deliberations, formulated and voted on recommendations. The voting panel was assembled for the ACR and Vasculitis Foundation’s broad effort to develop recommendations for 7 forms of systemic vasculitis: giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, and the 3 AAV presented in this manuscript. The physicians on this panel included rheumatologists who could provide insight for all of these diseases, and did not to include other subspecialists who would not have experience with many of the other vasculitides addressed in this effort (e.g., pulmonologists who would not have experience with large- or medium-vessel vasculitis). The literature review team chair was a nephrologist. The patients on the voting panel presented the views of the patient panel, which consisted of patients with different types of vasculitis. Each recommendation required consensus from at least 70% of the voting panel. How to interpret the recommendations: A strong recommendation is usually supported by moderate or high-quality evidence (e.g., multiple randomized controlled trials). For a strong recommendation, the recommended course of action would apply to all or almost all patients. Only a small proportion of clinicians/patients would not want to follow the recommendation. In rare instances, a strong recommendation may be based on low or very low certainty evidence. For example, an intervention may be strongly recommended if it is considered benign, low-cost, without harms, and the consequence of not performing the intervention may be catastrophic. An intervention may be strongly recommended against if there is high certainty that the intervention leads to more harm than the comparison with low or very low certainty about its benefit [ ]. A conditional recommendation is usually supported by lower quality evidence or a close balance between desirable and undesirable outcomes. For a conditional recommendation, the recommended course of action would apply to the majority of the patients, but the alternative is a reasonable consideration. Conditional recommendations always warrant a shared decision-making approach. We

benign, low-cost, without harms, and the consequence of not performing the intervention may be catastrophic. An intervention may be strongly recommended against if there is high certainty that the intervention leads to more harm than the comparison with low or very low certainty about its benefit [ ]. A conditional recommendation is usually supported by lower quality evidence or a close balance between desirable and undesirable outcomes. For a conditional recommendation, the recommended course of action would apply to the majority of the patients, but the alternative is a reasonable consideration. Conditional recommendations always warrant a shared decision-making approach. We specify some conditions under which the alternative may be considered. In some instances, the committee found that the evidence for a particular PICO question did not support a graded recommendation or did not favor one intervention over the other. However, the voting panel believed the PICO question addressed a commonly encountered clinical question and thus felt that providing guidance for this question was warranted. For these situations, we present ‘ungraded position statements’ which reflects general views of the voting panel. In this evidence-based guideline, we explicitly use the best evidence available and present it for the clinician and reader[ ]. In some instances, this includes randomized trials directly comparing the interventions under consideration. The GRADE system rates evidence that comes exclusively from the collective experience of the Voting Panel and patient panel members as “very-low-quality” evidence. For each recommendation, provides details regarding the PICO questions and GRADE evidence tables. RESULTS For the evidence report for GPA and MPA, 729 articles were reviewed to address 47 PICO questions. For the evidence report for EGPA, 190 articles were reviewed to address 34 PICO questions. Recommendations and Ungraded Position Statements for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis and Microscopic Polyangiitis GPA and MPA are recognized as different diseases for which disease-specific management approaches exist. However, many recommendations and ungraded position statements consider GPA and MPA together because pivotal trials have enrolled both groups and presented results for these diseases together. Thus, we present recommendations and ungraded position statements applicable to both GPA and MPA as well as recommendations and ungraded position statements only applicable to GPA. All recommendations for GPA/MPA are conditional, due in part to a lack of multiple randomized control trials supporting the recommendations. The complete list of studies reviewed to form the recommendations is provided in the evidence report ( ). Given that these diseases affect multiple organ systems, collaboration between rheumatologists, nephrologists, pulmonologists, and otolaryngologists can enhance the care of patients with GPA and MPA. presents the definitions for disease states described in the Recommendations and Ungraded Position Statements, including definitions of severe and non-severe disease, and the dosing regimens of medications used for remission induction and maintenance. presents the PICO questions contributing to each Recommendation and Ungraded Position Statement and subsequent discussion, along with level of evidence. represents a flowchart of key recommendations for the treatment of GPA and MPA. Remission induction for active, severe disease Recommendation 1: In patients with active severe GPA OR MPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with rituximab over cyclophosphamide for remission induction. Both rituximab and cyclophosphamide, in combination with glucocorticoids, have been used for remission induction for GPA and MPA. Rituximab (RTX) has been shown to provide similar benefits to cyclophosphamide (CYC) for remission induction in a randomized controlled trial [ ]. Although the current cumulative doses of CYC used are less than previous regimens, resulting in less toxicity per treatment course, RTX is still preferred. since RTX is considered less toxic than CYC..A single course of CYC can carry substantial risks such as neutropenia, bladder injury, and the small but present potential for infertility which can be devastating to a young patient. Risks of malignancy and infertility increase when repeated courses of CYC are used. RTX was also preferred by the patient panel. Retrospective studies suggest that the two remission induction regimens for rituximab used in adults, 375 mg/m 2 every week for 4 weeks (FDA-approved dosing schedule) and 1000 mg on days 1 and 15, are equally efficacious. The choice between these two regimens should be guided by patient preferences and values. CYC (dosing provided in ) may be used when RTX needs to be avoided or when patients have active disease despite use of RTX. It remains controversial whether CYC should be preferred for certain types of severe disease, such as acute renal failure (e.g., serum creatinine > 4.0 mg/dL). Clinicians can use either intravenous pulse or daily oral CYC [ , ]. For adults, the decision between these two options should be based on patient and physician preferences. In children, intravenous CYC may be preferred to facilitate compliance and limit toxicity. Data regarding the efficacy of combined CYC and RTX therapy for remission induction remains limited [ ], and potential toxicity of

be avoided or when patients have active disease despite use of RTX. It remains controversial whether CYC should be preferred for certain types of severe disease, such as acute renal failure (e.g., serum creatinine > 4.0 mg/dL). Clinicians can use either intravenous pulse or daily oral CYC [ , ]. For adults, the decision between these two options should be based on patient and physician preferences. In children, intravenous CYC may be preferred to facilitate compliance and limit toxicity. Data regarding the efficacy of combined CYC and RTX therapy for remission induction remains limited [ ], and potential toxicity of this combination remains a concern. The combination of RTX with CYC is not widely used in the US, and its efficacy compared to RTX or CYC alone is not established. This combination remains under study ( Clinicaltrials.gov NCT03942887 ) at this time. Recommendation 2: In patients with active glomerulonephritis, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend <italic toggle="yes">against</italic> the routine addition of plasma exchange to remission induction therapy. Plasma exchange should not be initiated for all patients with active glomerulonephritis but can be considered for patients at higher risk of progressing to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and accept a potential increased risk of infection. The recommendation is supported from data from the two largest trials of plasma exchange for the treatment of glomerulonephritis in AAV. The first trial, which required a serum creatinine ≥ 5.8 mg/dL for entry, showed that plasma exchange decreased the risk of ESKD but did not decrease mortality[ , ]. In a more recent randomized trial of plasma exchange in AAV [ ], the addition of plasma exchange to conventional remission induction therapy did not improve the composite outcome of ESKD or death; a decrease in ESKD was observed but the result was not statistically significant (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.57–1.13). However, combined data from these two trials (see ) show that there is probably decreased ESKD in patients with glomerulonephritis who received PLEX compared to those who did not (HR 0.72 [95% CI 0.53–0.98], moderate certainty). The benefit was most pronounced in patients at the highest risk of ESKD (118 fewer cases of ESKD per 1,000 cases of active glomerulonephritis [95% CI 217 fewer to 7 fewer]), although no difference in mortality was demonstrated (RR 1.15 [95% CI 0.78, 1.70], moderate certainty). Among four trials of plasma exchange in AAV, a higher risk of severe infection was observed with plasma exchange (RR 1.19 [95% CI 0.99, 1.42], moderate certainty). These findings suggest that for patients with a low risk of progressing to ESKD, the risk of plasma exchange may outweigh the benefit while in patients at higher risk of progression to ESKD, the decrease in risk of progressing to ESKD could outweigh the increased risk of serious infection with plasma exchange. Thus, the voting panel does not recommend plasma exchange for all patients with active glomerulonephritis but favors consideration of plasma exchange for patients at higher risk of progression to ESKD. Factors that could influence whether plasma exchange is initiated include the patient’s kidney function upon presentation, rate of loss of kidney function, response to remission induction therapies, and the patient’s ability to tolerate serious infections. Plasma exchange remains advisable in patients with GPA or MPA who also have anti-GBM disease. Recommendation 3: In patients with active severe GPA or MPA with alveolar hemorrhage, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend <italic toggle="yes">against</italic> adding plasma exchange to remission induction therapies. Two trials evaluated the use of plasma exchange in patients presenting with alveolar hemorrhage, and no differences in mortality or remission rates were observed. Thus, plasma exchange does not have an established benefit for patients with alveolar hemorrhage, and is associated with an increased risk of serious infection (Recommendation 2). Plasma exchange may be considered for certain patients with active glomerulonephritis (Recommendation 2), or patients who are critically ill and whose disease is not responding to recommended remission induction therapies (i.e., plasma exchange as “salvage” or “rescue” therapy). Plasma exchange remains advisable in patients with GPA or MPA who also have anti-GBM disease. Ungraded Position Statement A: In patients with active, severe GPA or MPA, either pulse intravenous or high-dose oral glucocorticoids may be prescribed as part of initial therapy. There are no trials comparing the efficacy of pulse intravenous to high dose oral glucocorticoids. Higher doses of glucocorticoids (such as pulse glucocorticoids) are generally used for patients with organ- or life-threatening disease manifestations but may be associated with an increased risk of infection[ ]. Recommendation 4: In patients with active severe GPA/MPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend a reduced-dose over a standard-dose glucocorticoid regimen for remission induction. A recent study[ ] reported a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen provided similar benefit to a standard-dose regimen for the composite outcome of end-stage renal disease or death and was associated with a decreased risk of infection. Given the

trials comparing the efficacy of pulse intravenous to high dose oral glucocorticoids. Higher doses of glucocorticoids (such as pulse glucocorticoids) are generally used for patients with organ- or life-threatening disease manifestations but may be associated with an increased risk of infection[ ]. Recommendation 4: In patients with active severe GPA/MPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend a reduced-dose over a standard-dose glucocorticoid regimen for remission induction. A recent study[ ] reported a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen provided similar benefit to a standard-dose regimen for the composite outcome of end-stage renal disease or death and was associated with a decreased risk of infection. Given the known toxicities associated with long-term glucocorticoid use, minimizing glucocorticoid exposure is critical to improving outcomes. Glucocorticoid dosing may be individualized for each patient. Of note, the reduced-dose regimen started with pulse methylprednisolone (3 daily pulses for maximum total dose of 3 g) and one week of high-dose oral glucocorticoids. The standard and reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen used in this study is provided in . Remission induction for active non-severe disease Recommendation 5: In patients with active non-severe GPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with methotrexate over cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Non-severe GPA is defined as GPA without life- or organ-threatening manifestations ( ). Methotrexate (MTX[ ]), RTX and CYC are effective at inducing remission in this patient group. However, like severe GPA, non-severe GPA can be a chronic disease that requires multiple courses of therapy. Thus, the voting panel favored using therapies with potentially less toxicity before utilizing therapies with potentially more toxicity. Therefore, MTX is preferred due to the greater toxicity of CYC. MTX is currently recommended over RTX because of the larger body of evidence and clinical experience with MTX use for this group of patients; a clinical trial is needed to compare their efficacy. RTX may be preferred in specific clinical situations, including patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction, recurrent relapses on MTX, or concerns regarding compliance. Recommendation 6: In patients with active non-severe GPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with methotrexate and glucocorticoids over glucocorticoids alone. MTX with glucocorticoids is recommended to minimize glucocorticoid exposure and toxicity. Overall, there are few clinical situations where treatment with glucocorticoids alone may be considered (e.g., arthralgias, or inability to tolerate other remission maintenance therapies), and close monitoring is needed should this treatment strategy be employed. Recommendation 7: For patients with active non-severe GPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with methotrexate + glucocorticoids over azathioprine + glucocorticoids or mycophenolate mofetil + glucocorticoids. Use of MTX for remission induction in this patient group is supported by more data[ ], but azathioprine (AZA) and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) can be considered. Comparative effectiveness trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy of MTX, AZA, and MMF for remission induction in active non-severe GPA. Clinical factors may influence the medication selected. For example, MTX should be used with caution or avoided in patients with moderate to severe renal insufficiency. AZA is the preferred agent in pregnant patients or in patients who cannot tolerate MTX or MMF. MTX or MMF is indicated in patients with total thiopurine-S-methyltransferase deficiency or high risk TPMT and/or NUDT15 genotypes. Recommendation 8: In patients with active non-severe GPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with methotrexate with glucocorticoids over sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim with glucocorticoids. MTX is considered more effective than sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (SMX/TMP) for remission induction given previous experience suggesting MTX is more effective than SMX/TMP for remission maintenance[ ]. Low-dose SMX/TMP may be given concurrently with immunosuppressive agents to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (see GPA/MPA Recommendation 24). Remission maintenance Recommendation 9: In patients with severe GPA or MPA who have entered remission after treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with rituximab over methotrexate or azathioprine for remission maintenance. RTX is associated with a lower relapse rate than AZA when used for remission maintenance after remission induction with CYC[ ] MTX and AZA have comparable efficacy for remission maintenance.[ ] Thus, RTX is favored over MTX or AZA. However, more long-term safety data is available for MTX and AZA, and cost and other factors may limit RTX use. Different doses of RTX have been used for remission maintenance, including 500 mg IV every 6 months[ ] (FDA-approved), 1000 mg IV every 4 months [ ], and 1000 mg IV every 6 months [ ]. No comparative trials have been conducted. Thus, the optimal dose of RTX for remission maintenance remains uncertain. If MTX or AZA is being considered for remission maintenance, the patient’s clinical situation, preferences, and values should guide selection between them, given their comparable efficacy. Recommendation 10: In patients with GPA/MPA using rituximab for remission maintenance, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend scheduled re-dosing over using ANCA titers or CD19 B cell counts to guide re-dosing. In one randomized trial, patients who received RTX for remission maintenance based on changes in CD19 B cell counts and/or ANCA titers had similar rate of relapse as those receiving RTX on a scheduled dose. However, this study was limited by the small sample size and there were wide confidence intervals for the effect size[ ]. This recommendation is based on part on the experience and expertise of the voting panel, which recognizes that flares can occur when patients are CD19 B-cell depleted and/or tests for ANCA are negative. Thus, CD19 B cell counts or ANCA titers may not accurately indicate the potential for a patient’s disease to flare. Recommendation 11: In patients with severe GPA or MPA who achieved remission after treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with methotrexate or azathioprine over mycophenolate mofetil for remission maintenance. MTX and AZA are equally efficacious for remission maintenance [ ]. AZA is favored over MMF because the relapse rate for MMF was higher than AZA when studied for remission maintenance[ ]. MMF may still be considered in those unable to tolerate or with contraindications to MTX, AZA, or rituximab (GPA/MPA Recommendation 9). Recommendation 12: In patients with severe GPA or MPA who entered remission after treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with methotrexate or azathioprine over leflunomide for remission maintenance. MTX or AZA is recommended over leflunomide due to the data supporting and clinical experience using MTX and AZA for remission maintenance. The data and clinical experience with leflunomide are more limited. In the one clinical trial comparing leflunomide to MTX[ ], leflunomide use had a decreased rate of relapse but a higher rate of drug withdrawal. The trial used a leflunomide dose of 30 mg/day, which may have contributed to toxicity. Recommendation 13: In patients with GPA who have entered remission, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with methotrexate or azathioprine over sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for remission maintenance. The voting panel strongly favored the use of MTX or AZA over SMX/TMP but this recommendation is conditional due to the lack of sufficient high-quality evidence comparing the two treatments. Recommendation 14: In patients with GPA who have entered remission, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend against adding sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim to other therapies (e.g., rituximab, azathioprine, methotrexate, etc.) for the purpose of remission maintenance. SMX/TMP may have benefit for patients with sino-nasal involvement[ ] but its use potentially increases toxicity (e.g., severe hypersensitivity reactions) and medication burden. SMX/TMP may still be indicated for prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (see GPA/MPA Recommendation 24). There is a potential drug interaction between MTX and SMX/TMP when SMX/TMP is dosed at 800 mg/160 mg twice a day. The SMX/TMP dose used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis is generally tolerated, but its use should be monitored when used in conjunction with methotrexate. Recommendation 15: In patients with GPA/MPA on remission maintenance therapy with rituximab who have hypogammaglobulinemia (e.g., IgG< 3 g/L) and recurrent severe infections, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend immunoglobulin supplementation. Immunoglobulin supplementation at replacement doses (e.g., 400–800 mg/kg/month) should be considered if patient has hypogammaglobulinemia and is experiencing recurrent infections. Immunoglobulin supplementation can also be considered for patients with hypogammaglobulinemia without recurrent infections but with impaired vaccine responses.[ ] These considerations should be made in collaboration with an allergist/immunologist. Treatment of relapse Recommendation 16: In patients with GPA/MPA who have relapsed with severe disease manifestations and are not on rituximab for remission maintenance, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with rituximab over cyclophosphamide for remission induction. RTX is more effective than oral CYC for re-induction of remission among patients who previously received CYC and then relapsed, based on subgroup analysis of a randomized controlled trial[ ]. In addition, the cumulative toxicity of CYC raises concerns for repeated use of this agent. Recommendation 17: In patients with GPA/MPA who have relapsed with severe disease manifestations while on rituximab for remission maintenance, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend switching rituximab to cyclophosphamide over receiving additional rituximab for remission induction. Multiple factors can influence whether RTX or CYC (IV or oral) is used, such as time since last RTX infusion and cumulative CYC dose. CYC is recommended if the patient recently received RTX, while a remission induction dose of RTX may be effective if an extended period has passed since the last RTX infusion. As standard for remission induction, these agents should be used in conjunction with glucocorticoids. Treatment of refractory disease Recommendation 18: In patients with refractory severe GPA/MPA after treatment with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for remission induction, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend switching treatment to the other therapy over combining the two therapies. Disease refractory to remission induction therapy is rare, and there is little data to guide treatment recommendations. Practitioners should evaluate whether other conditions such as infection could be mimicking vasculitis. However, if a patient’s disease is refractory to one remission induction therapy, it is important to change the remission induction strategy. We recommend changing to the other remission induction agent prior to using combination therapy. Recommendation 19: In patients with GPA/MPA refractory to remission induction therapy, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend adding intravenous immunoglobulin to current therapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) should not be used routinely to treat GPA/MPA but can be considered at treatment doses (e.g., 2 g/kg) as adjunctive therapy for short term control while waiting for remission induction therapy (i.e., rituximab or cyclophosphamide) to become effective (per Recommendation 17)[ ]. Other considerations Recommendation 23: In patients with GPA or MPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend against dosing immunosuppression based on ANCA titers alone. Increases in ANCA titers/levels are only modestly informative as an indicator of disease activity[ ] and are not reliable predictors of disease flares for individual patients. Increasing immunosuppression based on changes in ANCA titers/levels alone can result in unnecessary immunosuppression resulting in adverse events. Persistence of ANCA positivity does not necessarily indicate that continued immunosuppression is required. Instead, treatment decisions should be based on a patient’s clinical symptoms in conjunction with diagnostic studies (e.g., laboratory, imaging, biopsy findings). Recommendation 24: In patients with GPA or MPA receiving cyclophosphamide or rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend prophylaxis to prevent <italic toggle="yes">Pneumocystis jirovecii</italic> pneumonia. Prophylaxis to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is routinely used with CYC treatment. [ ] The prescribing information for RTX recommends prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia for at least 6 months after the last RTX dose for patients with GPA or MPA. While many on the voting panel felt strongly that patients with GPA or MPA on CYC or RTX should receive prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, this recommendation is conditional given the lack of moderate or high-quality evidence directly addressing this question and the potential toxicity of the medications used for prophylaxis. Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia should also be considered for patients taking moderate-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., > 20 mg/day) or higher in combination with MTX, AZA, or MMF[ ]. Prophylaxis is less commonly used in younger children receiving RTX but should be considered. Recommendation 25: In patients with GPA/MPA in remission and chronic kidney disease stage V, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend evaluation for renal transplantation. Outcomes of kidney transplantation in patients with ANCA associated vasculitis are similar to patients receiving transplants for other reasons, with relapses in the transplanted kidney being rare[ , ].GPA and MPA in remission should not be considered a contraindication to kidney transplantation, but these patients should be monitored for relapse after transplantation. IVIg should not be used routinely to treat GPA/MPA (GPA/MPA Recommendation 19). However, in the rare instances where patients with active disease may not be able to receive conventional immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., sepsis or pregnancy), IVIg can be used as a short-term intervention until conventional remission induction therapies can be used.[ ] Ungraded Position Statement E: The optimal duration of anticoagulation is unknown for patients with GPA/MPA who develop venous thrombotic events. AAV is associated with an increased risk of venous thrombotic events, including both deep vein thromboses and pulmonary emboli.[ , ] Venous thromboembolic events that occur in a patient with active disease and no other risk factors can be considered a provoked event with a transient risk factor (assuming subsequent disease control). Thus, short-term instead of life-long anticoagulation may be considered. Recommendations and Ungraded Position Statements for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): EGPA is characterized by diverse features, including asthma/allergic rhinitis, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, and vasculitis. As these clinical features can potentially have differing responses to treatment, the management approach is typically based on a patient’s disease features and their severity. The recommendations presented here focus primarily on the use of immunosuppressive medications to treat the vasculitic manifestations of EGPA. However, asthma and allergic manifestations are a significant component of EGPA, and measures directed towards these, including inhaled therapies and allergen avoidance, play an important role in management. Collaboration between rheumatologists, asthma/allergy specialists, and other medical disciplines can enhance the care of patients with EGPA. In contrast to GPA/MPA, there have been very few randomized controlled trials conducted to date in EGPA. Remission induction for active, severe EGPA Ungraded Position Statement A: In patients with active, severe EGPA, either pulse intravenous or high-dose oral glucocorticoids may be prescribed as initial therapy. There are no data to support favoring either pulse intravenous or high-dose oral glucocorticoids over the other option in active, severe EGPA. Which approach to use should be influenced by individual patient factors. In either instance, glucocorticoids should be combined with a non-glucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab (Ungraded Position Statement B). Ungraded Position Statement B: In patients with active, severe EGPA, either cyclophosphamide or rituximab may be prescribed for remission induction. CYC has been more commonly used for remission induction for patient with active severe EGPA given the experience with CYC with other forms of vasculitis.[ ]. Increasing experience with RTX in GPA/MPA has also led more patients with EGPA to be treated with RTX, and case-series suggest that RTX may also have efficacy for active, severe disease.[ ] Given the comparative effectiveness of CYC and RTX for EGPA is unknown, the voting panel felt both CYC and RTX could be considered for remission induction with active, severe EGPA. CYC would be preferred for patient with active cardiac involvement given the increased experience with CYC as cardiomyopathy has been found to be the main independent predictor of death in EGPA (25, 26). CYCcan also be considered for patients who are ANCA negative and have severe neurologic or gastrointestinal manifestations. RTX may be considered in patients with a positive ANCA, active glomerulonephritis, prior CYC treatment, or at risk of gonadal toxicity from CYC. Recommendation 1: In patients with active, severe EGPA we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with cyclophosphamide or rituximab over mepolizumab for remission induction. The efficacy of mepolizumab in severe EGPA has not been established, as patients with active severe disease were excluded from the randomized trial[ ]. CYC or RTX would be recommended over mepolizumab in this setting. Remission induction for active, non-severe EGPA Recommendation 2: In patients with active, non-severe EGPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with mepolizumab with glucocorticoids over methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil with glucocorticoids. A range of immunosuppressive agents may be considered in the treatment of active, non-severe EGPA, all of which are used with glucocorticoids. The clinical profile of these non-severe EGPA patients includes predominantly asthma, sinus disease, and non-severe vasculitis. While there is significant clinical experience with MTX, AZA, and MMF, there is limited data regarding their efficacy and these treatments have not been assessed in randomized clinical trials. The GRADE methodology used in the guideline development process weighs clinical trials more heavily than observational studies. Thus, mepolizumab is recommended as the first choice because it has been found to be efficacious for non-severe EGPA in a randomized trial[ ]. All patients in this trial had relapsing or refractory disease with 55% receiving an additional non-glucocorticoid immunosuppressive agent at the time of enrollment. A large proportion of patients in this trial had asthmatic and eosinophilic features, for which mepolizumab has also been found to be effective in non-EGPA disease settings. Although patients with non-severe vasculitic manifestations were represented in this trial, questions remain about the effectiveness of mepolizumab for all aspects of non-severe vasculitis. Individual factors, including disease manifestations, may impact the decision to use mepolizumab, in which case MTX, AZA, or MMF may be used instead. There are insufficient data to favor one of these medications (MTX, AZA, MMF) over the others; therefore, the choice should be influenced by individual patient factors. Recommendation 3: In patients with active, non-severe EGPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend initiating treatment with methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil with glucocorticoids over glucocorticoids alone. Patients should be treated with adjunctive MTX, AZA, or MMF rather than glucocorticoids alone to minimize glucocorticoid toxicity. One randomized trial that combined patients with EGPA, MPA, and polyarteritis nodosa without poor prognosis factors found the addition of AZA did not provide benefit beyond glucocorticoids alone.[ ] Particularly in patients with asthma, this may impact the decision to use MTX, AZA, or MMF concurrently with glucocorticoids and could lead to consideration of mepolizumab. Glucocorticoid monotherapy may be appropriate for mild asthma, allergic symptoms, during pregnancy, or other individual patient situations. While the comparative efficacy of MTX, AZA, MMF, and RTX is not well established, MTX, AZA, or MMF is favored given the longer experience with these agents in EGPA compared to RTX. However, RTX may be considered if other agents are not effective in controlling active non-severe disease, or the patient has non-severe vasculitis (which in some series included mononeuritis multiplex) and is positive for ANCA. CYC should be avoided in treating active non-severe disease due to its toxicity and is the least preferred option in this setting. Remission maintenance in EGPA Recommendation 5: In patients with severe EGPA who have entered remission with cyclophosphamide therapy, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil over rituximab for remission maintenance. Typically, a maintenance agent would be used after remission induction of severe EGPA to reduce toxicity and the risk of relapse[ ], although monophasic disease can occur[ ]. AZA has been commonly used in published series of EGPA[ ], but the lack of comparative evidence between AZA, MTX, or MMF in EGPA precludes recommending one agent over another. Use of MTX, AZA, or MMF is recommended over RTX because there has been less experience with the use of RTX for remission maintenance in EGPA. RTX could be considered if remission was induced with rituximab, or if there are contraindications to other choices. Recommendation 6: In patients with severe EGPA who have entered remission, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil over mepolizumab for remission maintenance. While there is limited data informing the use of remission maintenance therapy in EGPA, patients should be not continued on remission induction therapies (e.g., cyclophosphamide) indefinitely given the potential toxicity. Thus, MTX, AZA, or MMF can be considered for remission maintenance based on experience in GPA/MPA, expert opinion, and results from small studies [ ]. The primary experience with mepolizumab is in refractory non-severe disease, and thus it is difficult to extrapolate its efficacy as a remission maintenance agent for severe disease. Ungraded Position Statement C: The duration of glucocorticoid therapy in EGPA should be guided by the patient’s clinical condition, values, and preferences. There is insufficient published evidence to support a specific duration of glucocorticoid treatment and thus, the length of glucocorticoid therapy should be determined based on each patient’s clinical circumstances. Many patients with EGPA require some amount of glucocorticoid, generally at a low-dose, to maintain control of asthma and allergic symptoms. The minimum effective dose should be prescribed to minimize glucocorticoid toxicity. Treatment of Relapse: Recommendation 7: In patients with EGPA who have relapsed with severe disease manifestations after prior successful remission induction with cyclophosphamide, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with rituximab over cyclophosphamide for remission re-induction. RTX is favored based on the general desire to avoid retreatment with CYC if possible, as well as an observational study of RTX in relapsing or refractory EGPA[ ]. Recommendation 8: In patients with EGPA who have relapsed with severe disease manifestations after prior successful remission induction with rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend treatment with rituximab over switching to cyclophosphamide for remission re-induction. Re-induction with RTX is favored over CYC to minimize toxicity. However, the duration of remission prior to the onset of relapse should be examined. CYC should be considered if a severe relapse occurred quickly after use of RTX, or if cardiac involvement is present (see Ungraded Position Statement B and Recommendation 7). Recommendation 13: In patients with EGPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend obtaining an echocardiogram at the time of diagnosis. Cardiac involvement is the major cause of disease-related mortality in EGPA. [ ] Echocardiography has minimal risk and can identify cardiac involvement, which if present, would impact treatment decisions. Not identifying cardiac involvement could negatively impact patient outcomes. Thus, we recommend obtaining an echocardiogram in all newly diagnosed patients with EGPA, even in the absence of cardiac symptoms. Recommendation 14: In patients with EGPA, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend using the Five Factor Score to guide therapy. The Five Factor Score (FFS) first published in 1996[ ] was based on 342 patients with either polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), as it was then defined, or EGPA. These five factors include proteinuria greater than > 1 gram/day, renal insufficiency with serum creatinine above 1.58 mg/dL, GI tract involvement, cardiomyopathy, and central nervous system involvement. The FFS is primarily a prognostic tool in which higher scores have been associated with a worse outcome.[ ] It has been used to guide treatment[ ] but its applicability to newer therapies is unknown. The FFS was revisited in 2011 in a population of 1108 patients with GPA, MPA, EGPA, or PAN.[ ] The 2011 derivation included ENT parameters and age above 65. The 1996 FFS remains more commonly used and may be helpful in identifying organ-specific parameters associated with severe disease and guiding treatment. Although the definitions of severe and non-severe EGPA used in this guideline were not based on FFS, the FFS was felt to be useful to clinicians in making treatment decisions. and guiding treatment. Although the definitions of severe and non-severe EGPA used in this guideline were not based on FFS, the FFS was felt to be useful to clinicians in making treatment decisions. The components of the FFS can serve as markers of severe disease that warrant more aggressive treatment. Ungraded Position Statement E: In patients with sino-nasal involvement in EGPA, treatment with nasal rinses and topical therapies (e.g., antibiotics, lubricants, and glucocorticoids) may be considered. Allergic rhinitis and sino-nasal disease are frequent clinical features of EGPA. Although the efficacy of nasal rinses and topical therapies in EGPA is not well-established, select patients may benefit. Where possible, consultation with an otolaryngologist who has expertise in treating AAV should be obtained to guide the use and choice of these agents. These interventions can continue to be beneficial even when symptoms have improved or resolved. Recommendation 15: In patients with EGPA receiving cyclophosphamide or rituximab, we <underline>conditionally</underline> recommend prescribing medications for prophylaxis to prevent <italic toggle="yes">Pneumocystis jirovecii</italic> pneumonia. Prophylaxis to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is discussed in GPA/MPA Recommendation 24. The same considerations regarding prophylaxis to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii for patients with GPA/MPA also apply to patients with EGPA. Discussion In this guideline, we present the first ACR/Vasculitis Foundation recommendations for the management of GPA, MPA, and EGPA. Although these recommendations provide a general guide for disease management, patients’ clinical condition, preferences, and values should influence their treatment. Overall, these recommendations reflect the evolving management of these diseases, including the new roles for biologic therapies and aggressive strategies to minimize glucocorticoid toxicity. The recommendations for GPA/MPA are supported by a greater number of randomized trials than are currently available in EGPA. All of the recommendations made for these three diseases are conditional, reflecting that there are settings in which the evidence is not strong or an alternative is a reasonable consideration. These recommendations should not be used by any agency to restrict access to therapy or to require that certain therapies be utilized prior to other therapies. The physicians on the voting panel were primarily rheumatologists because the recommendations were being developed for rheumatologists in the US. Since the AAV are multi-system diseases, patients with AAV often receive care from other medical subspecialists (e.g., nephrologists, pulmonologists, and/or otolaryngologists). While the recommendations presented in this guideline are driven by the published data, other medical subspecialists may favor a different management strategy. We encourage rheumatologists to discuss treatment plans and coordinate care with other subspecialists as needed. Recently, a clinical trial of avacopan in patients with GPA and MPA was published.[ ] This guideline development effort did not include consideration of avacopan since the guidelines consider therapies that were approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use for any indication at the time of the last literature search. Therapies that are approved by the FDA after that date will be considered for inclusion in future updates to this guideline. This guideline highlights gaps in our knowledge for the treatment of AVV. Most glaring is the lack of biomarkers or other non-invasive diagnostic testing with minimal toxicity that can accurately assess disease activity and predict outcomes. In addition, while we have evidence from randomized clinical trials to support recommendations regarding initial remission induction and maintenance therapy, critical questions remain unanswered, such as the optimal duration of therapy. These gaps in knowledge reinforce the need for ongoing research in these diseases. Specific areas to investigate include: Biomarker studies to identify more specific, reliable indicators of disease activity that can guide treatment decisions Trials to clarify how best to use the medications currently available (e.g., dosing, duration, effective combinations, and in which population to use which drugs) Trials to identify novel, targeted, and/or glucocorticoid-sparing agents with minimal toxicity Long-term studies to understand the course of disease and safety of current therapies We hope significant progress will be made in these areas such that future recommendations provide a more tailored approach to disease management, minimize treatment toxicity, and prevent organ damage in these patients. documents.title: 2021 ACR VF guideline for the management of giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis

chunks.content: Introduction Giant cell arteritis (GCA) and Takayasu arteritis (TAK) are systemic vasculitides that primarily affect large and medium-sized vessels. GCA can present with both cranial and extracranial manifestations. Cranial manifestations include headaches, scalp tenderness, vision loss, and jaw claudication. Large vessel (“extracranial”) involvement results in arterial stenosis and aneurysms, causing absent pulses, and limb claudication. GCA is more common in individuals of Northern European descent who are older than 50 years of age. The diagnosis is based on the clinical presentation, pathological abnormalities on temporal artery biopsy, and/or evidence of large vessel involvement on vascular imaging. – Glucocorticoids are the mainstay treatment for GCA, but tocilizumab has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of GCA. , Takayasu arteritis (TAK) causes granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and its branches. It is more common in younger women. , Clinical manifestations include constitutional symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, and arterial stenosis and/or aneurysms resulting in limb claudication and absent pulses. Treatment options include glucocorticoids, non-glucocorticoid immunosuppressive agents, and surgical management of vascular abnormalities. As GCA and TAK share clinical manifestations, similar questions arise regarding their treatment and management. Recent studies have broadened treatment options for GCA, and vascular imaging is increasingly used for diagnosis and management. This guideline was developed to provide evidence-based recommendations for the evaluation and management of GCA and TAK. Methods This guideline follows the ACR guideline development process ( https://www.rheumatology.org/Practice-Quality/Clinical-Support/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines ) using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology to rate the quality of evidence and develop recommendations – . ACR policy guided management of conflicts of interest and disclosures ( https://www.rheumatology.org/Practice-Quality/Clinical-Support/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/Vasculitis ). presents a detailed description of the methods. Briefly, a Literature Review team undertook systematic literature reviews for pre-determined questions specifying the clinical population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes (PICO). An in-person Patient Panel of 11 individuals with different types of vasculitis, including 3 patients with GCA or TAK, moderated by a member of the Literature Review team, reviewed the evidence report (along with a summary and interpretation by the moderator) and provided patient perspectives and preferences about their personal experiences regarding clinical and treatment aspects of their disease. The Voting Panel comprised of nine adult rheumatologists, five pediatric rheumatologists, and 2 patients, reviewed the Literature Review team’s evidence summaries and, bearing in mind the Patient Panel’s deliberations, formulated and voted on recommendations. A recommendation required 70% consensus of the Voting Panel. How to interpret the recommendations: A strong recommendation is typically supported by moderate or high-quality evidence (e.g., multiple randomized controlled trials). For a strong recommendation, the recommended course of action would apply to all or almost all patients. Only a small proportion of clinicians/patients would not want to follow the recommendation. In rare instances, a strong recommendation may be based on low or very low certainty evidence. For example, an intervention may be strongly recommended if it is considered low-cost, without harms, and the consequence of not performing the intervention may be catastrophic. An intervention may be strongly recommended against if there is high certainty that the intervention leads to more harm than the comparison with low or very low certainty about its benefit . A conditional recommendation is generally supported by lower quality evidence or a close balance between desirable and undesirable outcomes. For a conditional recommendation, the recommended course of action would apply to the majority of the patients, but the alternative is a reasonable consideration. Conditional recommendations added always warrant a shared decision-making approach. We specify conditions under which the alternative may be considered. In some instances, the committee found that the evidence for a particular PICO question did not support a graded recommendation or did not favor one intervention over the other. However, the voting panel believed the PICO question addressed a commonly encountered clinical question which has not been fully clarified and requires further investigation and thus felt that providing guidance for this question was warranted. For these situations, we present “ungraded position statements” which reflects general views of the voting panel. In this evidence-based guideline, we explicitly use the best evidence available and present that in a transparent manner for the clinician reader/user . In some instances, this includes randomized trials directly comparing the interventions under consideration. The GRADE system rates evidence that comes exclusively from the collective experience of the Voting Panel and patient panel members as “very-low-quality” evidence . For each recommendation, provides details regarding the PICO questions and the GRADE evidence tables. Results For the GCA evidence report, 399 articles were reviewed to address 27 PICO questions. For the TAK evidence report, 347 articles were reviewed to address 27 PICO questions. For each recommendation, provides details regarding the PICO questions and the GRADE evidence tables. Results For the GCA evidence report, 399 articles were reviewed to address 27 PICO questions. For the TAK evidence report, 347 articles were reviewed to address 27 PICO questions.
