chunks.content: Introduction Epilepsy is a neurological disorder in which a person has a risk of recurrent seizures due to a chronic underlying process. Epilepsy is diagnosed after 2 recurrent unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart, after a single unprovoked or reflex seizure with a high risk of reoccurrence (at least 60% risk over the next 10 years), or diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome. , The incidence of epilepsy in the U.S. is 79 cases per 100,000 persons with a prevalence of 8 persons per 1000. Epilepsy exists in many forms with multiple causes encompassing structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune, and unknown etiologies. , An important aspect of diagnostic evaluation for epileptic seizure is classification based on seizure type: focal, generalized, or unknown. , Imaging is warranted in most adult patients presenting with a new-onset epileptic seizure, especially focal-onset seizure, or early epilepsy to identify underlying structural etiologies ( ). , , , In patients with a known seizure disorder, additional indications for imaging include refractory seizures, changes in seizure pattern, and surgical evaluation. In the pediatric population, imaging is recommended in children under age 3 presenting with a new-onset and afebrile seizure and in neonates presenting with a seizure. , Imaging is generally not required in most children with normal neurodevelopment presenting with generalized onset seizure and unambiguous history and examination suggesting a benign seizure disorder, such as simple febrile seizure or absence epilepsy. In the nonemergent setting, neuroimaging with MRI using specialized seizure or epilepsy protocols is performed for evaluation of structural brain lesions such as infarction, infection, trauma, tumors, vascular malformation, developmental abnormalities, and other seizure-associated brain pathologies. In the emergent setting, CT is the initial modality used to rapidly identify immediately treatable structural pathologies while retaining ready access to the patient. , , The presence of any of these entities must then be further evaluated with integration of clinical semiology and electroclinical studies by the epileptologist to establish a causal relationship between the structural lesion and the patient’s epilepsy. Identification of an epileptogenic lesion on MRI should prompt referral to a specialized epilepsy surgery center for surgical evaluation as the presence of a structural lesion is a strong indicator of anti-epileptic drug resistance. Furthermore, small lesions identified by MRI and electroclinical studies may be precisely targeted within highly eloquent regions using minimally invasive procedures such as stereotactic radiofrequency thermoablation and newer stereotactic laser ablation. , Imaging protocol/advanced techniques Specialized MRI epilepsy protocols are crucial for detection of various structural pathologies that may be missed by routine MRI. , The ILAE Neuroimaging Task Force identified a set of sequences known as HARNESS-MRI, consisting of high-resolution 3D T1-weighted gradient echo sequence (no interslice gap) with isotopic voxels of 1 mm or less for optimal evaluation of brain anatomy and morphology, high-resolution 3D fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) turbo spin echo sequence (no interslice gap) with isotropic millimetric voxel resolution for assessing signal anomalies, and high in-plane resolution 2D coronal T2WI turbo spin echo sequence with submillimetric voxel resolution (e.g., 0.4 × 0.4 × 2 mm 3 , no interslice gap) for assessing hippocampal internal structure, amygdala, and parahippocampal cortices. An important caveat for FLAIR is that it is not sensitive for epileptogenic lesions in children before 24 months due to incomplete myelination. Additional MRI sequences include T1WI with gadolinium for evaluation of suspected tumor, vascular malformation, or infectious process and susceptibility-weighted imaging for detection of venous blood, hemorrhage, iron deposits, and calcifications. Several of the entities discussed in this review, such as hippocampal sclerosis and cortical malformations, are better appreciated on scanners with magnetic fields of 3T or higher due to increased signal-to-noise ratio and resolution. Despite use of these specialized epilepsy protocols, patients with epileptogenic foci may still have visually normal MRI, which has prompted efforts to develop advanced neuroimaging sequences. Double inversion recovery (DIR) is a newer MRI structural protocol with high contrast between gray and white matter for better detection of epileptogenic lesions compared to FLAIR, T1WI, and T2W2 in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and extratemporal focal epilepsy. Fluid and white matter suppression (FLAWS) is a technique that suppresses white and cerebrospinal fluid signals to generate gray matter-specific images for better detection of focal cortical dysplasia. Edge-enhancing gradient echo (EDGE) is another technique for focal cortical dysplasia that directly visualizes the boundary between gray and white matter. Epileptogenic entities A wide spectrum of etiologies may produce seizures, only a subset of which can be detected via imaging. Non-structural factors contributing to seizures include metabolic derangements, channelopathies, and genetic syndromes. Structural abnormalities identifiable on neuroimaging include temporal lobe pathologies, developmental malformations, neoplastic lesions, vascular lesions, as well as infectious and inflammatory processes. Even when structural abnormalities are present, it is crucial to incorporate electrophysiological information and to pinpoint the abnormal structures that are truly epileptogenic foci. Temporal

Edge-enhancing gradient echo (EDGE) is another technique for focal cortical dysplasia that directly visualizes the boundary between gray and white matter. Epileptogenic entities A wide spectrum of etiologies may produce seizures, only a subset of which can be detected via imaging. Non-structural factors contributing to seizures include metabolic derangements, channelopathies, and genetic syndromes. Structural abnormalities identifiable on neuroimaging include temporal lobe pathologies, developmental malformations, neoplastic lesions, vascular lesions, as well as infectious and inflammatory processes. Even when structural abnormalities are present, it is crucial to incorporate electrophysiological information and to pinpoint the abnormal structures that are truly epileptogenic foci. Temporal lobe etiologies Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), also known as mesial temporal sclerosis, is the most common cause of medically refractory epilepsy. The underlying pathophysiology characterized by hippocampal neuronal loss and gliosis. In patients undergoing epilepsy surgery, HS was identified within specimens in 44% of adults and 15% of children. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy syndrome is associated with focal seizures with impaired consciousness, history of febrile seizures, family history of epilepsy, early onset, and intractable seizures not responsive to anti-epileptic medications. Findings on imaging may be bilateral but are usually unilateral or asymmetric. Characteristic features include hippocampal volume loss or atrophy, abnormal T2 hyperintensity, and obscuration of internal architecture ( ). Secondary signs include ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy, as well as enlarged temporal horn and choroidal fissure. Use of 3T, or higher, scanners enables quantitative assessment of hippocampal volume and visualization of hippocampal internal architecture. Furthermore, use of DIR has been reported to have superior detection of temporal white matter abnormalities compared to FLAIR. Abnormal findings should be integrated with clinical semiology and electrophysiological findings to identify the epileptogenic focus. Developmental etiologies Focal cortical dysplasia Malformations of cortical development (MCD) are a group of conditions, often with childhood onset, caused by abnormal cell proliferation or apoptosis, abnormal neuronal migration, or abnormal cortical organization. Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) is the most common MCD responsible for extratemporal epilepsy. Prevalence of FCD ranges from 5 to 25% depending on collection and imaging technique. FCD is present in 5–10% of epilepsy patients and has a prevalence of up to 50% in children with intractable focal epilepsy. Despite its prevalence in intractable epilepsy, it is potentially curable by surgery. FCD is classified into types and subtypes with varying degrees of abnormalites. FCD type I is characterized by mild cortical dyslamination without dysmorphic neurons and presents with absent or subtle MRI findings, such as mild focal cortical thickening, asymmetrical gyral pattern, and blurring of the gray–white matter junction. Type IIa is characterized by cortical lamination with dysmorphic neurons and is more reliably identified with MRI, presenting with cortical thickening, blurred gray–white matter junction, and hyperintense cortical and subcortical signals. Type IIb presents with even more pronounced imaging findings such as cortical thickening, marked blurring of the white–gray matter junction, and a highly specific but not always present transmantle sign or radial band that appears as T2 hyperintense wedge-shaped signal in the subcortical white matter ( ). , FCD type III is characterized by features of FCD type I or type II in association with other lesions, such as HS (type IIIa), tumors (type IIIb), vascular malformations (type IIIc), or acquired lesions (IIId). Due to subtle or absent signs, FCD type I is much less commonly detected compared to type II. Compared to isolated FCD type I and type II, FCD type III generally presents with more subtle or absent dysplastic changes in the cortex adjacent to the principal lesion and lacks the transmantle sign seen in type IIb. Diagnosis and identification of epileptogenic foci is improved with careful review of seizure semiology, EEG, and nuclear medicine studies if available. FDG PET is helpful if lesions are not visible or very subtle on MRI and can assist with identification of epileptogenic foci ( ). Furthermore, assessment of the gray–white matter junction may be enhanced by use of FLAWS, which enhances contrast between the gray and white matter, and EDGE, which improves direct visualization of the gray–white matter boundary. In FCD type III, accurate mapping of the entire epileptogenic zone, typically involving the principal lesion and adjacent FCD lesion, with multimodal evaluation is essential to achieving optimal post-surgical seizure control. Invasive EEG may be used in cases with no identifiable epileptogenic foci on imaging. Important alternative diagnoses to consider during evaluation of FCD include tuberous sclerosis, cortical neoplasm (DNET, ganglioglioma, low-grade glioma), incomplete myelination, and gliosis. FCD is distinguished from these other diagnoses by its characteristic focal cortical findings on imaging and lack of systemic clinical features. Polymicrogyria Polymicrogyria is a common MCD characterized by small and disorganized gyral convolutions with shallow sulci (“nodular cortex”) resulting from abnormal distribution of cortical neurons. The bilateral perisylvian region is the most commonly affected, but findings may also be unilateral. It

seizure control. Invasive EEG may be used in cases with no identifiable epileptogenic foci on imaging. Important alternative diagnoses to consider during evaluation of FCD include tuberous sclerosis, cortical neoplasm (DNET, ganglioglioma, low-grade glioma), incomplete myelination, and gliosis. FCD is distinguished from these other diagnoses by its characteristic focal cortical findings on imaging and lack of systemic clinical features. Polymicrogyria Polymicrogyria is a common MCD characterized by small and disorganized gyral convolutions with shallow sulci (“nodular cortex”) resulting from abnormal distribution of cortical neurons. The bilateral perisylvian region is the most commonly affected, but findings may also be unilateral. It is also often associated with other malformative lesions such as cerebellar hypoplasia, callosum agenesis, periventricular nodular heterotopia, and schizencephaly. On MRI of patients with complete myelination (greater than 2 years old), findings include an abnormally thickened and irregular cortex instead of small gyri ( ). In patients 1–2 years old, polymicrogyria presents with an abnormal sulcation pattern. In neonates (or younger than 1 year old), polymicrogyria is best visualized with thin T2WI. Patients 1–2 years old may also be imaged with 3D spoiled-gradient recalled echo (SPGR) T1WI. Alternative diagnoses to consider include microcephaly with simplified gyral pattern, hemimegaloencephaly, pachygyria, and cobblestone malformations. Polymicrogyria can be distinguished from these other diagnoses by its small, irregular gyri without reduced brain volume, hemispheric enlargement, broad and thick gyri, or disorganized cortex with indistinct gray–white matter junction. Schizencephaly Schizencephaly is another cortical malformation characterized by a cleft extending from the cortical surface to the ventricular ependyma. It is a rare condition with a prevalence of 1.54 per 100,000 births. The cleft is lined by dysplastic gray matter, often polymicrogyria, and may occur bilaterally or unilaterally, which is often associated with contralateral polymicrogyria. When the walls of the cleft are separated with CSF present in between, often bilaterally, the malformation is termed open-lipped ( ). When the walls of the cleft are in apposition without CSF in between, usually in unilateral schizencephaly, the type is close-lipped. Multiplanar sequences with or without volumetric acquisition are particularly useful for close-lipped schizencephaly. In patients with incomplete myelination, the gray matter lined cleft is best seen on T2WI. It is important to distinguish schizencephaly from porencephaly cyst, which is an acquired lesion characterized by smooth walls without a gray matter lining or associated cortical malformations, such as polymicrogyria with schizencephaly. Heterotopic gray matter Heterotopic gray matter is a rare disorder of abnormal neuronal migration that results in the formation of nodules of ectopic gray matter, consisting of mature neurons and glial cells, without defined lamellar organization. Heterotopia may occur anywhere from the periventricular region to the pia. Periventricular (subependymal) nodular heterotopia is the most common subtype ( ). Subcortical laminar heterotopia (double cortex) is a subtype that involves a continuous or semicontinuous band of gray matter below the cortical mantle. Other subtypes include subcortical nodular heterotopia and pial heterotopias (“cobblestone” cortex). Cobblestone heterotopia is characterized by an irregular, bumpy “cobblestone” brain surface with cortical dysplasia, disruption of the normal cortical contour, and agyria. Helpful MRI sequences for detection of heterotopia include 3D T1WI SPGR in patients with complete myelination and 3D T2WI fast spin echo (FSE). Alternative diagnoses to consider include TSC, closed-lip schizencephaly, ependymal spread of a tumor, polymicrogyria, and congenital CMV. Heterotopic gray matter is distinguished by its non-enhancing, isointense gray matter nodules without mass effect or systemic features. Ulegyria Ulegyria is a condition that usually results from perinatal global hypoxic ischemic brain injury producing cortical and subcortical lesions such as shrunken and flattened cortex and multiple cerebral convolutions ( ). In children with a history of term hypoxic-ischemic injury and cortical injury on imaging, ulegyria was identified in 66% of patients. Ulegyria is most commonly centered around the deepest portion of a gyrus and usually in the parasagittal watershed and posterior cerebral artery distributions. On MRI, ulegyria is characterized by a unique mushroom-shaped appearance resulting from small atrophic circumvolutions at the bottom of a sulcus underlying an intact gyral apex. Findings may be unilateral or bilateral. Associated clinical findings include cerebral palsy, mental disability, and intractable focal seizures often with visual auras and mean onset at 4 years old. Ectopic posterior pituitary Ectopic posterior pituitary (EPP) is a rare condition characterized by the absence, truncation, or thread-like appearance of the pituitary stalk leading to positioning of the posterior pituitary gland outside of the sella turcica. EPP is thought to arise from defective neuronal migration during embryogenesis. EPP is best seen on midline sagittal T1WI MRI and is commonly located along the median eminence of the tuber cinereum or truncated pituitary stalk ( ). As age increases, the pituitary bright spot dims and may appear absent on T1WI. Commonly associated abnormalities include heterotopia, optic nerve hypoplasia, and corpus callosum abnormalities. Alternative diagnoses to consider include surgical or

EPP is thought to arise from defective neuronal migration during embryogenesis. EPP is best seen on midline sagittal T1WI MRI and is commonly located along the median eminence of the tuber cinereum or truncated pituitary stalk ( ). As age increases, the pituitary bright spot dims and may appear absent on T1WI. Commonly associated abnormalities include heterotopia, optic nerve hypoplasia, and corpus callosum abnormalities. Alternative diagnoses to consider include surgical or traumatic stalk transection, central diabetes insipidus, and hypothalamic lipoma (in the tuber cinereum). EPP can be distinguished from these diagnoses by gradual progression of panhypopituitarism, presence of ectopic bright spot seen on fat-specific imaging. Septo-optic dysplasia Septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) is a rare congenital neurodevelopmental disorder with a wide range of clinical presentations ranging from normal cognitive and neurological function to developmental delay and epilepsy. SOD has prevalence at birth of 1.41 per 10,000 live births. It defined by the presence of at least 2 of the following three features: optic nerve hypoplasia (often asymmetric), midline brain abnormalities (typically malformations in the septum pellucidum and corpus callosum), and pituitary gland dysfunction (often ectopic posterior pituitary). There may be flat-roofed ventricles and inferiorly pointed frontal horns ( ). The presence of additional cerebral cortical malformations such as polymicrogyria and schizencephaly is known as SOD-plus syndrome. Imaging of SOD involves MRI with 3D acquisitions or multiplanar reformation (MPR) such as 3D GRE-based T1 and 3D-balanced steady state (SS) GRE. Cephalocele A cephalocele is another congenital anomaly that is characterized by extracranial extension of intracranial contents through a defect in the skull. These contents can include meninges, brain tissue, and CSF. It occurs in 0.8–4 per 10,000 live births. Cephalocele more commonly occurs in the occipital region but can also occur at the frontoethmoidal, parietal (atretic or cranial vault), or basal (nasopharyngeal) regions. On MRI imaging, a cephalocele will have a heterogeneous signal intensity of contents reflecting the brain parenchyma and CSF ( ). MRV can help to characterize venous relationships to the cephalocele, particularly in the occipital region. Alternative diagnoses to consider include dermoid or epidermoid cyst, nasal glial heterotopia (“nasal glioma”), sinus pericranii, and vascular anomalies such as neoplasms and malformations. These alternative diagnoses lack direction connection to the intracranial compartment and a skull defect or will show venous communication, such as in the case of sinus pericranii. Tuberous sclerosis complex Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare neurocutaneous disorder characterized by hamartomatous lesions or “tubers” in various organs and systems. , The incidence is estimated to be between 1:6,000 and 1:10,000 live births. TSC often initially manifests as infantile spasms in the first months of life, progressing to intellectual disability and intractable focal seizures. In the CNS, TSC is characterized by cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, and white matter lesions. On MRI imaging, tubers change with myelination, appearing hyperintense on T1 and hypointense on T2 in neonates and appearing hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 with poorly defined borders in older children ( ). , Cortical tubers may be difficult to differentiate between FCD. Unlike FCD, cortical tubers tend to be multifocal, affect any part of the cortex, are often associated with calcifications, and are present with other features of TSC. It is also important to consider cavernomas as a differential diagnosis in the evaluation of calcified tubers. Other alternative diagnoses include gray matter heterotopia, cortical dysplasias, and germinal matrix. TSC can be distinguished by the presence of subependymal nodules and systemic features. Sturge–Weber syndrome Sturge–Weber syndrome (SWS) is another rare congenital neurocutaneous disorder characterized by abnormal cortical venous development with an incidence of 3.08 per 100,000 people per year. – Clinically, patients with SWS often present with focal antiepileptic-resistant seizures, hemiparesis, cognitive impairment, and headaches. The hallmark features of SWS include facial capillary malformation, known as a port-wine stain typically involving the first division of the trigeminal nerve, leptomeningeal vascular malformations, and ocular abnormalities such as glaucoma. Imaging findings include ipsilateral leptomeningeal enhancement, ipsilateral enlarged choroid plexus, cortical atrophy, cortical calcification with a tram track appearance, calvarial thickening, and sinus hyperpneumatization ( ). Alternative diagnoses to consider include an acquired meningeal process, PHACES syndrome, blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome, Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome, and Wyburn–Mason syndrome. SWS is distinguished from these diagnoses by the presence of a port-wine stain with ipsilateral leptomeningeal enhancement and ocular involvement. Leigh disease Leigh disease or subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy is a rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by progressive neurodegeneration typically manifesting in infancy or early childhood. The prevalence is estimated to be between 1:30,000 and 1:40,000. Clinically, Leigh disease presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, ataxia, and respiratory. Lactate may be elevated in the

calvarial thickening, and sinus hyperpneumatization ( ). Alternative diagnoses to consider include an acquired meningeal process, PHACES syndrome, blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome, Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome, and Wyburn–Mason syndrome. SWS is distinguished from these diagnoses by the presence of a port-wine stain with ipsilateral leptomeningeal enhancement and ocular involvement. Leigh disease Leigh disease or subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy is a rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by progressive neurodegeneration typically manifesting in infancy or early childhood. The prevalence is estimated to be between 1:30,000 and 1:40,000. Clinically, Leigh disease presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, ataxia, and respiratory. Lactate may be elevated in the blood, CSF, as well as within the brain (on MR spectroscopy) due to mitochondrial dysfunction. The hallmark feature of Leigh disease is symmetrical “speckled” lesions in the basal ganglia or brainstem on MRI, which appear as hyperintensities on T2 and hypointensities on FLAIR ( ). Alternative diagnoses to consider include hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, Wilson disease, near drowning, kernicterus, Huntington disease, and encephalitis. Leigh disease is distinguished from these conditions by its progressive neurological symptoms, symmetric lesions in the basal ganglia on MRI, and elevated lactate on various testing modalities. Inflammatory/infectious etiologies Rasmussen encephalitis Rasmussen encephalitis is a rare immune-mediated progressive hemispheric encephalopathy characterized by childhood onset, intractable epilepsy, hemiparesis, and neurologic decline. The incidence is estimated to be 2.4 per 10 million people aged less than 18 per year. On MRI, there is progressive atrophy of one cerebral hemisphere, usually beginning in the insula, perisylvian region, caudate head, and putamen, with cortical hyperintensities on T2 and FLAIR ( ). Serial imaging may show fluctuations with regression followed by reappearance of lesions on FLAIR in the cortical and subcortical regions, predominantly in the frontoinsular and parietal regions. There may also be a crossed cerebellar diaschisis. Alternative diagnoses to consider include SWS, other autoimmune encephalitis (often with bilateral findings), and Dyke–Davidoff–Masson syndrome. Rasmussen encephalitis is distinguished by its progressive, unilateral cerebral atrophy with T2/FLAIR hyperintensities and without enhancement. Meningoencephalitis Meningoencephalitis is a condition of simultaneous inflammation of the meninges and brain parenchyma caused by a wide variety of infectious and non-infectious agents. It is typically a clinical diagnosis that presents with fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits with confirmation by CSF analysis showing pleocytosis, elevated protein, and elevated inflammatory markers. Imaging plays a role in identifying etiologies and assessing complications such as empyema, ischemia, hydrocephalus, cerebritis, and ventriculitis. Location of abnormalities provides a clue for the etiology with cerebral convexities suggesting a bacterial agent; basilar meninges suggesting TB, neurosyphilis, cryptococcus, sarcoidosis, and lymphoma; and meningoencephalitis suggesting a viral agent. These lesions may appear as hyperintense signals in sulci, cisterns, or brain parenchyma on T2 and FLAIR with enhancement of the meninges ( ). It is important to note that meningitis may be present even with normal imaging. Autoimmune encephalitis Autoimmune encephalitis (AE) is an immune-mediated disease with antibody-mediated inflammation of the brain. It has an incidence of 0.8 per 100,000 person-years. Paraneoplastic AE may occur as a neurologic complication of underlying malignancy outside the CNS, most commonly small cell lung carcinoma. The most common clinical paraneoplastic syndrome is limbic encephalitis. Clinically, limbic encephalitis presents with rapid onset of psychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment, temporal lobe seizures, and movement disorders. On imaging, limbic encephalitis is characterized by hyperintensities in the mesial temporal lobes and limbic system ( ). It is important to note that brain MRI is positive in only 30–50% of patients with anti-NMDAR paraneoplastic encephalitis. Alternative diagnoses to consider include HSV encephalitis, diffuse astrocytoma, status epilepticus, and gliomatosis cerebri. Limbic encephalitis, which may mimic HSV encephalitis, is typically associated with a subacute or chronic course. Neoplastic etiologies Long-term epilepsy associated tumors Long-term epilepsy associated tumors (LEATs) are encountered in approximately 30% of patients with long-term pharmaco-resistant epilepsy. The most common of these are gangliogliomas, which appear as cortically based enhancing cystic nodules on imaging ( ). They are most frequently found in the temporal lobe and can be supratentorial but can also be infratentorial. Calcifications are found in about 50% of cases. Most cases are also associated with cortical disorganization (FCD type IIIb). Differentiating features of FCD include the presence of cortical thickening and transmantle sign. Other alternative diagnoses to consider include pilocytic astrocytoma, DNET, xanthoastrocytoma, diffuse astrocytoma, and oligodendroglioma. Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) is a benign, slow growing, mixed-glial neuronal neoplasm. On imaging, DNETs appear as a T2-hyperintense “bubbly” cortical mass with minimal or no mass effect, no peritumoral edema, and typically with sharp demarcation ( ). Enhancement is significantly less common than with gangliogliomas. Some DNETs with less distinct margins may have associated focal cortical dysplasia. The most common site is the medial temporal lobe. Alternative diagnoses to consider include ganglioglioma, FCD, neuroepithelial cyst, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, and angiocentric glioma. Multinodular and vacuolating

alternative diagnoses to consider include pilocytic astrocytoma, DNET, xanthoastrocytoma, diffuse astrocytoma, and oligodendroglioma. Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNET) is a benign, slow growing, mixed-glial neuronal neoplasm. On imaging, DNETs appear as a T2-hyperintense “bubbly” cortical mass with minimal or no mass effect, no peritumoral edema, and typically with sharp demarcation ( ). Enhancement is significantly less common than with gangliogliomas. Some DNETs with less distinct margins may have associated focal cortical dysplasia. The most common site is the medial temporal lobe. Alternative diagnoses to consider include ganglioglioma, FCD, neuroepithelial cyst, pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, and angiocentric glioma. Multinodular and vacuolating nodular tumor Multinodular and vacuolating nodular tumor (MVNT) is a rare, benign neuronal tumor characterized by multiple nodules and vacuolated neuronal cells, primarily encountered as an epileptogenic lesion in the subcortical white matter. MVNT appears as a cluster of variably sized, confluent, and discrete nodules, often in a U-shaped configuration with no mass effect ( ). They can be found in the deep cortical ribbon and superficial white matter sparing the superficial gray matter and can also be found in the vermis of the cerebellum. On MRI, the lesions are isointense with the cortex on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI/FLAIR, very bright on DWI, and exhibit no enhancement. Alternative diagnoses to consider include DNETs, FCD, and enlarged perivascular spaces. Miscellaneous etiologies Cerebral cavernous malformations Cerebral cavernous malformations, also known as cavernomas, are benign vascular lesions made up of dilated sinusoids lined by thin, immature walls containing blood products of various ages. This results in hamartomatous or “berry-like” of vascular spaces without any intervening brain parenchyma. The peak incidence for cavernomas is 4–60 years old, and they are estimated to occur in 0.5% of the general population. On imaging, cavernomas have a heterogenous or “popcorn” appearance on T2, a hypointense hemosiderin rim, hypointensity on SWI, and absent or minimal enhancement (except in cavernomas with associated developmental venous anomaly) ( ). Sizes may range from microscopic to giant (larger than 6 cm), and they are most common in the supratentorial region compared to the infratentorial region and spinal cord. Alternative diagnoses to consider include diffuse axonal injury, intracerebral hematoma, neoplasm, and capillary telangiectasia. Cavernomas are distinguished by their “popcorn” appearance, hemosiderin rim, and lack of significant enhancement and edema. Gliosis Gliosis is a relatively common reactive process occurring after some time following most types of CNS injuries, such as trauma, infection, ischemia, and neurodegenerative disease. The prevalence of gliosis varies based on the underlying condition. In patients undergoing epilepsy surgery, glial scars were found in 4.9% of patients. Gliosis is characterized by focal proliferation and activation of glial cells, particularly astrocytes. Gliosis can be asymptomatic or be a seizure-focus. The presenting features of gliosis are typically related to the underlying condition causing the gliosis. On imaging, gliosis produces no volume loss, no mass effect, and appears hyperintense on T2/FLAIR and mildly hypointense on T1, with mildly facilitated diffusion on ADC ( ). It may also mimic a low-grade astrocytoma. On CT, small or subtle areas of gliosis may be invisible but more pronounced gliosis produces white matter hypoattenuation. Dual pathology Dual pathology refers to the coexistence of hippocampal sclerosis and another extrahippocampal epileptogenic entity, most commonly MCDs or acquired childhood lesions. Satisfaction of search after detection of either HS or another epileptogenic entity can result in failure to detect both conditions, ultimately reducing success of epilepsy surgery and highlighting the importance of a systematic approach. Multimodality imaging Several of the entities discussed above have subtle findings that make detection difficult, even resulting in labeling as “normal.” These conditions include focal cortical dysplasias, small gangliogliomas, and DNETs. Detection of these entities can be improved by selection of proper MRI techniques, incorporation of EEG and clinical findings, multimodality imaging with PET and SPECT, and a systemic approach for evaluating the epileptogenic lesions. Chart review should include age of seizure onset, seizure semiology, family history, and suspected localization from EEG findings. Multimodality imaging can also provide additional utility for epilepsy evaluation through confirmation or further mapping of the epileptogenic zone. In addition to being essential in the emergent setting for evaluation of acute hemorrhage, CT can also help detect conditions associated with calcifications. PET is helpful for detection of subtle FCD and surgical planning. SPECT can be used for interictal subtraction for localization, and fMRI is also commonly used for surgical planning. It is essential to avoid overinterpretation of structural lesions as epileptogenic foci without clinical correlation. Systematic approach Using a checklist approach or including pertinent positives and negatives in a reporting template can ensure a thorough search for possible etiologies. Grouping pathologies by location and broader categories of imaging appearance can reinforce a comprehensive search for the large diversity of the potential abnormalities, without requiring call-out of every entity. It is essential to avoid overinterpretation of structural lesions as epileptogenic foci without clinical correlation. Systematic approach Using a checklist approach or including pertinent positives and negatives in a reporting template can ensure a thorough search for possible etiologies. Grouping pathologies by location and broader categories of imaging appearance can reinforce a comprehensive search for the large diversity of the potential abnormalities, without requiring call-out of every entity. Sites or groupings of pathology that may be useful to specifically enumerate in a search pattern or report template include cortical sulcation abnormalities, hippocampal abnormalities, parenchymal signal abnormalities, subependymal/ventricular lining contour abnormalities, and midline fusion/developmental abnormalities ( ). For example, detection of abnormal cortical sulcation or contour can suggest entities such as FCD, polymicrogyria, and ulegyria. Hippocampal abnormalities or asymmetries should prompt consideration of hippocampal sclerosis. Detection of a parenchymal mass or nodule can raise suspicion for etiologies such as gray matter heterotopia, ganglioglioma, and other neoplasia. The presence of abnormal brain susceptibility should include consideration of cavernomas, neurocysticercosis, or mineralization or blood products within other cerebral lesions. Other abnormal (e.g., T2/FLAIR) brain signal is associated with a wide range of conditions including gliosis, ischemia, trauma, infection, metabolic, demyelinating, and autoimmune processes. Subependymal/ventricular contour abnormalities can be caused by TSC, schizencephaly, heterotopia, and neoplasms. Conditions with midline fusion abnormalities include holoprosencephaly, agenesis of corpus callosum, and SOD. Entities with other midline developmental abnormalities include EPP and hypothalamic hamartoma. Chunking of etiologies in this way facilitates not just workflows and reporting ( ) but also the recollection of epileptogenic lesions detectable on imaging. Conclusion Identification of epileptogenic foci can be facilitated with use of a systematic approach. Consideration of clinical semiology and electrophysiological information, recognition of the features of notable intracranial pathologies, use of specialized epilepsy protocols for certain relatively common conditions such as FCD and hippocampal sclerosis, and use of comprehensive epilepsy reporting templates can facilitate evaluation of structural causes of epilepsy on imaging.

chunks.content: Introduction Renal artery thrombosis is a rare but critical diagnosis that often presents with nonspecific symptoms, such as abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Renal infarction is an even rarer phenomenon, which may occur as a consequence of renal artery thrombosis, with an estimated incidence of 0.004%-0.007% [ , ]. Cardioembolic events are a common cause for renal artery thrombosis and are often associated with atrial fibrillation (AF) [ , , ]. AF is a leading cause of systemic emboli, but involvement of the renal vasculature—particularly the main renal artery—is uncommon and underrecognized. Other etiologies of renal infarction include renal artery injury, hypercoagulable states, and cryptogenic causes [ , , ]. One large retrospective review of 438 patients cites cardiogenic events as the most common etiology of renal infarction at 55.7% [ ]. On the other hand, another large retrospective review of 186 patients reports cardioembolic etiologies comprised a much lower 9.1% of renal infarctions, while renal artery lesions were the predominant etiology at 81.2% [ ]. For suspected renal artery occlusion, CT angiography (CTA) is the imaging modality of choice. CTA and other imaging modalities such as contrast-enhanced CT may reveal a wedge-shaped, non-enhancing region of parenchyma indicating renal infarction [ , ]. If over 50% of the kidney is involved, the infarction is described as global [ ]. Definitive treatment and therapeutic intervention remain unclear due to the rarity of global renal infarction. Though treatment approaches vary based on the underlying etiology, common interventions include systemic anticoagulation, thrombolysis, and endovascular revascularization [ , , ]. Regardless of treatment approach, outcomes can range from recovery of kidney function to recurrent renal infarction, acute kidney injury, new-onset chronic kidney disease (CKD), or end-stage renal disease [ , , , ]. We present a patient with acute-onset abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, found to have a right renal artery thrombosis resulting in global renal infarction. The patient underwent thrombectomy with partial removal of the thrombus and was treated with anticoagulation. Right renal function was reduced, as seen through technetium-99m mercaptoacetyltriglycine (Tc-99m MAG3) renogram. At follow-up, the patient was noted to have progression of his CKD. Case A 47-year-old man with a history of heart failure with improved ejection fraction (EF 40%-45%); paroxysmal AF (PAF) noncompliant with anticoagulation (CHA 2 DS 2 ‑VASc score of 3 for heart failure, hypertension, and diabetes); CKD (baseline creatinine 1.2 mg/dL); type 2 diabetes mellitus; and hypertension presented to the ED with acute-onset abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting that began 8 hours prior. He also endorsed hemoptysis of unknown duration. Initial workup revealed several laboratory abnormalities as seen in . CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed an occlusive thrombus in the right renal artery with evidence of global infarction ( and ). CT chest with contrast revealed patchy bilateral ground glass opacities consistent with infection versus alveolar hemorrhage. Anticoagulation with heparin was initiated 11 hours after symptom onset. The patient underwent interventional radiology-guided percutaneous thrombectomy 13 hours after symptom onset. A 5 French sheath was placed in the right common femoral artery, and C2 glide catheter was advanced into the right renal artery, at which point the sheath was exchanged for a long 6 French sheath. Digital subtraction angiography performed during planned thrombectomy confirmed an intraluminal thrombus in the distal right renal artery extending into branch arteries, without angiographic evidence of dissection or stenosis. A total of 10 passes with aspiration were completed. Approximately 60% of the thrombus was removed with the successful removal of the thrombus in the distal right renal artery and lower pole renal artery. However, there was persistent thrombus within the upper pole renal artery. There were no post-procedural complications. Catheter-directed thrombolysis was contraindicated due to ongoing hemoptysis. Alternatively, he was treated with continuous heparin infusion for the remaining thrombus. One day post-thrombectomy, approximately 36 hours after symptom onset, Doppler ultrasound of the right kidney revealed minimal flow and an inability to visualize arterial waveforms, which was consistent with continued perfusion deficits. He was also noted to be hypervolemic, so further workup with transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a left ventricular EF of 25%-30% with severe global hypokinesis of the left ventricle. The inferior vena cava was dilated (>2.1 cm) without collapse, and right atrial pressure was elevated at 15 mm Hg. Given his recent noncompliance and polypharmacy, this was thought to be an exacerbation of HF secondary to medication noncompliance. His GDMT was titrated appropriately with planned outpatient follow-up in the heart failure clinic. To assess the renal artery thrombosis, a hypercoagulable and autoimmune panel were obtained. Notably, the antithrombin III (AT-III) level was decreased at 63% (normal range 80%-125%), but the remaining workup (antiphospholipid antibodies, PNH testing, JAK2 V617F mutation, factor V activity, homocysteine, ANA, ANCA, C3, and C4) was within normal limits or negative. Given the CT chest findings and hemoptysis,

His GDMT was titrated appropriately with planned outpatient follow-up in the heart failure clinic. To assess the renal artery thrombosis, a hypercoagulable and autoimmune panel were obtained. Notably, the antithrombin III (AT-III) level was decreased at 63% (normal range 80%-125%), but the remaining workup (antiphospholipid antibodies, PNH testing, JAK2 V617F mutation, factor V activity, homocysteine, ANA, ANCA, C3, and C4) was within normal limits or negative. Given the CT chest findings and hemoptysis, he was treated with 5 days of intravenous antibiotics for suspected pneumonia, with resolution of hemoptysis at the time of discharge. Four days after thrombectomy, approximately 108 hours after symptom onset, Tc-99m MAG3 renogram showed significantly reduced perfusion and function of the right kidney with a differential function of 24% on the right versus 76% on the left ( , ). At this time, he was transitioned to oral anticoagulation with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and discharged approximately 114 hours after symptom onset. At discharge, kidney function had improved, with creatinine 1.91 mg/dL and eGFR 43 mL/min. Kidney function remained stable at 8 weeks post-discharge. Despite a decreased AT-III level, further workup was negative, suggesting that the most likely etiology of renal artery thrombosis in this case was embolic, secondary to PAF in the absence of therapeutic anticoagulation. Further follow-up, including any future imaging or assessment of kidney function, is not available. Discussion Renal artery thrombosis is a rare diagnosis, and subsequent global renal infarction is exceedingly rare. Renal infarcts generally present with nonspecific symptoms, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and even fever [ , ]. These symptoms may stem from several different etiologies, and the differential diagnosis often includes pyelonephritis, ureteric colic, and multiple gastrointestinal pathologies [ ]. Due to this broad differential, renal artery thrombosis is often initially missed, with fewer than 50% of patients being correctly diagnosed within 2 days. [ ] Current literature indicates that the triad of abdominal or flank pain, elevated LDH, and hematuria with proteinuria on urinalysis may point toward renal infarction and should prompt urgent imaging, typically CTA [ , ]. Our patient presented with nonspecific right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. However, given his significant cardiac history and acute renal dysfunction, a CT scan with contrast was chosen as the initial imaging modality. Initial workup for renal artery thrombosis often includes routine laboratory studies, such as urinalysis, CMP, CBC, and LDH [ ]. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis is CTA, which should be used as the first-line imaging modality for suspected infarct or occlusion [ ]. In select cases in which other imaging was obtained prior to CTA, noncontrast CT may reveal hypodensities or perfusion defects in the kidney with the “cortical rim sign” [ , , ]. One study examining the diagnosis of acute renal infarction in the emergency department through contrast-enhanced CT noted that all patients demonstrated a wedge-shaped area of nonenhancement [ ]. CTA can also help differentiate causes of renal artery occlusion and renal infarction, including thromboembolic, renal artery dissection, fibromuscular dysplasia, or atherosclerotic disease. Renal artery dissection is often characterized by the presence of separate lumens within the artery. Fibromuscular dysplasia may demonstrate a classic beading appearance due to alternating areas of narrowing and dilatation that can be seen on CTA. Finally, atherosclerotic disease is often characterized by calcified plaques within the artery [ ]. Risk factors for renal artery thrombosis include AF, hypertension, diabetes, hypercoagulable states, and prior embolic infarction [ ]. Our patient has a notable cardiac history, including heart failure with improved EF of unknown etiology diagnosed 11 years prior; PAF not appropriately anticoagulated diagnosed 3 years prior, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He was followed for several years in the heart failure clinic with appropriate treatment, including GDMT, cholesterol-lowering agents, and antihypertensives. However, there were several periods prior to presentation where the patient experienced difficulty obtaining medication, resulting in noncompliance. Further workup for underlying hypercoagulability revealed low AT-III, though in the setting of acute thrombosis and active treatment with heparin, this is not diagnostic of a hereditary deficiency [ ]. Hematology was consulted during the hospitalization with plans to repeat follow-up AT-III testing at a later date. Overall, the imaging findings and clinical picture were most consistent with a thromboembolic cause, given the lack of any other findings on CTA, including arterial wall irregularities, calcification, atherosclerotic plaque, or fibromuscular dysplasia. Previous studies have divided etiology of renal infarction into 4 categories: cardioembolic, renal artery injury, hypercoagulable state, and cryptogenic [ , , ]. Retrospective studies have examined the etiology of renal infarction but differ in reported frequencies. For example, 1 large study of 438 patients reports cardiogenic as the most

Hematology was consulted during the hospitalization with plans to repeat follow-up AT-III testing at a later date. Overall, the imaging findings and clinical picture were most consistent with a thromboembolic cause, given the lack of any other findings on CTA, including arterial wall irregularities, calcification, atherosclerotic plaque, or fibromuscular dysplasia. Previous studies have divided etiology of renal infarction into 4 categories: cardioembolic, renal artery injury, hypercoagulable state, and cryptogenic [ , , ]. Retrospective studies have examined the etiology of renal infarction but differ in reported frequencies. For example, 1 large study of 438 patients reports cardiogenic as the most common etiology at 55.7% [ ]. However, another study of 186 patients reports cardioembolic etiology in only 9.1% of patients, while renal artery lesions were the predominant etiology in 81.2% of patients [ ]. These differences may be attributed to sample size, single- versus multicenter design, and differing inclusion or diagnostic criteria. Overall, the estimated prevalence of AF in patients with renal infarction ranges from 18% to 48% [ , , ]. In patients with confirmed cardiogenic causes of infarction, the prevalence of AF is as high as 86% [ ]. Patients with renal infarction are typically in their 60s, while those with cardioembolic causes are known to be considerably older. This case is notable because the patient is younger than typical cardioembolic cohorts [ , ]. In the majority of reported renal infarcts, patients have a single lesion [ ]. Some patients have multiple lesions, which is more common in patients with identified cardioembolic causes [ , ]. Global infarction is defined as greater than 50% involvement of the kidney [ ]. Unilateral left and right kidney infarction appears to occur with equal frequency [ , ]. Although prior studies have demonstrated complete occlusion of one of the main renal arteries, the etiology of these complete occlusions is often not established [ , ]. Among patients with renal infarctions, most series do not specifically report the prevalence of global infarctions; however, in those that specify global versus focal, global infarcts represent a very small subset of cases [ , , ]. As discussed, although AF is a well-recognized risk factor for renal infarction overall, cases of global renal infarction secondary to AF are infrequently reported. Therefore, this case represents an uncommon instance of global renal infarction likely secondary to AF and cardioembolic etiology. Rapid diagnosis of renal artery thrombosis and renal infarction is essential for timely management and therapeutic intervention. In 1 study, the mean time from symptom onset to diagnosis by radiographic findings was 5 days, ranging from 0 to 11 days [ ]. Renal infarction was confirmed in our case within 12 hours of symptom onset, allowing for timely intervention. Treatment is not standardized as renal infarction is rare. Patients are typically managed with systemic anticoagulation, thrombolysis, or endovascular revascularization. If AF is suspected to be the underlying cause, continued anticoagulation is often necessary, as seen in this case [ ]. Despite anticoagulation, prior studies have shown that 2% to 17% of patients with renal infarction will have a recurrent systemic infarction [ , ]. Similarly, 1 study demonstrated that 17% of patients with acute renal embolism experienced recurrent embolism [ ]. Short-term mortality in hospitalized patients is low and appears to be higher in patients with renal artery injury or hypercoagulable states compared to cardiogenic etiologies [ , ]. Patients often initially present with acute kidney injury, but this typically resolves with treatment [ , ]. Outcomes vary, but 1 study cites that 10.9% of patients with renal infarction will have new-onset CKD with only 2.8% of patients progressing to end-stage renal disease requiring hemodialysis after renal infarction [ ]. This may be because patients develop atrophy of the injured kidney, though atrophy has not always been associated with a decrease in renal function [ ]. As we consider the prognosis for our patient, atrophy of the right kidney and progression of CKD are the most likely implications of the global infarction. The Tc-99m MAG3 renogram demonstrated decreased perfusion and function of the right kidney, which can provide a baseline measurement for serial assessment of the right kidney after revascularization. Follow-up imaging is not available at this time, but serial assessment with Tc-99m MAG3 renogram is planned. Our patient maintained stable kidney function for at least 4 weeks post-discharge and will continue to be monitored for long-term follow-up. Tc-99m MAG3 renography has many clinical applications, including the evaluation and diagnosis of congenital abnormalities, obstruction, renal failure, and renal function after transplant [ , , ]. Tc-99m MAG3 renography assesses the renal parenchyma, renal perfusion, and split renal function [ , , ]. Though the literature does not specifically mention its use after global renal infarction, by establishing a new baseline split renal function, we can more

this time, but serial assessment with Tc-99m MAG3 renogram is planned. Our patient maintained stable kidney function for at least 4 weeks post-discharge and will continue to be monitored for long-term follow-up. Tc-99m MAG3 renography has many clinical applications, including the evaluation and diagnosis of congenital abnormalities, obstruction, renal failure, and renal function after transplant [ , , ]. Tc-99m MAG3 renography assesses the renal parenchyma, renal perfusion, and split renal function [ , , ]. Though the literature does not specifically mention its use after global renal infarction, by establishing a new baseline split renal function, we can more appropriately assess the function of the injured kidney over time. In this study, we highlight a rare case of global right renal infarction due to AF. Global renal infarct is a rare phenomenon with a paucity of literature demonstrating consistent and established etiologies. To our knowledge, renal artery thrombosis with full occlusion resulting in a global renal infarct secondary to AF is rarely reported in the literature. This case underscores the importance of maintaining clinical suspicion for renal artery thrombosis and renal infarction in patients with nonspecific abdominal symptoms and a concomitant history of AF, especially those not receiving anticoagulation or having undergone left atrial appendage occlusion. Patient consent Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report.

documents.title: ACR practice parameter for performance of screening and diagnostic mammography

chunks.content: 1. Introduction The Tomosynthesis Mammography Imaging Screening Trial (TMIST) EA 1151, sponsored by ECOG ACRIN is being conducted to assess the effectiveness for breast cancer screening of digital breast tomosynthesis (TM) compared to digital mammography (DM) in an anticipated population of 128,905 women. Participants are randomized 1:1 into trial arms in which they are screened using conventional 2D mammography or where they receive tomosynthesis with additional 2D views or synthetic 2D depending on the preference of the site radiologist. TMIST is funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI). This report describes the quality control (QC) methodology used in TMIST and summarizes selected test results over the initial 5-y period from October, 2017 to December, 2022. It is important that all equipment is operated within appropriate parameters with regard to image quality and dose for the findings of the study to be valid and capture the true capacities of the two technology types. In the Digital Mammography Screening Trial (DMIST), , the QC tests for digital systems closely emulated those designed originally for testing Screen Film systems, and tests varied among manufacturers. In TMIST, there was an opportunity to take advantage of more sophisticated digital tools to assess stability and performance. Direct digital image transmission to a central Physics QC core (PQCC) also allowed automated analysis to be performed for many of the tests. Tomosynthesis systems are fairly mature and have been in the marketplace long enough for most of the initial problems to be worked out, however when the protocol was written, there was no consensus on what tests would be included in an optimal QC testing program. The American College of Radiology (ACR) has an approved comprehensive “alternative standard quality assurance” program for digital mammography and tomosynthesis. However, when TMIST commenced operation, this program was used by very few facilities; most still used the manufacturer specified QC program. Similarly, in principle, EUREF or EFOMP protocols – , could have been used to obtain data that could be compared across systems, but these are not commonly used in the U.S., would require different equipment and would have increased the workload for the site technologists or physicists. The TMIST QC program was designed specifically to allow measurement on systems from multiple vendors, located at many sites, with differing levels of medical physics support. It is complementary to existing federal requirements in the US, and requires that all systems are maintained and perform QC to meet applicable accreditation standards. In TMIST, a simple set of weekly and monthly tests was implemented to limit the additional workload on the technologist. Physicist reports (Mammography Equipment Evaluation) were used to ensure that performance of the equipment was at an acceptable level. Data on tube output and half-value layer (HVL) were gleaned from these reports and used to estimate subject radiation exposures. A set of physics tests to be performed annually by the QC technologist and analysed by the PQCC team was developed to consistently evaluate all tomosynthesis units involved in the trial. As in our development of the QC program for the earlier DMIST Trial, , the testing protocol and initial pass/fail criteria were established at the outset of the trial and designed so that, as much as possible, tests could be applied generically among the different tomosynthesis systems. Wherever appropriate, the design of the tests was based on the IAEA Quality Control Program for Digital Mammography. Limits were set to be consistent with equipment design to allow for expected day-to-day variability of test results, but sufficiently restrictive to identify systems with substandard imaging performance. The initial limits were established based on preliminary measurements with some of the equipment, however, with further experience it became necessary to adjust some tests (e.g., to accommodate file formats) during the trial. We aimed to closely adhere to the established protocol in order to enable consistent monitoring of performance across different types of equipment over a period of time. An important objective was to identify specific tests that could effectively identify issues with image quality or anticipate equipment failure. This information would be valuable in developing a well-structured quality control program for digital mammography and tomosynthesis. In this report, the unique QC tests for the weekly and monthly QC are described along with objectives and pass/fail criteria for the tests. Initially, it was planned that both “FOR PROCESSING” (raw) and “FOR PRESENTATION” images would be submitted, but because of technical constraints at some sites, the program was modified, to make submission of FOR PROCESSING images optional. This resulted in the loss of the ability to perform “linear systems” analysis on all images. Tests of subject contrast and resolution were carried out and tracked. The annual QC portion which tests automatic exposure control response vs thickness, resolution, noise levels and geometric accuracy will be described in a future paper. The

This resulted in the loss of the ability to perform “linear systems” analysis on all images. Tests of subject contrast and resolution were carried out and tracked. The annual QC portion which tests automatic exposure control response vs thickness, resolution, noise levels and geometric accuracy will be described in a future paper. The Physics QC protocol and additional detailed test results are available through a direct link in the online article’s section. 2. Methods 2.1. Data Collection and overall QC program structure All images in TMIST, including QC and study subject mammograms (both DBT projections and reconstructed volumes) for the study are collected by the ACR using its “Transfer of Images and Data” (TRIAD) software package. This software runs on a computer at each screening facility. The overall schematic of data flow as well as analysis and reporting operations is illustrated in . QC images are transferred from ACR to the PQCC using secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) to the “QC core” cloud servers (Amazon Web Services (AWS)), which automatically determine the image type and perform appropriate analysis. Results from each test are stored in a database, and available for review by personnel at the screening sites on a secure password-protected web application ( tmistqc.org ). Website access requires user registration and approval. Users are restricted to view data only from the clinical site(s) for which they are approved. After associating a given set of subject images with an assigned study subject ID, TRIAD then removes any Protected Health Information (PHI) from the DICOM header and transmits these images to ACR for future reader studies and secondary uses. Each de-identified subject image header is also sent to the PQCC without the clinical image pixel data so that technical factors can be tracked and evaluated. Results for the analysis of header data will be presented in a companion paper (MS#22-2140). Please note that in several places in this report, for the readers’ convenience, we have reproduced some text and wording of the test criteria verbatim from the online TMIST Quality Control Manual, specifically developed for the program. 2.2. Site Initiation and Credentialing Requirements To ensure that all image files required for clinical imaging were appropriately sent through TRIAD , submission of a credentialing phantom was required. For this purpose, either the Mammographic Accreditation Phantom (MAP) or the new digital mammography phantom (DMP) as specified in the American College of Radiology (ACR) Mammography Accreditation Program and mandated by the Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA) could be used. Most sites already had, and were familiar with at least one of these phantoms. To complete the credentialing process, sites had to be able to transfer images of all required types via the TRIAD software (provided by ECOG/ACRIN). These include 2D mammograms, reconstructed tomosynthesis volumes, and synthetic 2D images (if used by the center). Depending on the site preferences, images are either transferred from the mammography unit directly to the TRIAD server or first sent to the local or research PACS and then moved to the TRIAD server. To verify that a site was providing at least a minimally acceptable level of image quality, their ACR (MAP or DMP) phantom was imaged both in DM and TM modes for each machine intended to be used for participant imaging in the trial. For each unit or new detector, phantom images were subjectively reviewed. Minimum scoring requirements were set based on ACR published standards ( e.g ., 4 specks, 3 masses and 3 fibers perceivable in the MAP phantom or 3 specks, 2 masses and 2 fibers in the DMAP phantom), as well as the requirement that images be free from obvious artifacts such as “dead” lines, hot or dead pixels, electromagnetic field (EMF) ripple or streaking. From the image headers of the credentialing images, the unique detector ID and station serial number were extracted to identify each machine enrolled in the program. As part of QC oversight, we requested that sites forward us all service reports and physicist’s reports for credentialed units. Service information was collected in our database so that it could be cross referenced with QC shifts and failures. 2.3. Description of the TMIST QC program The QC tests, frequencies, and objectives of the tests are summarized in . Only the weekly tests will be discussed in this report. Phantoms used in the tests, software analysis tools and results will be described in a later section. A governing philosophy for the QC approach used in TMIST is to assess the image quality in “patient imaging mode” as

Description of the TMIST QC program The QC tests, frequencies, and objectives of the tests are summarized in . Only the weekly tests will be discussed in this report. Phantoms used in the tests, software analysis tools and results will be described in a later section. A governing philosophy for the QC approach used in TMIST is to assess the image quality in “patient imaging mode” as would be used in the clinic and viewed by the radiologist. In other words, “FOR PRESENTATION” mammograms, reconstructed tomosynthesis planes and, if used by the radiologists, synthetic mammograms and optional “slab” views are evaluated in the tests. By choosing these images for evaluation, the QC captures the effects of the entire imaging chain – including non-linear reconstruction and image processing that may change behavior depending on underlying imaging conditions or changes to the system software. The technologists are asked to use the same compression paddles, compression force, grid and fully automatic exposure control (AEC) settings for the QC testing as would normally be used to image patients. It was emphasized that for consistency of operation, the same AEC setting, reconstruction mode and large paddle be used for the tests every time they are performed. Some sites were asked to use a semi-manual technique such as “AutoTime”, because we found that slight compression thickness variations could change AEC operation enough (usually kilovoltage (kV) changed) that the test results became inconsistent and outside control limits. Every test in the program has a baseline value established for each parameter based on up to five repeated measurements. Baselines were established at the beginning of QC accrual or whenever we were able to determine that a change in equipment or operating conditions had taken place. To meet the mammographic standard of practice for all digital mammography (DM) and tomosynthesis mammogram (TM) units used to image TMIST subjects, the mammography technologist and the site Qualified Medical Physicist (QMP) perform the standard QC tests required to maintain accreditation in the facility jurisdiction. Each report from the QMP is collected when they perform their testing, including the Annual Mammographic Equipment Evaluation (MEE) and any post-service MEE. In addition, all TMIST sites are provided with identical TMIST test phantoms (described in a later section) to harmonize the quality control across sites and vendors. Facilities used pre-existing uniform thickness PMMA phantoms (2.5 cm for GE, 4 cm for Hologic and Siemens) for flat-field tests. Using those phantoms, the technologists take a limited number of QC exposures. Image sets for each of the QC tests are sent to the TRIAD server and uploaded as “Site Qualification” images. To minimize the number of test images that must be acquired, several tests are performed within a single image acquisition. Additional testing was also performed on the synthetic 2D mammogram of the TMISTQC phantom (weekly) and a tomosynthesis acquisition of a uniform plastic block (monthly). There were varying (and initially low) rates of use of synthetic 2D images at sites, so we did not have adequate experience to include the data for analysis. Monthly uniform QC tests are not reported here because the detection of artifacts was qualitative, performed by individual site technologists, and information recording was often inconsistent. The images received from ACR are analyzed by automated software at the PQCC, and results are available for viewing on the tmistqc.org website by site personnel using a password-protected login. Automated Processing of Images As shown in , all images are transferred from the central ACR image repository via secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) to the TMIST QC file portal. An automated service excludes non-relevant DICOM files (such as screen-captures, dose reports and CAD reports) that may be included in the examination package. Such extraneous files are expected, because it is more effective and reliable to send the entire study content, rather than depending on each site to select only the relevant file types. Relevant files are pushed via DICOM protocols to a “watchdog” service that analyzes each incoming image to identify the phantom type (TMISTQC, uniform monthly (no disk), 2D SDNR (uniform with disk), MAP or annual phantoms). This identification is performed based on automatically detected structures in each image (e.g. shape: semicircular vs uniform vs small block) and by additional aluminum spheres (BBs) at expected locations (e.g. a binary-coded serial number is located in the corner of each TMISTQC phantom consisting of BBs and spaces). Further identification is based on a priori knowledge of the approximate locations of inserts in the phantom. For example, the sphere, 4 speck groups, and a single BB appear in predefined, otherwise uniform regions in the 2D image or volume, and simple thresholds identify the precise locations of the inserts. The speck groups are located at 10.5, 20.5 and 30.5 mm heights to evaluate slice height reporting accuracy. Images that cannot be identified by automatic means are flagged for review by a physicist who can redirect the image for the correct analysis by the watchdog service. Reporting and Display of Results The testing and display software was inspired by “Gladys” , , which was an early version of a centralized software for remote collecting and monitoring of mammography system performance. In the TMISTQC software, the results of each test, as well as DICOM tags for the image such as detector ID, time of acquisition, detector temperature and technical factors are captured in a database. Key results are published on the TMISTQC.org website and reviewed by the site technologist. Examples of time-charts of test results displayed at TMISTQC.org are shown in . For a system to be operating within acceptable limits, all plotted parameters are required to be within the control limits (red lines) indicated on the chart. Any out of range points are colored red. Marginal limits are also shown (orange lines) and marginal points are colored orange. For any CRITICAL or NONCOMPLIANT variances, alert emails are sent both to the site and the PQCC physicists. Alerts are also sent if the test results are submitted late or if the site technologist has not reviewed the tests in a timely manner. Details on the time frames used to determine when alert emails were sent are included in the in . Compression Thickness Accuracy & Compression Settings The TMISTQC phantom is known to be exactly 40 mm thick. Compression thickness errors can contribute to changes in AEC operating points and can potentially change the number of reconstructed planes in the TM volume, potentially causing tissue to be missed from the reconstructed image volume. So, it is important that the readout be accurate. When phantom thickness is reported to be higher (>47 mm) or lower (<35 mm) than the expected thickness, an alert is sent to have the image checked manually, and the PQCC requests that the system calibration be corrected. During the study we became aware that on System D the thickness readout could vary, depending on the compression setting chosen (“FAST” or “NORMAL”), resulting in changes to the kV, mAs and estimated dose. From that point forward, the compression setting tag (private tag 0x0019, 0x1025) was added to the list of tags extracted from the headers and stored in the database for troubleshooting. For all units where both paddle settings had been used for weekly TM QC image acquisition, the average reported thickness, kV, exposure and estimated dose were calculated for both settings. The absolute percent differences in exposure and reported dose were calculated, as well as the absolute difference in thickness (mm) and kV. Test Limits and Definitions of Variances At the outset of the trial, test parameters and limits were either estimated from previous experience in the DMIST QC program or from other protocols such as the European Reference Frame (EUREF) tomosynthesis QC protocol recommendations. Test limits are provided in . When a critical variance was detected, PQCC emailed the site, often requesting that the test be redone because there was an error in the positioning or compression of the phantom; or because the choice of technique factors was inappropriate or inconsistent. The technologist was instructed to report on the website if they had found an artifact on the image submitted for each test; and to describe any corrective actions on the website, if any chart parameters were found to be out of limits. Most frequently, they reported an error in performing the QC, such as not compressing appropriately or not selecting the correct operating mode. When an operator error occurred, the technologist was instructed to repeat the test exposure using the correct protocol and request that PQCC not display the erroneous point on the graph (nor use it in compiling failure statistics). Correspondingly, if PQCC staff observed a finding outside the limit, and an acceptable explanation for it, they would enter comments for a marginal or failing point on the graph, and set the point to not display, and not contribute to the data for analysis. Other causes of variances include performance degradation, but also may be a result of intentional changes in operation, triggered either by the PQCC or the site itself. The following are conditions that could cause variances from an indication of stability without necessarily impacting image quality: use of a different compression plate, variable compression pressure (among technologists), a different image size or slice thickness, dependence of automatic kV selection on compression thickness readout, different positioning of phantoms, use of different reconstruction algorithms or reconstruction parameter settings, recalibration of equipment (flat-fielding or software updates), improper performance of the test (phantom upside down or no compression). Correlation of QC failures with equipment service and clinical image quality When we became aware that service was performed on a system, this information was collected in a table in our QC database. To study the correlation of QC failures with equipment service, we cross referenced the dates of failing or marginal QC with the dates of service. We calculated the odds-ratios for service to the equipment following failing/marginal vs passing QC for the time period until the subsequent passing QC. In addition, the clinical image headers from the study subjects were automatically checked by the QC software against the QC status (Passing, Marginal, Failing, Overdue) of the mammography equipment at the time of image acquisition. Since the actual pixel data of the clinical images was not forwarded to our QC servers to protect patient privacy, any exams done while the QC for the equipment was failing were flagged for qualitative review by the ECOG/ACRIN clinical image QC core. 3. Discussion The automated QC system performed well, but because the QC images were not submitted directly from the acquisition workstations, and manual intervention by imaging staff was required to identify the appropriate images and push them to TRIAD, we did not achieve our desired instantaneous feedback of results to the mammographic technologist. Sites that used USB keys or DVDs to transfer images (“sneaker net”) had even longer delays between QC imaging and posting results to the website. In addition, there were a few rare problems related to uptime reliability caused at the following points of failure: a) TRIAD connectivity at the sites, b) TRIAD upgrades causing temporary outages, c) intermittent failures of the SFTP transfer of data to the QC core, d) software image analysis tools that failed without warning, and did not automatically restart (these were ultimately resolved) and e) connectivity problems with the Amazon Cloud data repository. We believe that the large standard deviation and large range of values seen in are due mainly to the wide variation of system designs, and therefore that harmonized QC testing employing universal threshold values would not be useful. In the case of the height of the calcification groups, Slice 0 was initially assumed to be the bottom of the volume. Some vendors “pad” the volume on the bottom by 3–5 mm to avoid missing tissue and some do not. This explains the wide range in the reporting of a measurement that should be both accurate and reproducible. On the other hand, when the test results are examined on the basis of machine type as in , it is seen that the ranges and standard deviations of all parameters are much tighter. There was also a large variation in the test results for the DM weekly test ( ). Some of the difference between systems can be attributed to differences in the vendor-supplied uniform blocks and their positioning for the measurement. Most of the sites with equipment from manufacturer 1 used the vendor-supplied 2.5 cm thickness of PMMA, while manufacturer 2 sites used the supplied 4.0 cm thick PMMA and manufacturer 3 sites used the supplied 4.0 cm thick block of PMMA that mounts at the tube port. Differences also were expected because “FOR PRESENTATION” images were analyzed, and thus image signal levels did not linearly track with x-ray fluence. We expected the signal and contrast values to differ among sites, but within a site, tests performed by the same staff using the same phantoms would yield consistent values of SDNR and dose, allowing reliable tracking at each site. As seen by the ratio of marginal results to failures described in and , the relatively low incidence of actionable problems detected by the TMIST QC program may be due to the dedication and initiative of the technologists who often detected problems during their testing and corrected them promptly, thus avoiding an actual recorded failure. As well, mammography equipment design has matured and computer control of components has resulted in quite tight control of electronic parameters such as kV and mAs which were problematic at the time of development of MQSA requirements.
