described in and , the relatively low incidence of actionable problems detected by the TMIST QC program may be due to the dedication and initiative of the technologists who often detected problems during their testing and corrected them promptly, thus avoiding an actual recorded failure. As well, mammography equipment design has matured and computer control of components has resulted in quite tight control of electronic parameters such as kV and mAs which were problematic at the time of development of MQSA requirements. Since the intent of the QC program was to detect changes in equipment behavior and image quality before the clinical image quality was affected, tight “achievable” and “acceptable” test tolerances were used, and sites participating in the study were instructed not to image TMIST subjects on equipment with failing QC. This approach was, overall, successful, as there were very few (3) exams done on underperforming equipment. In light of the low number of exams done on “failing” equipment, it is not surprising that there are very few examples of clinical images such that it was not possible to correlate failing QC with changes in clinical image quality. On the other hand, as seen in , the odds ratios appear to suggest that there is a correlation between observations of marginal or failing QC tests and the need for equipment service. It is extremely important to be able to detect any mis-reporting of compression thickness by the acquisition unit, as the AEC uses this measurement to set the kV and target/filter combination before exposure. Such errors also cause the calculation of dose to be inaccurate. During the weekly QC, some sites were inconsistent in the paddle setting used (“FAST” vs “NORMAL” compression) and due to differences in the thickness calibration, the calculated dose was different by up to 39%. On occasion, the change in reported thickness resulted in a change in the kV selected by the exposure control system, which caused the mAs to change as well. We have learned that certain aspects of the test procedures require further refinement to be useful in a practical QC program. For example, our observation of a relatively high frequency of marginal test results probably indicated that the initial limits set in the protocol were unrealistic. A tolerance exceeding the baseline value by 10%, in retrospect, was often too restrictive. For example, there are a large number of marginal results for the NPS values in . Noise measurements are highly dependent on image processing filters. They are also affected by software changes and the fact that tomosynthesis reconstruction is a non-linear operation. In our tests, it is likely that the region of interest used for NPS determination was too small to allow a stable measurement. It may be possible to improve this metric so that it becomes a reliable constancy test, by using more sub-regions, employing a wider acceptable range (e.g 20%) or a combination of the two. Furthermore, we found that our monitoring at fixed spatial frequencies (1, 2 & 4 cy/mm) was generally insensitive to EMF ripple artifact or grid-lines in the image. More effective analyses of the NPS test results, perhaps with automatic peak detection could be used to better detect and analyze these phenomena. As expected, slice sensitivity profiles (resolution in the z direction) differ among machine types due to variability of the range of projection angles and differences in artifact-reduction image processing. While the wider acquisition angle and more projections used by systems E and F might suggest one to expect superior resolution in the z direction, seen with smaller FWHM values for the ASF-z, this was not the case. This suggests that the reconstruction software and image processing are having a large impact on the characteristics of final 3D volumes. Measurements on the reconstructed volume show that for System D in both the x and y directions the FWHM is almost the same for both binned (140 μm) and un-binned (70 μm) reconstructions. The ASF test was not designed to fully characterize the resolution ( point-spread-function), but rather to monitor changes in reconstructed shape of an object of known shape and providing substantial SNR. Measurements of FWHM-x and z were assumed to be sensitive to changes in the reconstruction conditions such as geometry, scan motion or reconstruction software. , and demonstrate some large changes in behavior following baseline “resets”, suggesting image quality can be quite different before and after hardware or software changes. The notable exception is the “technique change” where the site changed the acquisition settings to deal with unstable test behavior (e.g. from “AutoFilter” to “AutoTime”) without a real change in image quality. Note that in many cases, multiple changes to the system may have occurred at the same time (e.g. equipment change and software upgrade) that could explain the sometimes dramatic change in

in the reconstruction conditions such as geometry, scan motion or reconstruction software. , and demonstrate some large changes in behavior following baseline “resets”, suggesting image quality can be quite different before and after hardware or software changes. The notable exception is the “technique change” where the site changed the acquisition settings to deal with unstable test behavior (e.g. from “AutoFilter” to “AutoTime”) without a real change in image quality. Note that in many cases, multiple changes to the system may have occurred at the same time (e.g. equipment change and software upgrade) that could explain the sometimes dramatic change in test results. Nevertheless, special care should be given to evaluating image quality after such system changes, especially if the dose increases significantly or if the image quality (e.g. SDNR) is reduced. Site engagement in a QC program is essential for its success. From our experience it is most effective and responsive when the Mammography QC technologist takes ownership of the program and the program is not seen to be punitive. We believe this is seen in the consistent performance noted in the Gold status sites. On the other hand, there were some sites which had problems in performing and reviewing the tests. For example, we noted that “Pass” was assigned to a test result even when there was a clear chart failure and /or clear presence of artifacts in the thumbnail images. Although support material (videos, “cheat sheets”, manuals, and presentations) were provided, we believe that additional training on reviewing the website results would be beneficial. COVID-19 had a serious impact on the TMIST study, with many sites stopping screening for long periods (> 3 months), staff illness and burnout. A number of the sites put accrual on hold for extended periods, and a few ceased new recruitment of subjects to the trial. Large gaps in QC data points were seen, and when the sites returned to the TMIST QC program, it was often necessary to set new baselines, because system values drifted at some sites or unreported service interventions occurred during the downtime. 5. Conclusions The QC test results demonstrated that, overall, the tomosynthesis mammography equipment used in TMIST operates in a consistent and repeatable manner for all machine types. The tests were useful in verifying that the systems were operating correctly. It is encouraging that changing trends could be seen in certain parameters such as tube output (mAs) drifting preceding a tube failure. This suggests that detecting trends may serve as an early warning for incipient system failure, although further study is required to reliably detect these trends. Because the Automatic Exposure Control and display software can compensate for changes in equipment performance, subjective assessment of severity of artifacts, variability of system signal levels and noise characteristics are unreliable. Similarly, gradual degradation of performance, such as spatial resolution is difficult to detect subjectively. This motivates the use of quantitative tests like ASF and SDNR, which are easy to perform on a digital system and are not observer dependent. Our experience was that SDNR and other metrics frequently changed whenever there was a software or image processing algorithm change. There was added value in having the responsible site QC technologists review both the images and the web charts to encourage them to take ownership of the process, but the effectiveness of this is highly dependent on the motivation and diligence of each individual. Compression thickness errors are potentially a large source of variation in image quality and dose. We saw up to a 39 % difference in reported dose on the phantom when sites switched between the FAST and NORMAL paddle settings, because of differences in thickness readout. These differences in reported thickness can result in changes in the AEC behavior, such as a choosing a lower or higher kV. The change in beam quality could lead to changes in contrast and noise and deposited dose. As shown in our paper on compression thickness errors, there is also a clinical implication due to the exclusion of tissue from the reconstructed volume if the thickness is under-reported. A comprehensive evaluation of the compression thickness accuracy, or the effect of using a different compression paddle is not performed by most physicists during their surveys, so it is recommended that this test be included in any Mammographic Equipment Evaluation. Our charts provided much more data than would be needed in a regular QC program, and in future work we will present a suggested minimal set of tests. Further investigation of the long-term failure characteristics of digital mammography systems is advisable, and continued tracking of QC at TMIST sites will generate adequate statistics to enable the detection of trends. Since many changes in noise characteristics occur when software is upgraded or image processing filters are changed, it will be necessary to capture information

during their surveys, so it is recommended that this test be included in any Mammographic Equipment Evaluation. Our charts provided much more data than would be needed in a regular QC program, and in future work we will present a suggested minimal set of tests. Further investigation of the long-term failure characteristics of digital mammography systems is advisable, and continued tracking of QC at TMIST sites will generate adequate statistics to enable the detection of trends. Since many changes in noise characteristics occur when software is upgraded or image processing filters are changed, it will be necessary to capture information about such changes, available from “private tags” in the DICOM header to isolate the effect of trending changes caused by software upgrades and other minor system adjustments. Automated QC is effective and timely if it can be accomplished without the need for manual upload of images as was required in this clinical trial. Cloud based solutions which can meet the requirements for security of PHI are available. There is the opportunity to improve efficiency, reducing both labor costs and variability through automation of many of the routine QC tests, thereby allowing technologists to focus on imaging patients. It is worth mentioning that there are special challenges in creating and operating a physics QC program embedded within a large multisite clinical trial. The clinical environment of an imaging facility focusses on managing a demanding workload of imaging procedures (some within and others outside the study) and the time and effort required to carry out nonstandard QC activities and data submission is often viewed as extra labor and distraction from the primary mission. This is especially true when the equipment generally appears to be functioning well and reliably and failures are uncommon. For this reason there is a necessary tension between operating a comprehensive QC program and the cooperation of the participating sites in the study. In practice this drove several changes in the QC protocol over time, changes that attempted to relieve some of the labor burden of the QC procedures while attempting to ensure consistent imaging performance. In our program, these changes included: making the submission of DICOM FOR PROCESSING images optional and reducing required frequency of additional dedicated TMIST tests for systems that are demonstrating consistent performance. Finally, based on our experience in TMIST, we believe that it is reasonable to streamline QC for both tomosynthesis and digital mammography considerably. chunks.content: Background Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is a clinical condition where the placenta does not detach spontaneously during delivery and cannot be removed without causing significant bleeding [ , ]. Prior cesarean delivery (CD) and placenta previa are reported as important independent risk factors for the occurrence of PAS [ , ]. PAS is associated with a high risk of severe bleeding, peripartum hysterectomy, and potential complications during surgery, which can lead to high rates of maternal morbidity and mortality [ , ]. Accurate diagnosis of PAS is critical for preventing these complications and the management of PAS requires careful antenatal monitoring [ ]. Ultrasound is an essential first-line diagnostic tool for identifying PAS [ ]. Ultrasound is convenient and non-invasive and allows multiple assessments throughout pregnancy, facilitating vigilant monitoring of PAS and allowing prompt clinical intervention and treatment [ ]. However, the identification of the ultrasound features of PAS still depends on the expertise and skill of the sonographer [ ], as certain subtle nuances within the images are not easily discernible by visual inspection [ ]. Radiomics is a developing field of scientific research that aims to understand the complexities of lesions, including their heterogeneity, by carefully extracting and quantitatively analyzing radiological features obtained from medical images [ , ]. This methodology shows promise in aiding clinical problem-solving strategies [ ].Previous studies have reported the application of radiomics in placental diseases. Hu et al. [ ] developed and validated a clinical-radiomic model based on Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) T2WI images to predict PAS. The area under the curve (AUC) value of the model was 0.84 in both the training and testing cohorts. MRI is considered safe during pregnancy for certain conditions, but caution is advised [ , ]. Ultrasound examination remains the preferred technique for screening abnormalities in pregnant women, providing real-time imaging with good spatial resolution [ ].Ultrasound radiomics, an emerging image analysis technique, addresses this limitation by extracting numerous quantitative features from medical images that are imperceptible to visual inspection and converting them into actionable data for clinical decision support [ ]. To our knowledge, there are few studies on the construction of ultrasound radiomics models for predicting the occurrence of PAS [ ].To support accurate diagnosis of PAS and provide a basis for reasonable clinical decisions in PAS patients, as a two-center study, this study constructs a favorable and comprehensive nomogram prediction model by integrating clinical variables and ultrasound radiomics features. Materials and methods Patient This two-center retrospective study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University and Guizhou Anshun Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital. Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study. Pregnant women with placenta previa between January 2017 and December 2024 were enrolled from the two participating centers. According to the TRIPOD statement [ ], 190 patients from the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University were assigned to the training cohort. In comparison, 81 patients from Guizhou Anshun Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital constituted the external validation cohort. The patient recruitment flowchart is shown in Fig. . The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Ultrasound diagnosis of placenta previa; (2) Singleton pregnancy; (3) Ultrasound examination performed between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. The exclusion criteria were: (1) Poor-quality ultrasound images (insufficient for radiomic feature extraction), (2) Patients with incomplete clinical data, and (3) Fetal congenital malformations. Both participating centers function as regional tertiary referral hubs for high-risk obstetrics, including suspected PAS. Consequently, the enrolled population represents a clinically enriched cohort referred for specialized assessment and management, rather than an unselected population of all placenta previa cases. Clinical data available at or before the index ultrasound were collected, including maternal age years, blood pressure (mmHg), obstetric history (gravidity, parity, number of prior cesarean deliveries), and placental characteristics (location, previa subtype). Placenta previa definition and classification Placenta previa was defined and classified according to standard obstetric criteria [ ]. Placental location and subtype were documented based on the index ultrasound examination (28–32 weeks) for all patients. The subtypes included: placenta previa(placenta overlies the internal os to any degree). a low-lying placenta (the lower placental edge lies within 2 cm of the internal cervical os). For consistency in terminology, all cases meeting the diagnostic criteria for placenta previa (regardless of subtype) were included in the study. Ultrasound examination All ultrasound examinations from two centers were performed by GE Voluson E8 or E10 ultrasound instruments with a convex array probe (obstetric mode; frequency 3-5 MHz in obstetric mode). All pregnant women with placenta previa were independently examined by two senior sonographers with more than 10 years of experience in obstetric ultrasound. Two-dimensional grayscale images depicting the maximum longitudinal section of the placenta (focused on the

placental edge lies within 2 cm of the internal cervical os). For consistency in terminology, all cases meeting the diagnostic criteria for placenta previa (regardless of subtype) were included in the study. Ultrasound examination All ultrasound examinations from two centers were performed by GE Voluson E8 or E10 ultrasound instruments with a convex array probe (obstetric mode; frequency 3-5 MHz in obstetric mode). All pregnant women with placenta previa were independently examined by two senior sonographers with more than 10 years of experience in obstetric ultrasound. Two-dimensional grayscale images depicting the maximum longitudinal section of the placenta (focused on the placental lower edge and internal cervical os) were saved in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format and stored on a secure hard disk. Follow up All pregnant women who underwent the index ultrasound examination were followed up to obtain their pregnancy outcomes. Pregnant women with incomplete clinic data were excluded from the study. The definitive diagnosis of PAS was established based on intraoperative findings and pathological confirmation, which served as the reference standard for this study. Intraoperative diagnostic criteria for PAS [ ]:During cesarean section, the placenta is found to be densely adherent to the endometrium, with uncontrollable bleeding during placental removal; the placenta implanted into the myometrium requires removal via curettage; macroscopic invasion of the placenta through the full thickness of the uterine wall, even extending beyond the uterus to surrounding organs. Pathological diagnostic criteria for PAS [ ]: Under light microscopy, placental villi are observed invading the superficial myometrium or deeper into the myometrial layer, or reaching the uterine serosa or extra-serosal tissues. Intraoperative and pathological evaluations were performed independently by separate teams. In cases of discordance between intraoperative impressions and histopathological results, a consensus panel consisting of two senior obstetricians and one perinatal pathologist reviewed the operative notes, gross specimen photographs, and microscopic slides to determine the final diagnosis. Among the finally enrolled patients, the training cohort included 119 PAS-positive cases and 71 PAS-negative cases, while the external validation cohort comprised 52 PAS-positive cases and 29 PAS-negative cases (Table ). Among the 171 cases classified as PAS-positive, 168 (98.2%) were confirmed by histopathology. Three cases in the training cohort were classified as PAS-positive based on definitive intraoperative criteria and consensus panel review despite the unavailability of pathological specimens (due to patient declination after hysterectomy). All 100 PAS-negative cases included in the study were primarily confirmed by intraoperative clinical findings (spontaneous, complete placental separation without macroscopic signs of PAS). Additionally, postoperative pathological examination was performed for 42 of these 100 cases (42.0%)—due to concurrent indications such as suspected chorioamnionitis—and all pathological results were consistent with the absence of PAS. This study did not include cases managed with conservative strategies such as placenta left in situ or uterine artery embolization. Image segmentation, multi-center feature harmonization radiomics feature extraction Image acquisition and preprocessing This study included ultrasound images acquired from different scanning devices with variable imaging conditions. To enhance data comparability and improve model stability, preprocessing steps were performed following the guidelines of the Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI): (1) Grayscale normalization: Z-score normalization was applied to standardize pixel intensity distributions across cohorts. Additionally, grayscale values within each image were sorted and constrained to the 0.5–99.5 percentile range to exclude extreme outliers. (2) Spatial resampling: The original pixel spacing of images ranged from 0.38 to 0.62 mm across different devices. All images were resampled to a uniform pixel spacing of 0.50 × 0.50 mm using cubic interpolation, while segmentation masks were resampled using nearest-neighbor interpolation to preserve ROI boundary integrity. (3) Gray-level discretization: A fixed bin width of 25 was used for gray-level discretization, consistent with the default settings of Pyradiomics for ultrasound imaging. No additional denoising or smoothing filters were applied before feature extraction. (4) Wavelet feature derivation: Wavelet features were generated using a 3D Coiflet-1 wavelet filter, in accordance with IBSI recommendations. The full IBSI-compliant parameter settings for preprocessing and feature extraction are provided in Supplementary Table (PyRadiomics YAML file). ROI segmentation and reproducibility Assessment Ultrasound images for radiomics analysis were acquired by two experienced senior sonographers (X.T.S. and M.X.L., each with > 10 years of clinical experience) who performed imaging independently without access to patients’ clinical or pathological data. The region of interest (ROI) was manually segmented along the placental boundary using 3D Slicer (version 4.11, https://www.slicer.org/ ), with careful exclusion of the bladder, cervix, and surrounding soft tissues to avoid non-target tissue interference. To verify segmentation reproducibility, a stratified random sample of 20 cases was selected, balanced by placental accreta spectrum (PAS) status and placenta location. Intra- and inter-observer reproducibility were evaluated using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) [ ] and mask-overlap analysis: Intra-observer reproducibility: One sonographer (X.T.S.) first performed ROI segmentation on the 20 selected cases. Two months later, the same sonographer repeated

clinical or pathological data. The region of interest (ROI) was manually segmented along the placental boundary using 3D Slicer (version 4.11, https://www.slicer.org/ ), with careful exclusion of the bladder, cervix, and surrounding soft tissues to avoid non-target tissue interference. To verify segmentation reproducibility, a stratified random sample of 20 cases was selected, balanced by placental accreta spectrum (PAS) status and placenta location. Intra- and inter-observer reproducibility were evaluated using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) [ ] and mask-overlap analysis: Intra-observer reproducibility: One sonographer (X.T.S.) first performed ROI segmentation on the 20 selected cases. Two months later, the same sonographer repeated the segmentation process to minimize memory bias. Inter-observer reproducibility: A second independent sonographer (M.X.L.) segmented the same 20 cases following the same standardized protocol. A two-way random-effects ICC model with absolute agreement was used to quantify reproducibility, where an ICC ≥ 0.75 was considered indicative of good consistency. The intra-observer agreement showed high reliability (ICC = 0.88; 95% confidence interval CI: 0.84–0.92), and the inter-observer agreement demonstrated similar reproducibility (ICC = 0.83; 95% CI: 0.78–0.88). Mask-overlap analysis confirmed high spatial consistency, with intra- and inter-observer Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) of 0.89 and 0.85, respectively. Radiomics features with an ICC < 0.75 were excluded to ensure robustness, resulting in 651 reproducible features retained for subsequent model development. Multi-center feature harmonization Given that radiomics features may be affected by scanner-related heterogeneity even within the same vendor family, multi-center batch effects were formally evaluated and addressed: (1) Heterogeneity assessment: Feature distributions between centers were visually compared using density plots and statistically analyzed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. (2) Harmonization implementation: To mitigate scanner-related batch effects, ComBat harmonization (pyCombat implementation) was applied with “center” specified as the batch variable. To avoid information leakage, ComBat harmonization parameters were estimated exclusively using the training cohort (Center 1). The fitted ComBat transformation was then applied unchanged (“frozen”) to the external validation cohort (Center 2), without refitting and without incorporating any validation data or outcome information. Both harmonized and non-harmonized feature sets were used for model development to assess the robustness of the radiomics signature. (3) Sensitivity analysis: As a complementary approach, “center” was included as an additional covariate in multivariable logistic regression models to test whether scanner identity exerted an independent influence on predictive performance. Per-center model performance was also evaluated to further validate the harmonization effect. Notably, although both centers used GE Voluson E8 or E10 systems with similar image acquisition settings, potential scanner-related heterogeneity was still evaluated and addressed to ensure the generalizability of the radiomics signature. Feature selection and model development The workflow of radiomics analysis is depicted in Supplementary Material ( ) The full modeling pipeline (training-only fitting vs. external validation application without refitting) is shown in Supplementary Material ( ) All feature selection and model development steps were performed using the ComBat-harmonized radiomics feature set, where ComBat parameters were estimated on the training cohort and then applied unchanged to the external validation cohort. Clinical model development Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to calculate the odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) for each clinical factor. Clinical factors with a statistical significance of P < 0.05 were retained to construct the clinical model using logistic regression (LR). Radiomics feature extraction and selection Radiomics features were extracted using Pyradiomics, a Python-based open-source toolbox (implemented in Python 3.8.8; http://www.python.org ), which integrates a comprehensive set of predefined algorithms for feature extraction from ultrasound images. A total of 849 radiomics features were initially extracted, including shape features, first-order intensity features, texture features, and wavelet-filtered features. To minimize overfitting and select robust features, a two-step selection process was adopted as described in the literature [ ]: Univariate filtering: Independent samples t-test was performed to compare feature distributions between the case group (PAS-positive) and control group (PAS-negative). Features with no significant between-group differences ( P ≥ 0.05) were excluded. LASSO regression: The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) algorithm was applied to the remaining features for dimensionality reduction and optimal feature selection. The algorithm was implemented with 10-fold cross-validation, a maximum of 1000 iterations [ ], and the optimal regularization parameter (λ) was determined based on the 1-standard error (1-SE) criterion (Fig. ). Avoidance of information leakage and feature stability validation ComBat harmonization was fitted using training data only and then applied to the external validation cohort using the frozen parameters. To prevent information leakage, all preprocessing steps (including Z-score normalization, ICC-based feature filtering, univariate t-test filtering, and LASSO feature selection) were exclusively performed on the training cohort. After determining the optimal λ value, the radiomics model was refit on the full training cohort before external validation. To evaluate the stability of the feature selection process, 1000 bootstrap resamples were performed on the training cohort, and the selection frequency of each feature was recorded.

of information leakage and feature stability validation ComBat harmonization was fitted using training data only and then applied to the external validation cohort using the frozen parameters. To prevent information leakage, all preprocessing steps (including Z-score normalization, ICC-based feature filtering, univariate t-test filtering, and LASSO feature selection) were exclusively performed on the training cohort. After determining the optimal λ value, the radiomics model was refit on the full training cohort before external validation. To evaluate the stability of the feature selection process, 1000 bootstrap resamples were performed on the training cohort, and the selection frequency of each feature was recorded. The six retained radiomics features exhibited high stability, with selection frequencies ranging from 74% to 91%. For full reproducibility, the complete logistic regression coefficients (intercepts and predictor weights) for both the radiomics-only model and the combined clinical-radiomics model are presented in Supplementary Table . Evaluation of model efficacy and nomogram development The predictive performance of the model was evaluated using the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and area under the curve (AUC). The optimal cutoff values for the models were determined based on the Youden index. The DeLong test was used to compare the AUCs of the different models. Selected clinical independent risk factors were incorporated into the radiomics model to create the clinical-radiomic model. The clinical-radiomics model was visualized as a nomogram, and the calibration curve was used to assess the consistency between observed outcomes and predicted probabilities. The decision curve analysis (DCA) was employed to evaluate the net benefit of the model. In addition to AUC, comprehensive diagnostic metrics were calculated, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (LR+), and negative likelihood ratio (LR–). For each metric, 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using 1000 bootstrap resamples to enhance reliability. These metrics were reported at two types of thresholds: (1) the optimal threshold derived from the Youden index; (2) clinically meaningful risk thresholds (10–30%) that align with clinical decision-making for placental accreta spectrum (PAS) management. Calibration was assessed to evaluate the consistency between the model-predicted probabilities of PAS and the observed clinical outcomes. Three key calibration metrics were calculated: calibration-in-the-large (intercept), calibration slope, and Brier score (lower values indicate better calibration). Internal validation of calibration was performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples of the training cohort to obtain optimism-corrected estimates of calibration metrics and their 95% CIs. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was conducted to quantify the net clinical benefit of the three models across clinically meaningful threshold probabilities (10–30%). These thresholds correspond to critical decision points in PAS clinical practice: (1) ≥ 10% risk: referral to a tertiary PAS-specialized center; (2) ≥ 20% risk: preparation for potential cesarean hysterectomy or blood product mobilization; (3) ≥ 30% risk: activation of a multidisciplinary surgical team. Net benefit curves for the clinical model, radiomics model, and combined clinical-radiomics model were generated and compared against two extreme strategies (“treat-all patients” and “treat-no patients”). Additionally, risk distribution histograms were constructed to visualize the dispersion of predicted probabilities within the training and validation cohorts, providing insights into model stratification ability (Supplementary Material ). Statistical analysis We used the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) (version 26.0, IBM) to perform statistical analyses of clinical data and R (version 4.3.3, https://www.r-project.org ) to develop models. The median (Interquartile Range) of non-normally distributed continuous data was compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as numbers (percentages) and compared using the Chi-square test. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to selected clinical factors. ROC analysis, nomogram construction, calibration curve, and DCA were performed. DeLong test was performed to compare the AUCs of three models in the internal and external validation cohorts. A two-sided P -value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant in this study. Results Clinical characteristics of the patients A total of 271 pregnant women with placenta previa were included in this study. Center 1 ( n = 190) formed the training cohort, while center 2 ( n = 81) formed the external validation cohort, in a 2:1 ratio. There were 119 PAS-positive cases in the training cohort and 52 PAS-positive cases in the external validation cohort. The baseline clinical characteristics of patients in the training and external validation cohorts are shown in Table . There were significant differences between the PAS and non-PAS groups in gravidity, parity, and number of CD in the training cohort and the external validation cohort( p < 0.05). The distribution of placenta previa subtypes in the full cohort was: placenta previa 76.75%, and low-lying placenta 23.25%. Placental location was anterior in 56% and posterior in 44% of cases. Clinical model construction After univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses (Table ), the number of prior cesarean deliveries (CD) ( p < 0.001, OR: 3.82, 95%CI: 1.94–7.49) was identified

in the training and external validation cohorts are shown in Table . There were significant differences between the PAS and non-PAS groups in gravidity, parity, and number of CD in the training cohort and the external validation cohort( p < 0.05). The distribution of placenta previa subtypes in the full cohort was: placenta previa 76.75%, and low-lying placenta 23.25%. Placental location was anterior in 56% and posterior in 44% of cases. Clinical model construction After univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses (Table ), the number of prior cesarean deliveries (CD) ( p < 0.001, OR: 3.82, 95%CI: 1.94–7.49) was identified as the sole independent clinical predictor. Collinearity assessment using variance inflation factors (VIFs) showed all VIF values < 2.0, indicating no significant multicollinearity. The clinical model based on prior CD number exhibited moderate discriminatory performance: the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.728 (95% CI: 0.654–0.802) in the training cohort and 0.708 (95% CI: 0.599–0.816) in the external validation cohort (Table ; Fig. ). Sensitivity analyses using ridge and elastic-net logistic regression yielded AUC values nearly identical to the primary model (AUC difference < 0.01), confirming robustness. Additional sensitivity analysis evaluated the impact of maternal age. Although maternal age differed significantly between groups, age alone demonstrated only moderate discriminatory ability (AUC = 0.71). When incorporated into the multivariable model, age did not diminish the independent predictive contribution of the radiomics signature. A sensitivity analysis comparing an age-only model, a clinical model (age + parity), and the full clinical-radiomics model showed AUCs of 0.71, 0.76, and 0.82, respectively. Feature selection and radiomics model development In this study, a total of 849 radiomics features were extracted using the pyradiomics package in Python software. 651 features were retained for further analysis based on intra-observer and inter-observer correlation coefficients greater than 0.75, indicating good consistency. 307 features were retained in the training cohort based on T-test analysis. The remaining 307 features were further analyzed using the ten-fold cross-validated LASSO regression model, and the non-zero coefficient features were identified based on the one-standard-error criterion validation (Table ). Finally, six robust radiomics features were selected to construct the radiomics signature, comprising two shape features and four texture features derived from Gray Level Dependence Matrix (GLDM), Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), and Gray Level Run Length Matrix (GLRLM). (Fig. , Supplementary Material ) The Rad-score (RS) for each patient’s radiomics evaluation was calculated based on these features and their coefficients (Supplementary Material ). The radiomics model was constructed using logistic regression (LR) algorithm. The AUC was 0.853 (95% CI, 0.797–0.909) and 0.778 (95% CI, 0.672–0.884) in the training and external validation cohorts (Table ; Fig. ). Sensitivity analyses for multi-center radomics heterogeneity To address scanner-related and center-specific heterogeneity—a key challenge in multi-center radiomics studies—comprehensive sensitivity analyses were performed. ComBat harmonization was applied to calibrate radiomic features across centers, and the adjusted radiomics-only model yielded AUCs of 0.853 (training cohort) and 0.778 (external validation cohort), which were comparable to the original unadjusted model. Additionally, incorporating “center” as a covariate did not substantially alter model coefficients or diagnostic performance (AUC change < 0.01), confirming the radiomics signature’s robustness against center-specific biases. When evaluated by individual center, the radiomics model maintained stable diagnostic ability: Center 1 (training cohort, n = 190) achieved an AUC of 0.85, while Center 2 (external validation cohort, n = 81) had an AUC of 0.81. This indicated minimal impact of scanner-related variations on model performance. A prespecified subgroup analysis was conducted based on placental location (Table ). No significant interaction was observed between placental location and radiomics model performance (interaction p = 0.27). Model discrimination remained consistent across subgroups, with AUCs of 0.87 for anterior placentas and 0.82 for posterior placentas. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the radiomics signature is robust to multi-center heterogeneity and placental location variations, supporting its potential for clinical application across different institutions and patient subgroups. Nomogram development and efficacy evaluation To enhance preoperative predictive performance for PSA in pregnant women with placenta previa, we integrated the sole independent clinical risk factor (number of prior CD) with the radiomics signature to construct a combined clinical-radiomics model, which was visualized as a nomogram (Fig. ). Building on the radiomics-only model (AUC: 0.853 95% CI: 0.797–0.909 in the training cohort; 0.778 95% CI: 0.672–0.884 in the external validation cohort), the integration of prior CD number further improved diagnostic efficacy. The AUC increased to 0.859 (95% CI: 0.802–0.915) in the training cohort and 0.822 (95% CI: 0.724–0.920) in the external validation cohort (Fig. ). Delong test results indicated that the AUC improvement was not statistically significant in the training cohort ( P = 0.32) but reached statistical significance in the external validation cohort ( P = 0.036), confirming the added value of incorporating clinical factors in multi-center validation. The AUC increased to 0.859 (95% CI: 0.802–0.915) in the training cohort and 0.822 (95% CI: 0.724–0.920) in the external validation cohort (Fig. ). Delong test results indicated that the AUC improvement was not statistically significant in the training cohort ( P = 0.32) but reached statistical significance in the external validation cohort ( P = 0.036), confirming the added value of incorporating clinical factors in multi-center validation. Additional performance metrics are presented in Supplementary Table . At the Youden index threshold, the combined model achieved high sensitivity and specificity in both cohorts, with favorable positive (LR+) and negative (LR–) likelihood ratios. It should be noted that the PPV and NPV are influenced by the high prevalence of PAS in our study cohorts (≈ 64%). In clinical settings with a lower prevalence of PAS among all placenta previa patients, the PPV would be lower and the NPV higher for the same test characteristics. Its performance remained acceptable across clinically relevant probability thresholds (10–30%), supporting its applicability in clinical decision-making. Calibration assessment confirmed the reliability of the combined model: calibration-in-the-large values were close to 0, calibration slopes were near 1.0 (training: 0.98; external validation: 1.03), and Brier scores were low (training: 0.12; external validation: 0.15). Hosmer-Lemeshow tests yielded non-significant results in both the training ( p = 0.686) and external validation ( p = 0.953) cohorts, indicating good agreement between predicted and observed outcomes (Fig. a and b). Bootstrap internal validation (1000 resamples) showed minimal optimism (AUC difference < 0.01), further validating the model’s stability. Decision curve analysis (DCA) revealed that the nomogram provided the highest net benefit among the three models (Fig. a and b). At clinically relevant thresholds (10%, 20%, 30%), the combined model outperformed both single-modality models and the “treat-all”/“treat-none” strategies. In the training cohort, the combined model’s net benefit values were 0.21, 0.31, and 0.36 at these thresholds, compared with 0.11–0.24 for the radiomics-only model and 0.05–0.18 for the clinical-only model. Corresponding net benefit values in the external validation cohort were 0.18, 0.27, and 0.33. Supplementary Material shows risk distribution histograms with clear separation between PAS-positive and PAS-negative cases, further validating the model’s discriminatory ability. Discussion In this two-center study, we developed and validated predictive models for PAS in patients with placenta previa. Our key findings demonstrated that the number of prior cesarean deliveries (CD)emerged as the ‌sole independent clinical predictor, while six radiomics features-comprising shape, and texture measures-demonstrated significant associations with PAS risk. By integrating this clinical factor with the selected radiomics features, we constructed a clinical-radiomics nomogram. The results demonstrated good performance and clinical utility of this nomogram in diagnosing PAS in both the training and external validation cohorts. The incidence of PAS is currently on the rise, possibly due to the increasing rate of cesarean Sect [ ]. PAS is associated with severe maternal and fetal adverse outcomes, including massive hemorrhage and peripartum hysterectomy, underscoring the need for accurate preoperative prediction. Radiomics, a burgeoning quantitative imaging too, has been widely applied in tumor identification and disease prognosis analysis [ , ]. Previous studies have applied radiomics in evaluating the PAS [ ], and the results demonstrate that radiomics models constructed from imaging data have shown high efficacy in predicting the occurrence of PAS. Romeo et al. [ ] were the first to use radiomic features for machine learning and applied them to predict the occurrence of PAS in patients with anterior placenta previa. However, their study only utilized radiomic features to construct a radiomics model and did not evaluate with clinical factors. Hu et al. [ ] included patients diagnosed with PAS based on pathological and clinical criteria and successfully constructed a clinical-radiomics model by combining radiomic features and clinical factors, demonstrating good efficacy. Ultrasound is a more convenient and safe imaging modality commonly used in prenatal care. In our study, radiomics features of ultrasound images were extracted from two-dimensional gray-scale ultrasound images, and clinical-radiomics models were built based on these ultrasound images. We validated the model using two-center data and the results indicated its robust predictive performance. We ultimately selected six optimal radiomic features, including two shape descriptors and four texture features (e.g., LargeDependenceHighGrayLevelEmphasis, LargeAreaHighGrayLevelEmphasis), which primarily quantify placental textural heterogeneity and structural irregularity. In the context of PAS, these features are thought to capture underlying pathological alterations, such as the disorganized villous invasion, heterogeneous vascularization, and loss of the normal placental architecture, which manifest as increased echotexture complexity and spatial disorder on ultrasound images. In our study, we noticed that the same feature, LargeDependenceHighGrayLevelEmphasis (LDHGLE), was extracted under two different filter conditions (original and Wavelet). LDHGLE, a feature from the Gray Level Dependence Matrix (GLDM), quantifies the prevalence of large, interconnected areas with high echogenicity (brightness) within the placenta. We hypothesize that elevated LDHGLE values may biologically correspond to regions of focal fibrin deposition, aberrant villous clusters with dense stroma, or areas of disordered vascularization, all of which contribute to increased placental tissue heterogeneity. This heightened structural complexity and echotexture irregularity, as captured by LDHGLE, is a hallmark of the aberrant trophoblastic invasion in PAS. It is a part of The Gray Level Dependence Matrix (GLDM) feature, GLDM has been confirmed to be associated with tumor heterogeneity [ ], utilized in numerous studies for prognostic and response prediction purposes in diseases such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cervical cancer [ ]. LDHGLE is thought to be associated with changes in placental heterogeneity based on our studies. Our model has several advantages. Firstly, we reduced image variations caused by different ultrasound machines through image standardization, ensuring the reproducibility of the study. Given that our data were collected from two centers, we also assessed the potential influence of scanner-related heterogeneity. ComBat harmonization and center-adjusted analyses yielded AUCs that were nearly identical to those of primary model, and per-center performance remained stable, indicating that acquisition differences between the two GE Voluson systems did not materially affect the robustness of the radiomics signature. Secondly, the integration of clinical factors led to a statistically significant improvement in AUC in the external validation cohort; meanwhile, the combined model achieved the highest AUC and net benefit in both cohorts, supporting its clinical value. Decision curve analysis further supports the clinical applicability of the proposed model. At threshold probabilities commonly used to guide management of suspected PAS, the combined model provided consistently higher net benefit than isolated clinical or radiomic predictors. This suggests that the model could assist clinicians in determining which patients warrant referral to a tertiary PAS center, early multidisciplinary planning, or enhanced peripartum blood-product preparation. The risk distribution histograms demonstrated clear separation between PAS and non-PAS groups, highlighting the potential value of the model in real-world triage and operative planning. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, as a retrospective analysis, the studyis subject to inherent selection bias, and the moderate sample size may limit the statistical power and generalizability of the results. Second, although both participating centers used GE Voluson E8/E10 platforms, residual heterogeneity in image acquisition, including depth, gain settings, acoustic attenuation, and operator-dependent technique, may influence radiomics feature behavior. Maternal BMI and placental depth may also affect image quality, particularly for deeper or posterior placentas. Third, although ComBat harmonization and center-stratified analyses suggested that scanner-related variability had minimal influence on model performance, most included cases involved anterior placenta previa, and relatively few women lacked a history of cesarean delivery. Thus, generalizability to posterior placenta previa and to women with an unscarred uterus remains uncertain. Fourth, although dimensionality reduction via LASSO and multi-step feature filtering were used to mitigate overfitting, the high dimensionality of radiomics features relative to the sample size may still contribute to model optimism. To address this, bootstrap internal validation was performed, but future studies should include larger, prospective multicenter cohorts with standardized acquisition protocols to further strengthen reproducibility. Fifth, the high prevalence of PAS in our cohorts reflects their origin from tertiary referral centers specializing in high-risk placental disorders. When applied to a lower-prevalence, screening-oriented population (e.g., all patients diagnosed with placenta previa in a general obstetric ultrasound unit), the absolute probability estimates from the nomogram would require careful interpretation, and the PPV would be expected to decrease. Therefore, consecutively enrolled cohorts with a prevalence closer to the general population. Finally, this study relied solely on grayscale two-dimensional ultrasound images. Incorporating Doppler-based hemodynamic features, elastography, or three-dimensional

When applied to a lower-prevalence, screening-oriented population (e.g., all patients diagnosed with placenta previa in a general obstetric ultrasound unit), the absolute probability estimates from the nomogram would require careful interpretation, and the PPV would be expected to decrease. Therefore, consecutively enrolled cohorts with a prevalence closer to the general population. Finally, this study relied solely on grayscale two-dimensional ultrasound images. Incorporating Doppler-based hemodynamic features, elastography, or three-dimensional ultrasound radiomics may enhance diagnostic performance in future work. Conclusions In summary, we developed and externally validated a clinical-ultrasound radiomics nomogram for predicting placenta accreta spectrum in women with placenta previa. By integrating quantitative radiomic features with the number of prior cesarean deliveries, the combined model demonstrated favorable discrimination, good calibration, and meaningful clinical utility in both centers. This two-center study supports the feasibility of ultrasound-based radiomics for PAS risk stratification and may assist clinicians in preoperative planning, multidisciplinary coordination, and individualized management. Future prospective multicenter studies with standardized ultrasound acquisition and incorporation of Doppler or 3D imaging are warranted to further enhance reproducibility and generalizability. chunks.content: Background Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a pregnancy-related condition characterized by glucose intolerance, which can result in hyperglycemia [ , ]. This condition has been associated with a spectrum of adverse fetal outcomes, including macrosomia, birth trauma, and neonatal hypoglycemia [ , ]. The global prevalence of GDM is on the rise; in 2021, the worldwide incidence of diabetes during pregnancy was reported to be 21.1 million cases, with GDM accounting for 80.3% of these cases [ ]. Given the increasing global incidence of GDM, its impact on childbirth has become an area of growing concern for healthcare professionals [ – ]. Preliminary microscopic studies on the impact of GDM on umbilical cord histology reveal significant structural alterations, including endothelial lining rupture, increased permeability, hemorrhages in umbilical arteries, and dilation of the umbilical vein, alongside degeneration of smooth muscle fibers in vessel walls and disrupted fiber distribution with large empty spaces in Wharton’s jelly [ , ]. It is also established that GDM can substantially influence fetal metabolism, potentially leading to challenges with glucose regulation in neonates [ , ]. Furthermore, impaired placental function in GDM can affect fetal oxygen delivery [ , ]. These findings indicate that GDM may disrupt fetal oxygenation, increasing the risk of neonatal complications and potentially influencing long-term health outcomes [ , ]. Umbilical cord arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis has become an essential diagnostic tool for evaluating the respiratory and metabolic status of neonates at birth [ – ]. By assessing key parameters such as the potential of hydrogen (pH), partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO 2 ), partial pressure of oxygen (PO 2 ), bicarbonate (HCO 3 ), and base deficit (BD), it provides critical insights into the newborn’s acid-base balance, oxygenation adequacy, and potential metabolic disturbances [ – ]. This information is crucial for identifying conditions like hypoxia, respiratory acidosis, or metabolic acidosis [ ]. These conditions can be associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, including hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, long-term neurodevelopmental impairments, and longer neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, highlighting the importance of umbilical ABG analysis in timely diagnosis and intervention [ – ]. Previous studies on umbilical artery ABG in GDM pregnancies have yielded contrasting results, with some indicating no significant pH changes but reduced PO 2 and PCO 2 , alongside elevated lactate levels in GDM neonates [ ], while others report higher rates of umbilical cord blood acidosis in term GDM pregnancies [ ]. Therefore, there is a clear gap in understanding the effects of GDM on umbilical ABG, which directly reflects fetal oxygenation status, highlighting the need for further research to clarify these critical aspects. This study aimed to investigate differences in umbilical cord ABG values (pH, PCO 2 , PO 2 , HCO 3 , and BD) between term pregnancies with and without GDM undergoing elective cesarean section. As a secondary objective, neonatal outcomes (including birthweight, 1-minute and 5-minute Apgar scores, resuscitation at birth, and NICU admission) were compared between the two groups. We hope this study’s findings could offer critical insights into the impact of GDM on placental function and fetal oxygenation, informing clinical practice and optimizing management strategies for pregnancies complicated by GDM. Methods Study design and setting This retrospective cohort study included all consecutive eligible patients who underwent elective cesarean sections at term across four referral university-based hospitals in Iran. The study spanned from January 1, 2024, to July 1, 2024, and involved hospitals in four cities: (a) Yas Hospital Complex, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran; (b) Al-Zahra Hospital, Guilan University of Medical Sciences, Rasht, Iran; (c) Razi Hospital, Jundishapur University of Medical Sciences, Ahvaz, Iran; and (d) Shahid Beheshti Hospital, Isfahan University of Medical Sciences, Isfahan, Iran. The medical records of these patients were reviewed for eligibility, and data collection was conducted on those who met the inclusion criteria. The study adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines [ ]. Ethical considerations The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board (IRB) and the ethics committee of Tehran University of Medical Sciences (reference code: IR.TUMS.MEDICINE.REC.1403.117). All study stages strictly followed the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki [ ]. At the time of admission, informed verbal and written consent was obtained from all participants for the anonymous use and publication of their data. Eligibility criteria We reviewed the medical records from the four participating hospitals to identify all consecutive eligible singleton-term pregnancies (gestational age ≥ 37 weeks) that underwent elective cesarean section between January 1, 2024, and July 1, 2024. Elective cesarean sections were performed for various clinical reasons, including a history of previous cesarean delivery, breech or other abnormal fetal presentations, fetal macrosomia, and maternal factors such as personal preference, prior retinal detachment, or a history of myomectomy. The strict eligibility criteria

Eligibility criteria We reviewed the medical records from the four participating hospitals to identify all consecutive eligible singleton-term pregnancies (gestational age ≥ 37 weeks) that underwent elective cesarean section between January 1, 2024, and July 1, 2024. Elective cesarean sections were performed for various clinical reasons, including a history of previous cesarean delivery, breech or other abnormal fetal presentations, fetal macrosomia, and maternal factors such as personal preference, prior retinal detachment, or a history of myomectomy. The strict eligibility criteria of including only term pregnancies undergoing elective cesarean sections in our study were designed to examine a more homogeneous population of neonates. This approach allowed us to directly assess the effects of GDM on neonatal ABG findings while minimizing the confounding effects of variables such as gestational age at birth and mode of delivery, which are known to influence ABG results [ , ]. Given the high volume of elective cesarean sections performed in our study centers, we specifically chose this population for analysis. Elective cesarean sections, unlike emergency procedures, are performed in controlled settings with lower-risk pregnancies or based on maternal preference. This environment allows for a systematic assessment of neonatal outcomes immediately after birth [ , ]. Thus, we aimed to investigate the association of GDM with umbilical cord ABG findings in this specific population, minimizing potential confounding from other comorbidities and delivery-related factors. The exclusion criteria included maternal age under 18 or over 45 years, multiple pregnancies, vaginal delivery or emergency cesarean section during the current pregnancy, gestational age at delivery below 37 weeks, maternal history of pre-existing diabetes mellitus, maternal history of hypertensive, thyroid, metabolic, malignant, or autoimmune disorders, maternal smoking, opioid, or alcohol use during the current pregnancy, occurrence of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, or premature rupture of membranes during the current pregnancy, confirmed diagnosis of intrauterine growth restriction, unavailable umbilical cord ABG analysis data, and patient refusal to consent to the anonymous publication of their data. Additionally, we excluded cases diagnosed with GDM before weeks 24–28 of gestation outside the International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) [ ] criteria for routine GDM screening. Data collection The following data were collected from each study participant: (a) demographic information including age and body mass index (BMI); (b) obstetric history such as gravidity, prior abortions, molar pregnancies, and cesarean sections; (c) current pregnancy details, including the type of conception (spontaneous or assisted reproductive techniques), gestational age at delivery, diagnosis of GDM, and GDM management (lifestyle modification or medical treatment with insulin); (d) umbilical cord ABG analysis results, including pH, PCO 2 , PO 2 , HCO 3 , and BD; and (e) neonatal outcomes, including sex, birth weight, 1- and 5-minute Apgar scores, need for resuscitation at birth, and NICU admission. GDM was diagnosed uniformly across all participating centers based on the guidelines of IADPSG [ ]. Routine glycemic screening for GDM was conducted between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation, using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). For this test, venous blood samples were taken at fasting and 1 and 2 h after consuming a 75 g oral glucose load. The diagnosis of GDM was confirmed if at least one of the following glucose levels was observed: (a) fasting glucose ≥ 92 mg/dL, (b) 1-hour glucose ≥ 180 mg/dL, or (c) 2-hour glucose ≥ 153 mg/dL. Study outcomes The primary objective of this study was to compare umbilical cord ABG findings between pregnancies with and without GDM. A standardized protocol for umbilical cord blood collection was implemented across all four participating hospitals. This protocol involved immediate double-clamping of the umbilical cord at delivery, collection of blood from the umbilical artery using pre-heparinized syringes, and prompt analysis using calibrated blood gas analyzers at each site. Additionally, as secondary outcomes of our study, we aimed to compare neonatal outcomes between the GDM and non-GDM cohorts. These outcomes included birthweight, 1-minute and 5-minute Apgar scores, the need for neonatal resuscitation at birth, and rates of NICU admissions. Statistical analysis The statistical analyses were conducted using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS ® , IBM ® , Armonk, NY, USA), statistics software, version 25.0. Categorical data were presented as frequencies (percentages), while continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation [95% confidence interval]. To compare categorical variables between the study groups, the Chi-square test and Fisher’s exact test were used. For continuous variables, the independent t-test was employed. Additionally, Levene’s test for equality of variances was conducted for each independent t-test, and its results were considered when interpreting the t-test outcomes. A P-value of < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant for all analyses. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we adjusted

To compare categorical variables between the study groups, the Chi-square test and Fisher’s exact test were used. For continuous variables, the independent t-test was employed. Additionally, Levene’s test for equality of variances was conducted for each independent t-test, and its results were considered when interpreting the t-test outcomes. A P-value of < 0.05 was deemed statistically significant for all analyses. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we adjusted for multiple confounders, including age, BMI, gravidity, gestational age at delivery, and type of conception. For categorical variables that showed statistically significant differences between the GDM and non-GDM cohorts, we performed separate binomial multivariate logistic regression analyses. Additionally, we used multiple linear regression analyses for continuous variables with significant mean differences between the groups to account for potential confounding effects. It is noteworthy that in the logistic regression analyses assessing neonatal outcomes, the presence of an umbilical cord arterial pH < 7.2 was also included in the multivariate model to examine the independent predictive ability of GDM for these outcomes. Multicollinearity was assessed for all regression analyses using variance inflation factor and tolerance values, ensuring no significant multicollinearity among predictors. A P-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Furthermore, to assess the potential effects of GDM treatment on umbilical cord ABG findings and neonatal outcomes, we repeated the same analyses, comparing GDM pregnancies managed with lifestyle modifications versus those managed with medical anti-diabetic agents (insulin). Results Enrollment data Data from 658 singleton-term pregnancies were collected from four hospitals between January 1, 2024, and July 1, 2024. After reviewing their medical records against the eligibility criteria, 228 patients were excluded, leaving a total of 430 participants for inclusion in this study. A detailed breakdown of the data collection process and reasons for exclusion is illustrated in Fig. . The mean maternal age of the cohort was 31.8 ± 6.3 years, with a mean gestational age at delivery of 38.4 ± 0.8 weeks. Among the participants, 87 (20.2%) were diagnosed with GDM during their current pregnancy, while the remaining 343 (79.8%) did not have GDM. The detailed characteristics of the study participants are summarized in Table . The GDM cohort was significantly older than the non-GDM cohort (33.2 ± 6.0 vs. 31.4 ± 6.3 years; P-value = 0.014), with a higher proportion of pregnancies resulting from assisted reproductive techniques compared to the non-GDM cohort (21.8% vs. 11.1%; P-value = 0.008). However, no significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of BMI, gravidity, or gestational age at delivery (P-values > 0.05). Table provides a comprehensive comparison of the baseline characteristics of the GDM and non-GDM cohorts. Umbilical cord ABG findings The GDM cohort demonstrated significantly lower mean pH (7.33 ± 0.08 vs. 7.36 ± 0.06; P-value = 0.006) and greater BD (-1.82 ± 3.79 vs. -0.50 ± 2.74 mEq/L; P-value = 0.003) compared to the non-GDM group, with both remaining significant after adjusting for confounders (P-values = 0.001 and < 0.001, respectively). However, no significant differences were found for PCO 2 (47.59 ± 9.92 vs. 44.88 ± 19.81 mmHg; P = 0.215), PO 2 (13.13 ± 5.33 vs. 13.05 ± 5.74 mmHg; P-value = 0.902), or HCO 3 (22.85 ± 3.10 vs. 22.95 ± 2.58 mEq/L; P-value = 0.760) between the two cohorts (Table ). The results of our subgroup analysis of the GDM cohort, stratified by treatment approach (lifestyle modifications or medical therapy), are presented in Table . Our findings indicate no significant differences between the lifestyle modifications and medical management groups in umbilical cord ABG parameters, including pH, PCO 2 , PO 2 , HCO 3 , and BD (P-values > 0.05). Neonatal outcomes No significant differences were observed in the mean birthweight, 1-minute, or 5-minute Apgar scores between the GDM and non-GDM cohorts (P-values > 0.05). However, a significantly higher percentage of neonates in the GDM group required resuscitation at birth (28.7% vs. 12.0%; P-value < 0.001) and NICU admission (34.5% vs. 16.9%; P-value < 0.001). These differences remained significant after adjusting for potential confounders, including maternal age, BMI, gravidity, gestational age at delivery, type of conception, and presence of an umbilical cord arterial pH < 7.2 (both P-values = 0.006) (Table ). Our further subgroup analysis, based on the GDM treatment method, found no significant differences in mean birthweight between the lifestyle modification and medication treatment groups (P-value = 0.062). However, we observed significantly higher 1-minute Apgar scores (8.2 ± 1.2 vs. 7.2 ± 1.3; P-value = 0.001) and 5-minute Apgar scores (9.4 ± 0.7 vs. 8.8 ± 1.0; P-value = 0.001), as well as a lower rate of resuscitation at birth

potential confounders, including maternal age, BMI, gravidity, gestational age at delivery, type of conception, and presence of an umbilical cord arterial pH < 7.2 (both P-values = 0.006) (Table ). Our further subgroup analysis, based on the GDM treatment method, found no significant differences in mean birthweight between the lifestyle modification and medication treatment groups (P-value = 0.062). However, we observed significantly higher 1-minute Apgar scores (8.2 ± 1.2 vs. 7.2 ± 1.3; P-value = 0.001) and 5-minute Apgar scores (9.4 ± 0.7 vs. 8.8 ± 1.0; P-value = 0.001), as well as a lower rate of resuscitation at birth (17.0% vs. 42.5%; P-value < 0.001) in the lifestyle group compared to the medication group. These differences remained significant after adjusting for potential confounders, including maternal age, BMI, gravidity, gestational age at delivery, type of conception, and presence of an umbilical cord arterial pH < 7.2 (P-values = 0.010, 0.021, and 0.021, respectively). Additionally, the lifestyle management group had a significantly lower rate of NICU admissions compared to the medication group (23.4% vs. 47.5%; P-value = 0.018), although this difference did not remain significant after adjustment for confounders (P-value = 0.066) (Table ). Discussion Our findings demonstrated a significantly lower pH and greater BD in the umbilical cord blood of pregnancies complicated by GDM compared to non-GDM pregnancies. However, it is noteworthy that while the observed difference in umbilical cord pH is statistically significant (7.33 vs. 7.36), it may not represent a substantial clinical difference. Nonetheless, these results suggest that fetuses from GDM pregnancies may experience impaired oxygenation and a higher risk of hypoxia, contributing to increased umbilical cord blood acidity. While research on the impact of GDM on umbilical cord ABG findings is limited, existing studies align with our results. A prospective cohort study of 593 non-diabetic and 80 GDM pregnancies reported a higher incidence of umbilical cord acidosis in GDM cases, with cord blood acidosis independently linked to adverse neonatal outcomes [ ]. Also, another study analyzed data from a total of 2081 pregnancies undergoing elective cesarean sections and found a greater prevalence of acidemia in neonates born to mothers with GDM, further supporting our study’s findings [ ]. The development of fetal acidosis in GDM is primarily driven by the hyperglycemic environment resulting from maternal insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance. In GDM, elevated maternal blood glucose levels transfer excess glucose across the placenta to the fetus [ ]. This excessive glucose stimulates the fetal pancreas to produce increased amounts of insulin, a condition known as fetal hyperinsulinemia [ , ]. While insulin enables the fetus to utilize glucose for energy and storage, the abundance of glucose simultaneously increases fetal metabolic activity [ ]. A key consequence of this enhanced metabolic activity is an increased demand for oxygen [ ]. However, GDM affects not only fetal metabolism but also placental function. One of the principal consequence of GDM is the development of placental insufficiency [ ]. In GDM-affected pregnancies, the placenta may undergo both structural and functional alterations, including villous immaturity, thickening of the villous membrane, and decreased placental blood flow [ ]. These changes impair the placenta’s capacity to efficiently transfer oxygen from the mother to the fetus [ ]. As a result, chronic fetal hypoxia may develop, creating conditions favorable for the onset of metabolic acidosis. In addition to these structural abnormalities, GDM also is associated with altered placental expression of growth factors and cytokines, triggering inflammatory responses and oxidative stress [ , ]. These inflammatory processes can further degrade placental tissue, worsening placental insufficiency [ ]. Oxidative stress, in particular, may lead to endothelial dysfunction within the placenta, further hindering blood flow and nutrient exchange between the maternal and fetal circulations [ , ]. During episodes of hypoxia, the fetus begins to metabolize stored glycogen and fatty acids for energy. This metabolic shift generates acidic byproducts, such as ketones, which contribute to the development of acidosis [ ]. The cumulative effect of these pathways results in a reduction in fetal blood pH, a hallmark of acidosis that can be identified through fetal arterial ABG analysis. The clinical implications of umbilical cord acidosis in neonates born to mothers with GDM are substantial and necessitate careful scrutiny. Evidence indicates that neonates from GDM pregnancies have significantly lower umbilical cord pH levels compared to those born to non-diabetic mothers, underscoring the potential for adverse neonatal outcomes. Umbilical cord acidosis reflects chronic fetal hypoxia and metabolic stress, which can precipitate complications such as neonatal hypoglycemia, respiratory distress syndrome, and impaired cardiac function [ , ]. Additionally, the presence of acidosis may be associated with long-term neurodevelopmental issues, including an elevated risk of cerebral palsy and cognitive deficits [ , ].
