chunks.content: Introduction The US National Lung Cancer Screening Trial (NLST) and other randomized clinical trials in Europe , , , have shown that low-dose (LD) computed tomography (CT) is a viable screening tool for reducing lung cancer mortality among long-term smokers. However, screening entails harms in the form of false-positive screening test referrals and follow-up diagnostics. The efficiency of cancer screening using CT depends in part on optimized criteria for reporting and managing lung nodules; therefore, radiologic and oncologic expert societies have developed guidelines , , , , for using nodule characteristics as predictors of malignancy and as decision-making indicators to guide further diagnostic work. For nodules detected by CT for which there is an absence of information on nodule growth, several research groups have developed statistical models to determine the likelihood of malignancy based on radiologic features and patient-related attributes, such as age, sex, smoking history, presence of emphysema or other respiratory diseases, and personal or family history of cancer. Initial models were based on data from clinical settings, such as at the Mayo Clinic, US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) clinics, or Peking University People’s Hospital (PKUPH). However, these models were fitted to data from patients with high pretest probability of malignancy, focused on larger, mostly solid and often solitary nodules detected incidentally or in symptomatic individuals, and may overestimate malignancy risk for nodules detected in screening contexts. Malignancy prediction models were first developed in a screening setting at Brock University, Toronto, Canada, using data from prevalence screenings in the Pan-Canadian Early Detection of Lung Cancer Study (PanCan) LDCT screening trial. Initial PanCan models (sometimes also referred to as Brock models ) were generated using either a parsimonious (hereafter, PanCan-1 ) or a comprehensive (hereafter, PanCan-2 ) approach for variable selection without (PanCan-1a and PanCan-2a) or with (PanCan-1b and PanCan-2b) nodule spiculation among the radiologic variables. The more comprehensive model including spiculation, PanCan-2b, was recently updated by replacing nodule diameter with multidimensional measurements: mean diameter (PanCan-MD) or volume (PanCan-VOL). Independently of PanCan, a new model was developed recently in the context of the UK Lung Cancer Screening (UKLS) trial using nodule volume. The PanCan models have been externally validated for discrimination in the NLST , and Danish Lung Cancer Screening Trial, but they have not been externally validated for calibration. The recent UKLS model has not been externally validated, to our knowledge. Using data from the German Lung Cancer Screening Intervention (LUSI) trial, , we evaluated the earlier and more recent versions of the PanCan models, as well as the UKLS model, in terms of discrimination ability, calibration, and operational performance (eg, sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive values). For comparison, we also present findings for the Mayo Clinic, VA, and PKUPH models, as well as for pulmonary nodules first observed in follow-up (ie, incidence) screenings. Methods Study Design and Participants The LUSI trial , is a screening trial among adults aged 50 to 69 years with a history of heavy smoking (defined as ≥25 years of smoking ≥15 cigarettes per day or ≥30 years smoking ≥10 cigarettes per day and ≤10 years since smoking cessation) randomized into a screening intervention group, which included an LD multislice CT scan at time of randomization and 4 annual follow-up screening examinations, and a control group with no intervention. Participants were recruited as a random sample from population registries in Heidelberg, Germany, and surrounding areas and were assigned to the CT screening group or the control group. All participants provided written informed consent. The LUSI trial was approved by the ethics committee of the University of Heidelberg and the German Federal Office for Radiation Protection. This analysis of LUSI trial data is covered under the original ethical board approval per regulations of the ethics committee of the University of Heidelberg. This study followed the Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy ( STARD ) reporting guideline for diagnostic studies. Image Acquisition and Reading Computed tomography scans were obtained using a Toshiba 16-row scanner from October 23, 2007, to December 31, 2009, or a Siemens 128-row scanner from March 18, 2010, until the end of the screening phase of the LUSI trial on May 25, 2016. We used Median computer-aided detection software (Median Technologies) to read CT images, and nodule measures were derived, with largest diameter given in millimeters, perpendicular diameter given in millimeters, and volume given in millimeters-cubed. Perifissural nodules with oval or triangular shape and/or smooth delineations were excluded under the assumption that they were lymphatic nodules. Further data collected for each CT scan included nodule identifier, location, type (ie, solid or subsolid), shape and border characteristics (eg, presence of spiculation, translucence), and calcification. Presence of emphysema was determined on CT images using a densitometry method. Nodule Evaluation and Management All CT images were evaluated by 2 trained chest radiologists (including S.D.), and

read CT images, and nodule measures were derived, with largest diameter given in millimeters, perpendicular diameter given in millimeters, and volume given in millimeters-cubed. Perifissural nodules with oval or triangular shape and/or smooth delineations were excluded under the assumption that they were lymphatic nodules. Further data collected for each CT scan included nodule identifier, location, type (ie, solid or subsolid), shape and border characteristics (eg, presence of spiculation, translucence), and calcification. Presence of emphysema was determined on CT images using a densitometry method. Nodule Evaluation and Management All CT images were evaluated by 2 trained chest radiologists (including S.D.), and decisions were made based on nodule size and growth (in cases of nodules that had previously been recorded) (eTable 1 in the ). Participants with a lung cancer diagnosis made later than 1 year after the last CT scan or for whom the malignant nodule(s) could not be identified in earlier CT images were excluded. Spirometry Data In all study participants, spirometry was performed using MasterScreen IOS (VIASYS Healthcare) to determine 1-second forced expiratory volume (FEV 1 ) and forced vital capacity (FVC), and FEV 1 to FVC ratios were calculated from the largest FEV 1 and FVC values recorded in any 1 of 2 repeated assessments. Detailed descriptions of imaging, nodule, and lung function assessments are given in the eAppendix in the . Statistical Analysis All nodules detected during screening were analyzed using data from the LDCT image in which they were first seen. For participant-related characteristics, we used the Mann-Whitney U test for differences in continuous data and the χ 2 test or Fisher exact test for categorical data, as appropriate. For differences in nodule-specific characteristics, we used mixed-effects logistic regression with participant as the random effect. We applied 8 models from 6 published studies to our data to calculate the probability of nodule malignancy (eTable 2 in the ): 4 PanCan models (PanCan-1b : parsimonious model including spiculation; PanCan-2b : full model including spiculation; PanCan-MD : PanCan-2b with the mean of the largest and perpendicular diameters as nodule size; and PanCan-VOL : PanCan-2b with nodule volume as nodule size), the recently developed UKLS model ; and the models developed in VA clincs, the Mayo Clinic, and PKUPH clinics. We explored associations of radiologic parameters and participant-related characteristics with risk of nodule malignancy by fitting multivariable logistic regression models via generalized estimating equations using prevalence and incidence screening rounds combined and accounting for the correlation structure of multiple pulmonary nodules per individual on the LUSI data. Model selection was based on the quasi–Akaike Information Criterion (eAppendix in the ). For each selected model, the ability to discriminate nodules by malignancy status was evaluated through cluster-adjusted receiver operating characteristic curves and the corresponding area underneath the curve (AUC). Given the correlation structure of nodules within participants, sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values were estimated using generalized estimating equations. , , For comparison, we also estimated the discrimination capacity of models fitted on LUSI databased on a larger set of variables using cluster bootstrapping ( B = 1000). Model calibration was assessed by examining observed vs predicted nodule malignancy rates by category of nodule size (<5 mm, 5 to <8 mm, 8 to 10 mm, or >10 mm; as used in the LUSI CT evaluation algorithm) as well as by deciles of predicted risk. The Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit test was used to examine the fit between predicted and observed malignancy probabilities across deciles of predicted risk, and Brier scores (BS) and Spiegelhalter z test were used to assess the overall deviance of risk predictions estimated by models vs observed rates. Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness of fit and χ 2 for independence P values were 1-sided, and all other P values were 2-sided. Statistical significance was set at .05. All analyses were performed using R statistical software for version 3.5.1 (R Project for Statistical Computing), with packages gee, Hmisc, lme4, MuMIn, rms, pROC, and ROCR, as well as the clusteredROC function. Data analysis was performed from February 1, 2019 to December 5, 2019. Results Study Participants and Pulmonary Nodule Findings During 5 screening rounds, 1182 participants in the LUSI LDCT arm showed at least 1 noncalcified pulmonary nodule. A total of 62 participants were diagnosed with lung cancer up to 12 months after their last LDCT screening participation: 56 cancers detected via screening and 6 interval cancers. For 54 of 56 cancers detected via screening, malignancy was linked to 1 (51 participants) or more (3 participants) nodules. For 2 cancers detected via screening without nodules, the decision of referral to further diagnostic work was based on other pulmonary abnormalities. For 2 of 6 interval cases, no nodules were observed on LDCT screenings; for the remaining 4 cases with nonsuspicious nodules, no information was available to unequivocally link any of these

of 62 participants were diagnosed with lung cancer up to 12 months after their last LDCT screening participation: 56 cancers detected via screening and 6 interval cancers. For 54 of 56 cancers detected via screening, malignancy was linked to 1 (51 participants) or more (3 participants) nodules. For 2 cancers detected via screening without nodules, the decision of referral to further diagnostic work was based on other pulmonary abnormalities. For 2 of 6 interval cases, no nodules were observed on LDCT screenings; for the remaining 4 cases with nonsuspicious nodules, no information was available to unequivocally link any of these to malignancy. Nodules with benign-appearing calcification and individuals with lung cancer whose lung tumors could not be linked back to a specific nodule were excluded from statistical analyses. After removing participants with a lung cancer diagnosis made later than 1 year after the last CT scan or for whom the malignant nodule(s) could not be identified in earlier CT images, data was available for 3903 pulmonary nodules from 1159 individuals (median [range] age, 57.63 [50.34-71.89] years; 763 [65.8%] men) (eFigure 1 in the ). Detailed nodule counts by diameter, type (solid vs subsolid), malignancy status, and screening round of first observation (prevalence or incidence) are presented in eTable 3 in the . Of 3903 nodules observed, 2883 nodules (73.9%; 32 of these [1.1%] identified as malignant) were first seen during the prevalence screening, whereas 1020 nodules (26.1%; 31 of these [3.0%] identified as malignant), were first observed in 1 of 4 incidence screenings. Irrespective of screening round, more than 70% of malignant nodules (prevalence round: 25 of 32 nodules [78.1%]; incidence rounds: 25 of 31 nodules [80.6%]) had a diameter of 8 mm or greater. For these nodules 8 mm or greater, the malignancy rate was higher among nodules first observed in the prevalence round (12.8% [95% CI, 8.6%-18.5%]) than among those first observed in the incidence round (8.6% [95% CI, 5.7%-12.5%]); conversely, mean malignancy rate was higher for nodules smaller than 8 mm first observed in incidence rounds (0.8% [95% CI, 0.3%-1.9%]) than those first observed in the prevalence round (0.3% [95% CI, 0.1%- 0.6%]). Irrespective of screening round of first detection, compared with benign nodules, malignant nodules were significantly more often located in the left upper lobe (561 nodules [14.6%] vs 23 nodules [36.5%]; P < .001), were larger in terms of diameter (median [range], 4.8 [2.2-65.6] mm vs 11.6 [3.5-107.7] mm; P < .001) and volume (median [range], 41.4 [5.0-28947] mm 3 vs 357.1 [19.3-17466] mm 3 ; P < .001) and more often had spiculated borders (193 nodules [5.0%] vs 23 nodules [36.5%]; P < .001) ( ). Compared with patients with benign nodules, patients with malignant nodules were statistically significantly more likely to be older (median [range] age, 57.38 [50.34-71.89] years vs 59.88 [51.90-69.98] years; P < .001), have emphysema (474 patients [42.9%] vs 35 patients [64.8%]; P = .002), and have lower FEV 1 (median [range], 2.88 [0.66-6.11] L vs 2.66 [1.26-4.24] L; P = .009); whereas sex, smoking status at randomization, smoking duration and intensity, self-reported history of extrathoracic cancer, years since smoking cessation, presence of asthma or bronchitis, and FVC showed no significant association with malignancy diagnosis in the LUSI data ( ). Data on family history of cancer were not available in our data set. Evaluation of Predictive Models For nodules detected at the participants’ first screening (prevalence round), all PanCan models showed high discrimination accuracy. Among the PanCan variants, the comprehensive PanCan-2b model achieved only marginally better discrimination (AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.89-0.99]) than the parsimonious PanCan-1b model (AUC, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.87-0.99]), and there was no improvement in discrimination with the use of volume in the PanCan-VOL model (AUC, 0.90 [95% CI, 0.90-0.98]) or 2-dimensional perpendicular mean diameter in the PanCan-MD model (AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.91-0.98]). The discrimination by UKLS was poor (AUC, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.46-0.70]). A reduced UKLS model (eTable 2 in the ) that ignored variables with definitions or prevalence markedly differing from LUSI performed better in our data (prevalence round: AUC, 0.79 [95% CI, 0.68-0.89]; incidence rounds: AUC, 0.60 [95% CI, 0.49-0.70]) compared with the original version. For comparison, the models originally developed in clinical settings showed moderately good discrimination, (VA : AUC, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76-0.92]; Mayo Clinic: AUC, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.82-0.97]; PKUPH: AUC, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.79-0.995]) ( ). Compared with the prevalence round, all models (except for UKLS) showed useful, although reduced, discrimination when applied to nodules first noticed in any of the incidence rounds (PanCan-1b: AUC, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.87-0.99]; PanCan-2b: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.89-0.99]; PanCan-MD: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.91-0.98]; PanCan-VOL: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.90-0.98]; UKLS: AUC, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.46-0.70]; VA: AUC, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76-0.92]; Mayo Clinic: AUC, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.82-0.97]; PKUPH: AUC,

clinical settings showed moderately good discrimination, (VA : AUC, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76-0.92]; Mayo Clinic: AUC, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.82-0.97]; PKUPH: AUC, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.79-0.995]) ( ). Compared with the prevalence round, all models (except for UKLS) showed useful, although reduced, discrimination when applied to nodules first noticed in any of the incidence rounds (PanCan-1b: AUC, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.87-0.99]; PanCan-2b: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.89-0.99]; PanCan-MD: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.91-0.98]; PanCan-VOL: AUC, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.90-0.98]; UKLS: AUC, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.46-0.70]; VA: AUC, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.76-0.92]; Mayo Clinic: AUC, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.82-0.97]; PKUPH: AUC, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.79-0.97]) (eFigure 2 in the ). This difference may be explained by reduced variability in nodule size ( ; eTable 3 in the ). Regarding model calibration, for nodules detected at the prevalence screen, visual inspection of predicted absolute probabilities of malignancy and observed malignancy rates within categories defined by nodule size suggested best agreement for PanCan-1b ( ; eTable 4 in the ). Additional comparisons within deciles of the predicted probability scores (eTable 5 and eTable 6 in the ) combined with Hosmer-Lemeshow (HL) tests for deviance between predicted and observed rates showed acceptable calibration for PanCan-1b (HL = 7.71; P = .56), PanCan-2b (HL = 7.23; P = .61), and PanCan-VOL (HL = 10.89; P = .28) but not for PanCan-MD (HL = 30.53; P < .001) or UKLS (HL = 158.99; P < .001) (eTable 7 in the ). Alternatively, using BSs and Spiegelhalter z tests, acceptable calibration was found for PanCan-1b (BS = 0.009; Spiegelhalter z = −1.081; P = .28), PanCan-2b (BS = 0.009; Spiegelhalter z = 0.436; P = .67), and UKLS (BS = 0.012; Spiegelhalter z = −1.076; P = .28) but not for PanCan-VOL (BS = 0.009; Spiegelhalter z = 1.978; P = .05) or PanCan-MD (BS = 0.009, Spiegelhalter z = 3.888; P < .001) (eTable 7 in the ). Malignancy probabilities estimated by models developed in clinical contexts were all strongly overestimated (VA: Spiegelhalter z = −25.24; P < .001; Mayo Clinic: Spiegelhalter z = −12.63; P < .001; PKUPH: Spiegelhalter z = −19.35; P < .001) ( ) and were poorly calibrated according to all tests performed (VA: BS = 0.063; HL = 774.38; P < .001; Mayo Clinic: BS = 0.014; HL = 162.32; P < .001; PKUPH: BS = 0.094; HL = 1119.9; P < .001). None of the models showed acceptable calibration on nodules first observed in incidence screens. shows estimated sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values for malignancy at 2%, 5% or 10% model probability thresholds for nodules observed in the prevalence screening for the PanCan and UKLS models. PanCan-1b yielded highest sensitivities at 2% risk threshold (0.81 [95% CI, 0.67-0.94]), and 10% risk threshold (0.52 [95% CI, 0.32-0.71]), but lower specificities (2%: 0.90 [95% CI, 0.89-0.92]; 10%: 0.99 [95% CI, 0.98-0.99]) than the other models. The highest specificities at the 2% and 10% risk thresholds were observed for PanCan-MD (2%: 0.96 [95% CI, 0.95-0.97]; 10%: 0.99 [95% CI, 0.99-1.00]) but were accompanied by lower sensitivities (2%: 0.72 [95% CI, 0.56-0.86]; 10%: 0.43 [95% CI, 0.25-0.61]). The lowest positive predictive values at 2% or 5% risk thresholds were for PanCan-1b (0.08 [95% CI, 0.05-0.12]; 5%: 0.19 [95% CI, 0.11-0.27]), while the highest were for PanCan-MD (2%: 0.17 [95% CI, 0.10-0.24]; 5%: 0.33 [95% CI, 0.20-0.45]). On our data, PanCan-1b showed very similar estimates for sensitivity and specificity compared with those from the original PanCan study data. However, the recent PanCan-VOL and PanCan-MD updates in PanCan showed higher sensitivity and lower specificity in our study but similar PPV. External validation of PanCan-2b in the NLST also showed higher sensitivity, lower specificity, and comparable PPV compared with estimates in LUSI ( ). The UKLS model showed inferior sensitivity (2%: 0.25 [95% CI, 0.11-0.39]; 5%: 0.20 [95% CI, 0.07-0.33]; 10%: 0.14 [95% CI, 0.01-0.27]) and specificity (2%: 0.83 [95% CI, 0.81-0.85]; 5%: 0.92 [95% CI, 0.91-0.94]; 10%: 0.97 [95% CI, 0.96-0.98]) compared with PanCan models. Logistic regression models fitted via generalized estimating equations on LUSI data combined with model selection via backward elimination based on the quasi–Akaike Information Criterion resulted in a model retaining age (β coefficient = 0.06 [95% CI, 0.01 to 0.11]; P = .02), years since quitting smoking (β coefficient = 0.83 [95% CI, −0.15 to 1.82]; P = .10), bronchitis (β coefficient = −1.23 [95% CI, −2.29 to −0.17]; P = .03), nodule mean diameter (β coefficient = 0.14 [95% CI, 0.09 to 0.19]; P < .001), nodule location (β coefficient = 1.23 [95% CI, 0.35 to 2.11]; P = .01), and spiculation (β coefficient = 1.72 [95% CI, 1.02 to 2.42]; P < .001) as significant variables (eTable 8 in the ), whereas sex, self-reported history of extrathoracic

retaining age (β coefficient = 0.06 [95% CI, 0.01 to 0.11]; P = .02), years since quitting smoking (β coefficient = 0.83 [95% CI, −0.15 to 1.82]; P = .10), bronchitis (β coefficient = −1.23 [95% CI, −2.29 to −0.17]; P = .03), nodule mean diameter (β coefficient = 0.14 [95% CI, 0.09 to 0.19]; P < .001), nodule location (β coefficient = 1.23 [95% CI, 0.35 to 2.11]; P = .01), and spiculation (β coefficient = 1.72 [95% CI, 1.02 to 2.42]; P < .001) as significant variables (eTable 8 in the ), whereas sex, self-reported history of extrathoracic cancer, smoking duration, emphysema (based on CT results), FVC, nodule type, and nodule count per scan showed no further association with malignancy. This final model yielded discrimination AUC of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.83-0.93) (bootstrap AUC, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.84-0.92]) for nodules detected in the prevalence round and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.71-0.90) (bootstrap AUC, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.73-0.87]) for nodules first detected in the incidence round. Discussion Using data of the German LUSI trial, this diagnostic study found that 4 variants of the PanCan prediction model, developed in context of the Canadian Early Detection of Lung Cancer Study, each provided good discrimination between malignant and nonmalignant pulmonary nodules observed at individuals’ first (prevalence) LDCT screening, whereas more moderate discrimination was observed for 3 models originally developed on the basis of patient data from the Mayo Clinic and VA and PKUPH clinics. By contrast, discrimination for the model recently developed in context of the UKLS was poor. To our knowledge, these analyses are the first to provide external validation of the recent UKLS model and a complete external validation for PanCan-MD and PanCan-VOL models. Our analyses showed no clear superiority for the PanCan-VOL or PanCan-MD models over the older PanCan model versions, confirming observations in PanCan but not those from Horeweg et al. In LUSI, diameters were retrieved by software, thus based on a 3-dimensional estimation, which possibly led to a more accurate estimation of nodule diameter compared with manual diameter measurements used in other studies. Overall, our observations are in line with those from other validation studies, in context of incidentally or symptomatically detected pulmonary nodules , , , , , , , or in LDCT screening settings, , , , , , which mostly have also shown discrimination indices of AUCs of approximately 0.80 and higher, and similar ranking by discrimination capacity when comparing performance of the PanCan, VA, Mayo Clinic, and PKUPH models. Aside from good discrimination, PanCan-1b, PanCan-2b, and PanCan-VOL, but not PanCan-MD or UKLS, also showed acceptable calibration of estimated absolute malignancy probabilities when applied to data from the prevalence screening. In the original study leading to development of the initial PanCan models, acceptable calibration was reported on validation on data from a chemoprevention trial by the British Columbia Cancer Agency, and for PanCan-1b and PanCan-2b in NLST data , and a pilot LDCT screening trial in Queensland, Australia. , For the more recent PanCan-MD and PanCan-VOL models, by contrast, Tammemägi et al reported lower calibration accuracy by such tests in NLST data. The PanCan-1b model showed similar sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive values at selected (2%, 5%, or 10%) probability thresholds in LUSI and PanCan data, while among LUSI, PanCan, and NLST data, these estimates were somewhat more variable for PanCan-2b, PanCan-VOL, and PanCan-MD. , For the models developed in clinical settings, we found overestimated malignancy risk estimates, which were also observed for the VA and Mayo Clinic models on NLST data. None of the models (including the PanCan variants) showed acceptable calibration when applied to nodules first observed in incidence screens. Depending on the context (ie, clinical or screening) in which they were developed, malignancy prediction models include different sets of predictor variables. While age is an established factor for lung cancer risk, it was not retained as predictor in most PanCan models (PanCan-1b, PanCan-MD, or PanCan-VOL) or in those fitted in LUSI. However, in the UKLS model, age appeared together with smoking duration. With regard to smoking, while lifetime smoking status (ever vs never) is not relevant in LUSI or other screening contexts, including UKLS and PanCan, as screening generally is targeted to long-term smokers, our data and the analyses for the development of UKLS model show that in multivariable models that include age and detailed nodule characteristics, additional smoking-related information may improve malignancy prediction in combination with CT imaging, even among individuals at high risk who are eligible for lung cancer screening. Sex, associated with increased risk of malignancy for women based on the PanCan and UKLS models, showed no predictive value in our data and was found to be associated with lower malignancy risk in the Danish Lung Cancer Screening Trial. The female-to-male sex ratio for lung cancer incidence varies across populations

smokers, our data and the analyses for the development of UKLS model show that in multivariable models that include age and detailed nodule characteristics, additional smoking-related information may improve malignancy prediction in combination with CT imaging, even among individuals at high risk who are eligible for lung cancer screening. Sex, associated with increased risk of malignancy for women based on the PanCan and UKLS models, showed no predictive value in our data and was found to be associated with lower malignancy risk in the Danish Lung Cancer Screening Trial. The female-to-male sex ratio for lung cancer incidence varies across populations and by age, in relation to variable prevalence of and changing trends in smoking habits among women, which could explain population differences in the predictive value of sex for nodule malignancy. Also, among patients with lung cancer, women more often have adenocarcinomas as opposed to other histologic tumor subtypes. , Adenocarcinomas develop from slowly growing nodules with longer lead time until clinical relevance, which makes a benefit from lung cancer screening in terms of mortality reduction more likely. , , Thus, it may be relevant to refine malignancy prediction by sex and tailor models to specific screening populations. The PanCan and UKLS models, which were fitted on data from a first prevalence screening, may be less applicable to new nodules in follow-up screenings. In NLST, the malignancy risk of nodules 4 to 6 mm or larger or 6 to 8 mm or larger was higher than that of nodules found at the baseline screening, and malignancies associated with new nodules were significantly less likely to be adenocarcinomas. We could not confirm these observations in LUSI data because of small numbers (eTable 3 in the ). Strengths and Limitations Our study has some strengths, including that (with only 2 exceptions), malignancy was linked to specific nodules, as opposed to NLST in which malignancy was assumed to be always linked the largest nodule observed. , , Also, our study is the first, to our knowledge, to compare and document differences in the performance of malignancy risk predictions for models applied to nodules detected in prevalence or incidence screenings and for models originally developed in screening vs clinical settings. Our study also has some limitations. One limitation is the missing information in LUSI for several risk factors, including family history of lung or extrathoracic cancer and possible differences in CT-based assessment of emphysema as compared with PanCan. A limitation of all models examined in this analysis is that they do not incorporate measures of longitudinal nodule growth as a predictor of malignancy. For nodules of intermediate size, current diagnostic criteria for determining malignancy include early recall examinations for the determination of volume doubling time of nodules observed at an individual’s first screening or a direct assessment of longitudinal growth for nodules already noted at earlier visits when screening participants return for annual follow-up screenings. Detection algorithms are now being developed that integrate relevant nodule and nonnodule features on repeated CT screening examinations over time to predict the presence of lung cancer. , Variables difficult to standardize across populations, such as lung disease diagnosis and nodule type categories, may hinder model transferability. In fact, a reduced UKLS model (eTable 2 in the ) that ignored variables with definitions or prevalence markedly differing from LUSI performed better in our data compared with the original version. A more general limitation not only of LUSI but also other studies, including PanCan and UKLS, is the relatively small study size, with 2028 participants at baseline screenings in UKLS, 2029 participants at baseline screenings in LUSI, and 2537 participants at baseline screenings in PanCan, and limited numbers of malignant nodules observed. Accuracy of variable selection and model calibration may be improved in data from larger studies (eg, based on pooled data worldwide). Conclusions Our findings suggest that the PanCan models have good discrimination and confirmatory evidence for calibration accuracy of predicted malignancy risks when applied to nodules observed in an individual’s first (prevalence) screening examination, suggesting that such models may become useful tools for optimizing nodule management in population screening settings. Estimates of current models seem most applicable to nodules detected on a first screening examination, the specific context in which PanCan and UKLS were developed. For individuals screened at regular intervals, as in organized screening programs, models may be further developed to incorporate estimates of nodule volume doubling times, determined on early recall follow-up CT or determined directly for nodules already noted on an earlier visit when individuals return for annual incidence screenings.

chunks.content: Introduction Transient lateral patellar dislocation (TLPD) occurs most often in young active individuals. Although relatively common, they tend to spontaneously reduce and can be difficult to detect on clinical examination. While the typical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings following TLPD have been well documented in the literature and are known to frequently result in osteochondral lesion (OCL), the emergence of cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) as an imaging technique is in its relative infancy and the imaging findings on CBCT post TLPD are less well established. We describe a series of three cases of TLPD and the similar pattern of findings on CBCT, which were used as an adjunct to imaging with MRI. Case series The first case is of a 25-year-old patient with two previous patellar dislocations, presenting following a third TLPD, unable to straight leg raise or fully extend the knee. A small bony fragment was seen within the knee joint on plain radiographs (see A). CBCT showed a displaced curvilinear 1.9 cm bony fragment adjacent to the inferior pole of the patella, wrongly reported as likely from the medial patellar facet, and a small knee joint effusion (see B and C). MRI showed this to be a large OCL arising from the lateral aspect of the left lateral femoral condyle, in addition to the typical contusion pattern of TLPD, with marrow oedema in the medial aspect of the patella and the lateral aspect of the lateral femoral condyle (see D). The second case is of a 34-year-old patient who fell onto their knee and presented with swelling and medial knee pain. Radiographs showed no fracture but soft tissue swelling medially and a small knee joint effusion (see A). CBCT showed an intra-articular curvilinear 1.2 cm bony fragment in the medial aspect of the suprapatellar recess, in addition to a small fracture fragment adjacent to the medial patellar facet and a small knee joint effusion (see B and C). Again, this was reported as likely an avulsion fracture fragment from the medial patellar facet. However, MRI showed this to be an OCL arising from the weight-bearing surface of the lateral femoral condyle, in addition to the typical TLPD oedema pattern, partial thickness tears of the medial patellar retinaculum and the medial patellofemoral ligament and a tear of the body of the lateral meniscus (see D). The third case is of a 23-year-old patient who fell onto their knee and presented with swelling and generalized knee pain. Radiographs again showed a small bony fragment, in this case anterior to the distal femur in the patellofemoral space (see A). CBCT showed a curvilinear 1cm bone fragment anterior to the intercondylar space (see B and C). MRI confirmed this to be an OCL arising from the lateral femoral condyle, but only visible on sagittal imaging and felt to be better assessed on CBCT (see D). In addition to the typical TLPD oedema pattern, it also showed a partial thickness tear of the medial patellar retinaculum. Discussion Transient lateral patellar dislocation is a common cause of acute knee trauma, particularly among adolescents and young athletes. Despite its clinical frequency, it remains frequently misdiagnosed, especially in emergency settings where initial radiographs may appear normal. The consequences of a missed diagnosis are significant, including chronic instability, recurrent dislocations and the development of patellofemoral osteoarthritis [ ]. While MRI plays a central role and is the mainstay in confirming diagnosis and identifying associated injuries such as OCLs and damage to the adjacent ligamentous structures, there is mixed evidence on its sensitivity, as discussed below. The use of CBCT as an adjunct to MRI is less well established but the ease of access and better resolution of bone and bony detail than on MRI makes it an excellent additional screening tool to be used alongside, rather than instead of, MRI. Incidence The incidence of patellar dislocation in the general population is estimated to be approximately 5.8 to 77 per 100,000 people per year, depending on demographic and activity levels [ , ]. Adolescents and young athletes, particularly females, are at the highest risk, with peak incidence occurring during puberty due to increased ligamentous laxity and skeletal immaturity. Kirsch et al. [ ] were among the first to describe the typical pattern of MRI findings of TLPD, emphasizing that the condition is frequently misdiagnosed as a simple knee contusion or sprain. This underreporting contributes to an unclear understanding of the true incidence. Taljanovic et al. [ ] in the ACR Appropriateness Criteria, reinforce the need for early MRI in cases of acute knee trauma when patellar dislocation is suspected, even if initial radiographs are unremarkable. First-time versus recurrent dislocation First-time dislocations are most often due to noncontact injuries involving a twisting mechanism with the foot planted. These injuries typically result in tearing of the medial patellofemoral ligament

This underreporting contributes to an unclear understanding of the true incidence. Taljanovic et al. [ ] in the ACR Appropriateness Criteria, reinforce the need for early MRI in cases of acute knee trauma when patellar dislocation is suspected, even if initial radiographs are unremarkable. First-time versus recurrent dislocation First-time dislocations are most often due to noncontact injuries involving a twisting mechanism with the foot planted. These injuries typically result in tearing of the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL), bone contusions and potentially OCLs, which are more commonly seen in acute than recurrent TLPD [ ]. In up to 70% of cases, OCLs may accompany the dislocation [ ], which, if undiagnosed, can lead to poor outcomes. As is clear from this case series, larger OCLs are visible on CBCT and while they may be misdiagnosed as avulsion fracture fragments, it is clear that they should raise the suspicion for an OCL. Qiu et al. [ ] conducted a systematic review which concluded that MRI is the preferred modality to identify intra-articular pathology after first-time dislocation. Early detection of OCLs and MPFL tears allows early consideration of surgical stabilization, thereby reducing the risk of recurrence. Recurrent dislocations are often related to anatomic predispositions such as trochlear dysplasia, patella alta or rotational limb abnormalities. These are more common in individuals who have had prior dislocations managed conservatively without addressing structural contributors. Kapur et al. [ ] noted that recurrent cases often present with chronic signs such as lateral patellar tilt, maltracking and thickening or scarring of the MPFL, all of which are detectable on MRI. These features are less dramatic than those seen in acute cases but equally important in surgical planning. Recurrent dislocations are less likely to involve large OCLs but may exhibit more diffuse cartilage wear and early degenerative changes. Smith et al. [ ] noted that MRI has lower sensitivity for partial-thickness OCLs, which are more likely in chronic cases; however, they concluded that it remains the most useful modality in this context. MRI findings MRI is widely accepted as the imaging modality of choice in both acute and recurrent TLPD due to its ability to detect: - Bone contusions on the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella [ ] - MPFL injury, typically as a tear near its femoral origin [ , ] - OCLs and loose bodies [ ] - Chondral lesions (without osseous element), particularly full-thickness defects [ ]. These signs collectively form the “classic MRI triad” for TLPD, namely typical bone oedema pattern involving the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella, MPFL disruption and joint effusion. Although well documented in the literature as the primary modality for assessment of OCLs, there is mixed evidence on the effectiveness of MRI in their diagnosis. A study by Baker et al. [ ] of 87 patients with patellar instability who subsequently underwent knee arthroscopy demonstrated that the sensitivity and specificity of identifying OCLs on MRI were 0.43 and 0.81 and on radiographs were 0.08 and 0.97, respectively. However, a systematic review by Qiu et al. highlighted that MRI detects associated OCLs in up to 70% of first-time dislocations [ ]. Sanders et al. demonstrated that a significant number of these OCLs were found to involve the mid-lateral weight-bearing portion of the lateral femoral condyle and are often more posterior than would be expected after TLPD [ ]. Role and limitations of CT While CT offers excellent osseous resolution, its role in TLPD has to date been limited. The ACR Appropriateness Criteria currently recommend CT only in specific scenarios, such as pre-operative planning, evaluation of trochlear morphology or when MRI is contraindicated [ ]. CT does not adequately visualize soft tissues such as the MPFL or cartilage surfaces and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation, particularly important in pediatric and adolescent populations. However, MRI has been shown to over-estimate the size of OCLs due to the high signal of surrounding oedema, an important factor in surgical planning [ ]. The ease of access and the excellent resolution of CBCT, in addition to an emerging pattern of findings following TLPD, means that CBCT is excellently placed as an adjunct to MRI when TLPD is known or suspected. This case series demonstrates that OCLs from the lateral femoral condyle following TLPD are visible on CBCT as a distinctive curvilinear fragment of bone within the joint space and may be misdiagnosed as an avulsion fracture fragment from the medial patellar facet on initial plain radiographs. This case series demonstrates that OCLs from the lateral femoral condyle following TLPD are visible on CBCT as a distinctive curvilinear fragment of bone within the joint space and may be misdiagnosed as an avulsion fracture fragment from the medial patellar facet on initial plain radiographs. CBCT is good at assessing the size, location and morphology of OCLs, important factors in surgical planning – in one of the cases from this series, the OCL was much better assessed on CBCT than MRI and as noted above, MRI often overestimates the size of an OCL. While CBCT is able to accurately detect some soft tissue injuries such as knee joint effusion and soft tissue swelling, it is not able to detect most of the various soft tissue injuries detected on MRI. However, given difficulty and time delays in accessing MRI, CBCT is an excellent adjunct with its own particular benefits and as with the second case, may lead to the initial diagnosis of a fracture/suspected OCL not seen on initial radiographs. CBCT has the benefits of lower dose than multi-detector CT, in addition to lower cost and ability to be performed while weight-bearing and can be an effective triage tool to assess who needs an MRI and how urgently [ ]. Conclusion TLPD is a common but often underdiagnosed condition. MRI remains the gold standard for its evaluation, enabling accurate detection and diagnosis of pattern of bone oedema, MPFL tears and OCLs. While early MRI following a first-time dislocation remains crucial to prevent recurrence and long-term complications, this case series demonstrates that the superior osseous resolution of CBCT and the ability to visualize OCLs means CBCT is an excellent adjunct to MRI. Ease of access means it can be performed prior to MRI and can provide extra information for the interpretation of the MRI, rather than being performed afterwards for surgical planning, as has largely been the case to date. documents.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria shoulder pain atraumatic

chunks.content: Background Shoulder pain is a highly prevalent musculoskeletal complaint in the United States (US). A wide spectrum of bone and soft tissue pathologies can cause shoulder pain. The extensive existing diagnostic labels are based on the traditional pathoanatomic diagnostic classification, which attempts to identify a specific tissue pathology responsible for shoulder symptoms [ ]. However, making a definitive specific diagnosis of shoulder pain is challenging at both primary and specialist care levels [ ]. The immediate challenges surrounding the pathoanatomic diagnosis of shoulder pain include limited diagnostic value of physical examination tests, weak association between imaging findings and symptoms, co-existence of multiple pathoanatomic conditions [ , ]. Numerous reviews have highlighted the poor reliability of physical examination tests in the assessment of patients with shoulder pain [ – ]. Hegedus et al. examined the diagnostic accuracy of numerous shoulder physical examination tests and concluded that no single clinical test was sufficiently reliable to establish a pathognomonic diagnosis [ ]. In addition, many studies have questioned the weak correlation between clinical shoulder symptoms and radiologic abnormalities [ , ]. Barreto et al. prospectively evaluated bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings in 123 individuals with unilateral shoulder pain and demonstrated that most abnormalities seen on MRI were not different in frequency between symptomatic and asymptomatic shoulders [ ]. Consequently, the use of the term non-specific shoulder pain (NSSP) as a non-specific diagnostic label has been proposed [ ]. The definition of NSSP in the published literature is shoulder pain without specific recognizable pathology or physical signs [ ]. The extensive use of NSSP labels reflects uncertainty in traditional pathoanatomic labeling for shoulder pain and intention to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches to diagnosis [ , ]. NSSP might be considered as a common independent disease entity, rather than an indeterminate diagnosis that needs to be clarified [ ]. However, comprehensive national data on the characteristics of ambulatory visits with NSSP labels are lacking. The value of physical therapy (PT) as the first-line treatment of specific shoulder pain (SSP) is widely accepted [ , ]. The published clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) strongly recommended PT to improve pain, mobility, and function in patients with SSP, such as rotator cuff injuries and adhesive capsulitis of shoulder [ , ]. Although, the widely recognized CPGs for NSSP have not yet been established, the evidence supporting the PT as an effective intervention for patients with NSSP is also increasing and strengthening [ , , ]. Recently, a new Norwegian guideline strongly recommended simple clinical examination and advice for exercises in the primary care of NSSP [ ]. Dolder et al. assessed the effectiveness of exercise for the treatment of NSSP and demonstrated high quality evidence that exercise therapy was effective to relieve the shoulder pain [ ]. There is limited research focused on the use of PT for patients with NSSP compared to SSP. Therefore, the aim of our study was to identify the differences in the utilization of PT for ambulatory visits with NSSP labels and SSP labels, by using the 2007–2016 National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS) database. Methods Data source The NAMCS launched by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) provides a nationally representative estimate of office-based ambulatory care visits in the US. This annual survey captures information on the characteristics of patients and visits, such as patients’ age, sex, race, expected source of payment, metropolitan statistical area (MSA) status, reasons for visit (RFVs), major reason for this visit (new problem, chronic problem routine, chronic problem flare-up), continuity of care (new patient, established patient), clinical diagnoses, medical comorbidities. The NAMCS data also include the diagnostic screening and examination, education/counseling, and therapeutic services ordered or provided during the visits. Given the publicness and de-identification of NAMCS database, this study did not require institutional review board approval. Study population The NAMCS was queried from 2007 to 2016 to identify the ambulatory visits for shoulder pain. The sample consisted of visits by adults with a diagnosis of shoulder disorder in the top 3 diagnoses and a complaint of shoulder pain in the top 3 RFVs. We excluded visits involving diagnoses of pregnancy, malignancy or neoplasm, infectious diseases, visits classified as preventative care, pre-surgery or post-surgery. From this sample population, we further excluded the visits for infectious or inflammatory arthropathy of shoulder, pathological fracture of shoulder, open fracture or open dislocation of shoulder, because of the significant heterogeneity in the management of these diseases. The shoulder related diagnoses were dichotomized as NSSP and SSP based on the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) and International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes. A diagnostic label described a symptom without specific pathology was classified as NSSP, including effusion of joint, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71901; ICD-10 code: M25411 , M25412 ), hemarthrosis,

From this sample population, we further excluded the visits for infectious or inflammatory arthropathy of shoulder, pathological fracture of shoulder, open fracture or open dislocation of shoulder, because of the significant heterogeneity in the management of these diseases. The shoulder related diagnoses were dichotomized as NSSP and SSP based on the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) and International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes. A diagnostic label described a symptom without specific pathology was classified as NSSP, including effusion of joint, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71901; ICD-10 code: M25411 , M25412 ), hemarthrosis, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71911; ICD-10 code: M25011 , M25012 ), pain in joint, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71941; ICD-10 code: M25511 , M25512 ), stiffness of joint, not elsewhere classified, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71951; ICD-10 code: M25611 , M25612 ), other symptoms referable to joint, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71961), unspecified disorder of joint, shoulder region (ICD-9 code: 71991; ICD-10 code: M259). A diagnostic label identified a clear structural pathoanatomic origin of shoulder pain was classified as SSP. The comprehensive NSSP and SSP diagnosis codes were listed in Table . If none of the top 3 diagnoses was a SSP diagnosis, this visit would be assigned to the NSSP group. If one of the top 3 diagnoses was a SSP diagnosis, this visit would be assigned to the SSP group. To limit the visits mainly for shoulder pain, we used top 3 RFVs in addition to the top 3 diagnoses to identify the study sample. A complaint of shoulder pain was determined based on the RFV classification code number (19400–19405,19450–19455) and the top 3 RFVs were reviewed in our analysis. According to the RFV classification, 19,400 represents shoulder symptoms, 19,401 represents pain, ache, soreness, discomfort of shoulder, 19,402 represents cramps, contractures, spasms of shoulder, 19,403 represents limitation of movement, stiffness, tightness of shoulder, 19,404 represents weakness of shoulder, and 19,405 represents swelling of shoulder, 19,450 represents arm symptoms, 19,451 represents pain, ache, soreness, discomfort of arm, 19,452 represents cramps, contractures, spasms of arm, 19,453 represents limitation of movement, stiffness, tightness of arm, 19,454 represents weakness of arm, and 19,455 represents swelling of arm. Study variables Data on patient sociodemographic characteristics such as age, sex (male, female), race (white, black, and other), expected source of payment for this visit (private insurance, Medicare/Medicaid, worker’s compensation, and other), and MSA status (yes, no) were included, as variables in both descriptive and adjusted analyses. We also included the practice and visit characteristics such as the major reason for this visit (new problem, chronic problem routine, chronic problem flare-up), presence of injury related to current visit (yes, no), referred for this visit (yes, no), continuity of care (new patient, established patient), number of medical comorbidities (0, 1, 2, ≥ 3) and physician specialty (primary care specialty, surgical care specialty, medical care specialty). The variables with missing rate exceeding 20% were excluded from the statistical models because of the inability to make reliable estimates using these variables, which included tobacco use (missing rate 26.96%), temperature (missing rate 78.33%), body mass index (missing rate 41.36%), systolic blood pressure (missing rate 47.89%), and diastolic blood pressure (missing rate 47.96%) (Supplementary Table ). Considering the information on a variety of services and treatments captured in NAMCS, this study focused on the differences in the utilization of PT for ambulatory visits with NSSP labels and visits with SSP labels. In addition, this study also described the use of diagnostic imaging included x-ray, MRI, ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), as well as pain medications across both groups. Pain medications were classified into four categories according to the Multum drug classification, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (drug codes 061 and 278), narcotic analgesics (drug codes 060 and 191), skeletal muscle relaxants (drug codes 178 and 179), and other pain medications (drug codes 059, 062 and 063) [ ]. Recommendations for diet/nutrition, exercise, injury prevention, stress management, tobacco use/exposure, weight reduction were all included as health education/counselling services. Mental health counseling and psychotherapy were combined into one variable for analysis. Statistical analysis In order to identify the differences between the two groups, all analyses were stratified by NSSP group versus SSP group. We described the sample according to the patient and visit characteristics. Differences in these characteristics and clinical management for two groups were tested, by using the Rao-Scott Chi-square test for categorical variables and the Student’s t-test for continuous variables. We constructed multivariable logistic regression analyses to evaluate the influence of diagnostic labels on PT utilization. The covariables in the regression analysis included age, sex, race, expected source of payment for this visit, MSA status, major reason for this visit, presence of injury related to current visit, referred for this visit, continuity of care, number of medical comorbidities, and physician specialty.

We described the sample according to the patient and visit characteristics. Differences in these characteristics and clinical management for two groups were tested, by using the Rao-Scott Chi-square test for categorical variables and the Student’s t-test for continuous variables. We constructed multivariable logistic regression analyses to evaluate the influence of diagnostic labels on PT utilization. The covariables in the regression analysis included age, sex, race, expected source of payment for this visit, MSA status, major reason for this visit, presence of injury related to current visit, referred for this visit, continuity of care, number of medical comorbidities, and physician specialty. The results of regression analyses were presented as odds ratio (OR) with the corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI). To accommodate the multistage probability sampling design of NAMCS, all estimates were weighted to yield nationally representative estimates. The multiple imputations were applied to address missing data by using the MICE (Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations) package. In the sensitivity analysis, we conducted the regression analysis again by excluding the visits with closed fracture and closed dislocation of shoulder. Subgroup analyses and interaction tests were performed using the adjusted model to explore heterogeneity in the associations across different subgroups. All statistical analyses were conducted with the statistical computing language R software (version 4.1.3), with p values < 0.05 considered as the threshold for statistical significance. Results From 2007 to 2016, approximately 62.17 million (71.9%) visits were assigned to SSP labels, while the remaining 24.31 million visits (28.1%) were assigned to NSSP labels. Significant visit characteristic differences were observed between NSSP group and SSP group (Table ). The proportion of visits with the presence of injury in NSSP group was 9.9%, which was significantly lower than the proportion in the SSP group (42.4%). 20.6% of NSSP group were referred for this visit, which was lower than proportion in the SSP group (36.0%). The proportion of established patients in NSSP group (85.1%) was higher than proportion in the SSP group (78.3%). For the physician specialty, the proportion of primary care specialty in the NSSP group was significantly higher than the proportion in the SSP group (56.0% versus 25.8%), and proportion of surgical care specialty in the NSSP group was significantly lower than the proportion in the SSP group (25.1% versus 54.3%). The proportion of visits with no comorbidities was 40.1% in the NSSP group, which was significantly higher than the proportion in the SSP group (21.2%). Besides that, no statistically significant differences were identified with regard to patient age, sex, race, expected source of payment for this visit, MSA status, or the major reason for this visit between two groups (Table ). For visits with NSSP labels, x-ray (23.7%) was the most common imaging examination, followed by MRI (11.3%), ultrasound (0.3%) and CT (0.3%). It was interesting to see visits with NSSP labels received far fewer ultrasound compared with visits with SSP labels (0.3% versus 4.1%). Besides that, the use of medical imaging was similar for visits with SSP labels, and no differences were observed in use of x-ray, MRI, or CT between the two groups (Table ). For both NSSP and SSP groups, the most frequent medications prescribed were NSAIDs, and the use of NSAIDs were similar in the NSSP (31.9%) group and SSP (27.6%) group. It was noteworthy that visits with NSSP labels had a significant higher frequency of narcotic analgesics prescriptions compared to visits with SSP labels (25.8% versus 15.6%). Skeletal muscle relaxants occurred at 11.5% of visits with NSSP labels and 8.7% of visits with SSP labels. The health education/counselling was more common in the SSP group (23.2%) than that in the NSSP group (14.5%). No difference in the mental health counseling between the two groups was identified (Table ). Combining all years, PT was prescribed in approximately 19.0% of the overall adult ambulatory visits for shoulder pain (Table ). Our results revealed a significant lower frequency of PT for visits with NSSP labels (10.8%) versus visits with SSP labels (22.2%). The baseline characteristics of sample population stratified by utilization of PT were presented in Table . Multivariable logistic regression analysis was employed to identify the factors associated with ambulatory utilization of PT for shoulder pain (Table ). Visits assigned to NSSP labels had significantly lower odds of prescribing PT compared to visits assigned to SSP labels (adjusted OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.94), after adjustment for covariates including age, sex, race, expected source of payment, MSA, major reason for this visit, injury related, referred for this visit, continuity of care, number of medical comorbidities, and physician specialty. Meanwhile, the surgical care specialty had higher odds of prescribing PT compared to primary care specialty (adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI: 1.62–3.29). Meanwhile, the surgical care specialty had higher odds of prescribing PT compared to primary care specialty (adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI: 1.62–3.29). Visits covered by worker’s compensation had higher odds of receiving PT than visits covered by private insurance (adjusted OR = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.30–3.31). In the sensitivity analysis, visits assigned to NSSP labels still had significantly lower odds of prescribing PT compared to visits assigned to SSP labels (adjusted OR = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.39–0.92), after adjustment for covariates and excluding the visits with closed fracture and closed dislocation of shoulder (Table ). The results of subgroup analyses among shoulder pain visits are shown in Fig. . A significant negative association was observed between NSSP group and PT among age less than 60 years old, female, white, those from MSA, with routine chronic problem, without referred for this visit. Additionally, no significant interactions were identified between diagnosis labels and any covariates (all P values for interaction > 0.05, Fig. ). Discussion Our research was the first study focused on the differences in the utilization of PT for visits with NSSP labels and visits with SSP labels by using NAMCS database. The most noteworthy finding was that visits assigned to NSSP labels had significantly lower frequency of PT compared to visits assigned to SSP labels (10.8% versus 22.2%). Logistic regression analyses identified the influence of non-specific diagnostic labels on the utilization of PT after adjusting for the covariates. However, the evidence of a lower use of PT coupled with higher prescribed narcotic analgesics for visits with NSSP labels compared to visits with SSP labels needed to be interpreted with caution. Accurate and prompt diagnosis is crucial for clinical management of shoulder pain [ ]. Currently, the majority of diagnostic labels assigned to patients with shoulder pain are based on the pathoanatomic diagnostic classification [ ]. In typical ambulatory shoulder care, physicians often rely on physical examination tests and imaging modalities to reach a definitive diagnosis of shoulder pain [ , , ]. However, achieving a definitive and specific diagnosis of shoulder pain is challenging, and the basis for them has been questioned [ , , ]. Many studies have highlighted the poor reliability of physical examination tests in the field of shoulder disorders [ , ]. May et al. systematically reviewed the reliability of physical examination procedures in 2010 and found that majority of studies indicated poor reliability for the procedures used in the clinical examination of patients with shoulder pain [ ]. Several studies suggested that combinations of physical examination tests might provide better diagnostic accuracy [ , , ]. Given the limited diagnostic value of physical examination tests for shoulder pain, diagnostic imaging has become increasingly important for detecting shoulder disorders [ , ]. According to the American College of Radiology (ACR) appropriateness criteria for evaluating atraumatic shoulder pain, MRI is considered to be the gold standard with its excellent ability in depicting the soft-tissue streuctures [ ]. However, abnormal radiological findings may not be the source of clinical symptoms [ , ]. Barreto et al. found that abnormalities on MRI were not different in frequency between symptomatic and asymptomatic shoulders, after evaluating bilateral MRI findings in 123 individuals [ ]. Eliason et al. recruited 115 consecutive patients with unilateral subacromial pain syndrome from primary care centers and reported ultrasound findings of structural abnormalities in almost 90% of the asymptomatic shoulder [ ]. Consequently, the use of the term NSSP as a non-specific diagnostic label has been proposed [ ]. NSSP has been defined in various ways, the most common definition of NSSP is shoulder pain without specific recognizable pathology or physical signs. In our study, a diagnostic label described a symptom without specific pathology was classified as NSSP. A diagnostic label identified a clear structural pathoanatomic origin of shoulder pain was classified as SSP, such as rotator cuff tear or rupture, impingement syndrome, and adhesive capsulitis of shoulder. During 2007–2016, about 28.1% of ambulatory visits for shoulder pain were assigned to NSSP labels in the US. This occurrence rate of NSSP was consistent with literature reports and clinical practice [ , ]. Non-specific diagnostic labels have traditionally been considered as the consequence of inadequate expertise to diagnose the specific structural cause of symptoms, which may be different in the field of shoulder pain [ ]. Sometimes, it was difficult to establish a specific diagnosis at the initial visit for shoulder pain, and further examinations were needed. However,

This occurrence rate of NSSP was consistent with literature reports and clinical practice [ , ]. Non-specific diagnostic labels have traditionally been considered as the consequence of inadequate expertise to diagnose the specific structural cause of symptoms, which may be different in the field of shoulder pain [ ]. Sometimes, it was difficult to establish a specific diagnosis at the initial visit for shoulder pain, and further examinations were needed. However, these assumptions were not supported by the results of our study. There were no significant differences in the ordering of x-ray, MRI, or CT between the two groups, which indicated that visits with NSSP labels did not undergo more imaging. Meanwhile, the proportion of established patients in the NSSP group was higher than the proportion in the SSP group (85.1% versus 78.3%), that indicated the majority of visits with NSSP labels were made by established patients, rather than new patients. These results could be attributed to the uncertainty in traditional pathoanatomic labeling for shoulder pain and the improvement in understanding NSSP diagnosis in clinical practice. NSSP can be considered as a common independent disease entity, rather than an indeterminate diagnosis that needs to be clarified, which is supported by our research findings and published literature [ , ]. In addition to the lack of national data on the management of NSSP, there is limited research comparing the utilization of PT for NSSP and SSP. Feleus et al. performed a large prospective cohort study on the differences in management of different diagnostic groups in non-traumatic arm, neck and shoulder complaints by general practitioner in the Netherlands, and found that patients with a non-specific diagnosis were more frequently referred for physiotherapy [ ], which was contrasted with our results. This difference reflected variation in research characteristics and populations observed, also reflected the different beliefs of physicians about the treatment of NSSP from different academic backgrounds and regions. Many factors can influence the utilization of PT, including clinical diagnosis, seriousness of illness, PT supply, insurance policy, physician experience and training [ , ]. In our study, the physician specialty could be a significant potential confounder to the association between the diagnosis type and PT use. To evaluate the potential impact of physician specialty, we included the physician specialty as a covariable in the regression model, and found that visits assigned to NSSP labels had significantly lower odds of prescribing PT compared to visits assigned to SSP labels (adjusted OR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.94). Our result could be partially explained by the perception and recognition of the effectiveness of PT for NSSP and SSP in the clinical practice. PT has a fundamental role in the management of SSP, such as rotator cuff injuries and adhesive capsulitis of shoulder [ , ]. Doiron-Cadrin et al. assessed the methodological quality of 9 CPGs on the management of rotator cuff disorders and found all CPGs recommended active treatment modalities, such as an exercise program in the management of rotator cuff disorders [ ]. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by Mertens et al. found that range of motion, function, and pain in patients with frozen shoulder improved with both solely exercises and programs with exercises [ ]. In recent years, the evidence supporting PT as an effective intervention for patients with NSSP is also increasing and strengthening [ , , ]. Dolder et al. assessed the effectiveness of exercise for the treatment of NSSP and demonstrated high quality evidence that exercise therapy was effective to relieve the shoulder pain [ ]. Abdulla et al. conducted a systematic review and suggested that supervised strengthening and stretching were equally effective to corticosteroid injections or multimodal care for NSSP [ ]. Recently, a new Norwegian guideline strongly recommended simple clinical examination and advice for exercises in the primary care of NSSP [ ]. The gap in physicians’ awareness and understanding of NSSP, might lead to the lower utilization rate of PT for NSSP. Our study might identify this gap in the utilization of PT for NSSP and provided valuable information on improving the ambulatory management of NSSP. Findings from recent studies indicate that diagnostic labels for shoulder pain may influence patients’ perceived seriousness of the condition, need for imaging or surgery, recovery expectations, and clinical outcomes [ – ]. Zadro et al. analyzed 2024 responses and found labeling as rotator cuff tear increased perceived need for surgery, imaging, absence from work and to see a specialist compared to labelling as bursitis [ ]. valuable information on improving the ambulatory management of NSSP. Findings from recent studies indicate that diagnostic labels for shoulder pain may influence patients’ perceived seriousness of the condition, need for imaging or surgery, recovery expectations, and clinical outcomes [ – ]. Zadro et al. analyzed 2024 responses and found labeling as rotator cuff tear increased perceived need for surgery, imaging, absence from work and to see a specialist compared to labelling as bursitis [ ]. Cuff et al. suggested that using the term subacromial impingement syndrome (SIS) potentially contributed to the negative influence on the expectations of positive outcome with physiotherapy [ ]. Patients assigned to SSP labels might have higher perceived treatment need compared to patients assigned to NSSP labels, leading to a significantly higher use of PT for SSP compared to NSSP. The influence of non-specific diagnostic labels on the treatment intentions might explain the lower rate of PT for NSSP, but it was unable to explain the higher rate of narcotic analgesics prescriptions for NSSP compared to SSP, which was a contradiction needed further investigation. Limitations These limitations are worth noting. Firstly, due to the retrospective and cross-sectional nature of our study, no causal relationship can be inferred between the risk factors and the use of PT. Secondly, the accuracy of the diagnoses recorded in the NAMCS database could not be determined, and the recorded diagnoses more reflected the doctors’ diagnosis and treatment mode. Thirdly, variation exists across the current management of NSSP due to the lack of recognized CPGs for NSSP. Despite these limitations, the differences we observed in the utilization of PT for NSSP compared with SSP may signal gaps in the ambulatory management of NSSP, which warrants further investigation. Conclusion The results of this retrospective cross-sectional study identified the significant differences in the utilization of PT for visits with NSSP labels and SSP labels by using NAMCS database. Multivariable logistic regression analyses confirmed the influence of non-specific diagnostic labels on utilization of PT. After adjusting for the covariates, visits assigned to NSSP labels had significantly lower odds of prescribing PT compared to visits assigned to SSP labels. These findings may help improve physician prescribing practices, diminish management disparities, and improve appropriate use of PT in the ambulatory management of shoulder pain. chunks.content: Introduction Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) have been utilized in direct shoulder MR arthrography (MRA) – , recognized for its high accuracy in evaluating intra-articular structures despite the invasiveness involved. Some practitioners opt for a saline-only approach to potentially reduce the risk of contrast reactions and achieve cost savings , – . However, advantages such as clearer delineation of intra-articular structures, improved signal-to-noise and contrast-to-noise ratios, attributed to the T1 shortening effects of diluted gadolinium, have been noted . GBCAs have proven safety, stability, and efficacy over more than 30 years of use in various clinical settings – . However, in direct MRA, concerns have been raised by certain in vitro studies regarding potential adverse effects on chondrocytes , with conflicting findings reported – . Additionally, preclinical studies in rats have shown detectable levels of gadolinium in joint tissues following intra-articular injection of both linear and macrocyclic GBCAs , though the clinical significance of this is yet to be fully determined. Efforts to find alternatives to GBCA have led to the development of non-GBCA, particularly iron-based or manganese-based ones, aiming to replace the T1 shortening effect , . Recently, an iron (Fe)-based contrast agent designed for direct MRA, NEMO-103 (codename), has been developed by Inventera Inc., Seoul, South Korea , . It comprises a biocompatible dextran core with an iron shell (supramolecular amorphous iron oxide) and has a molecular weight of approximately 32 kDa and like gadolinium, functions as a T1-positive contrast agent. Interestingly, NEMO-103 exhibits a longer joint cavity residence time (> 2 h) compared to typical GBCAs (~ 1 h) due to its larger molecular size. It is excreted from the joint cavity within 24 h after administration. On the other hand, intra-articular injection of GBCAs lacks approval from the United States Food and Drug Administration and is considered an off-label use , , . GBCAs need to be diluted hundreds of times for direct MRA, with the ideal concentration range for optimum signal-to-noise ratio being 1.25–2.5 mmol/L – . Injecting GBCAs outside the optimal concentration range (e.g., 0.7–3.4 mmol/L) inadvertently leads to a decrease in the signal of the injected substance . However, NEMO-103 can be used directly without the need for dilution, eliminating concerns related to concentration variability. While no studies have directly compared image quality between NEMO-103 and GBCAs, NEMO-103 is considered a promising alternative for direct shoulder MRA. The aim of this study is to demonstrate, through both objective and subjective evaluations that MRA using NEMO-103 are comparable to those obtained with GBCAs. Additionally, we aim to show superior image quality during the delayed phase (30–60 min post-injection), attributed to NEMO-103’s longer joint-cavity residence times. Materials and methods Study design and data The intra-articular administration of the investigational contrast agent NEMO-103 was conducted under a prospective clinical trial sponsored by Inventera Inc. (Trial ID: IVT_NEM_P1_20), which received prior approval from the Korean Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS). The present study is a retrospective secondary analysis of the imaging data obtained during that trial, and was separately approved by our institutional review board (No. 3-2023-0339). Informed consent was waived as the data were fully de-identified. All procedures were performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki. A total of 138 direct shoulder MRAs from 90 patients were reviewed. After excluding 9 scans acquired at 120 min post-injection and 30 scans at 24 h post-injection (intended for pharmacokinetic analysis only), 99 MRAs remained eligible for image quality comparison. Two time-based comparison groups were defined: comparison 1 (0–30 min post-injection): 31 NEMO-103 MRAs versus 38 GBCA MRAs and Comparison 2 (30–60 min post-injection): 8 NEMO-103 MRAs versus 12 GBCA MRAs. Exclusion criteria included inadequate MR sequences, scanty intra-articular contrast agent (e.g., massive rotator cuff tear or technical error), or non-comparable scanner parameters (Fig. ). All subjects in both the NEMO-103 and GBCA groups were symptomatic patients referred for clinical MRA due to suspected rotator cuff or labral pathology. No healthy volunteers were included. Preparation of NEMO-103 NEMO-103 was synthesized according to a previously reported procedure , . Briefly, 20 mM Dextran T10 (551,000,109,001; Pharmacosmos) solution was mixed with a sodium hydroxide solution and epichlorohydrin (45,340; Sigma-Aldrich), followed by the addition of ethylenediamine (E26266; Sigma-Aldrich). The cross-linked dextran was purified via a 10 kDa cutoff ultrafiltration filter (UFC9010; Millipore). The terminal amine was further modified to form a carboxyl functional group. After ultrafiltration, the carboxyl-functionalized dextran was reacted with an iron chloride solution for 1 h. The final products were purified and concentrated by ultrafiltration. Phantom study Phantom images were acquired using a 3 T magnet machine (MAGNETOM Vida; Siemens Healthineers AG). Several concentrations of NEMO-103 and the GBCA (Dotarem®) were prepared (0.125, 0.25, 0.5, and 1.0 mM) in sealed tubes filled with 0.9% normal saline to minimize image artifacts. To obtain the
