Research on PNI has primarily focused on cancers with a strong neurotropic tendency, such as pancreatic and prostate adenocarcinomas, whereas breast cancer has historically been characterized by its primary dissemination through lymphatic and vascular channels [ ]. The complexity of characterizing and identifying PNI in breast cancer may have contributed to its underrepresentation in pathological reporting. 3. Prevalence and Clinicopathological Correlates of Perineural Invasion in Breast Pathology Despite varying definitions of PNI, it has been extensively studied and recognized as an important prognostic marker in malignancies such as pancreatic [ , ], colorectal [ , ], prostate [ , ] and head and neck [ , ] cancers, where it is associated with decreased patient survival due to high recurrence rates and therapy resistance [ ]. In breast pathology, PNI has been identified and reported in both benign and malignant conditions [ , , , , ] ( ), yet its independent prognostic role is debatable. While a collective appreciation of its pathophysiology is emerging, lack of standardized diagnostic criteria and underreporting may have hindered efforts to define its frequency and clinical impact in breast pathology [ ]. 3.1. Perineural Invasion in Pre-Malignant and Benign Breast Lesions The first reported case of benign breast PNI was documented by Ackerman in 1957, marking the initial recognition of this phenomenon outside of malignancies [ ]. Further research has strengthened this finding, where PNI has been reported in ADH, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), florid hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, and radial scars ( ). Gobbi et al. (2001) provided substantial evidence of PNI prevalence in non-invasive breast pathologies. Examination of 10,000 breast cases, excluding invasive mammary carcinoma, identified 14 cases of PNI within a distribution of specific patterns: five cases of ADH, three cases of DCIS (cribriform and comedo types), five cases of florid hyperplasia, and one case of ductal adenoma [ ]. Nine cases developed within complex sclerosing lesions or radial scars (CSL/RS), four in sclerosing adenosis (SA), and one at a prior biopsy site of ductal adenoma [ ]. These findings highlight the occurrence of PNI in non-invasive breast lesions, aligning with Taylor and Norris’s (1967) study, reporting PNI in 20 out of 1000 sclerosing adenosis cases (2%) [ ]. Follow-up for 17 of those 20 patients was available, and all were well (median, 7 years) [ ]. Additionally, Davies (1973) identified PNI in four out of 316 benign breast lesions (1.3%) [ ]. Research has also identified PNI in cases involving cystic lesions, papillomatosis, oncocytic metaplasia, and periductal inflammation, where epithelial cells were observed involving nerve bundles [ , , ]. Among these, radial scar, papillomatosis, intraductal papillomas, and sclerosing adenosis exhibited a higher propensity for PNI [ , , , , , ], further supporting the occurrence of nerve invasion beyond invasive carcinoma. A detailed histological evaluation by Elfituri and Emmadi (2019) also provided noteworthy insight into the complexity of PNI presentation in ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) PNI with multiple architectural patterns—cribriform, papillary, micropapillary—accompanied by findings of microcalcifications and focal necrosis [ , ]. Similarly, another case report that shows PNI presence in a benign breast condition is that of Fellegara et al. (2007), which described a case of florid adenosis [ ]. 3.2. Perineural Invasion in Breast Cancer There is considerable variability in the documented rate of PNI in breast cancer [ , , ] ( ). Karak et al. (2010) reported low PNI rates of 1.14% [ ], while Duraker et al. (2006) reported higher rates, as high as 25.73% [ ]. This difference may be due to the variability in tumor type, cohort size, and patient population [ ]. Specifically, in Karak’s study, PNI was identified in a relatively low percentage (1.14%; 13 of 1136 patients) of invasive mammary carcinoma cases, of which almost half (5/13) of the patients with PNI also had lymphovascular invasion (LVI). Results from this study demonstrated that PNI occurred 10 times less frequently than LVI, yet both PNI and LVI were associated with aggressive tumor features such as higher T-stage and intermediate to high histologic grade [ ]. Nevertheless, due to the limited number of PNI-positive cases, establishing PNI as an independent prognostic factor was not feasible [ ]. In Duraker’s study, a relatively high frequency of PNI (25.73%) was reported in invasive breast carcinomas (IBCs), with an even higher prevalence (up to 68.7%) observed in more aggressive pT4 tumors [ ]. Despite this, the analysis found no significant association between PNI and disease-free survival, LRR, or distant metastasis. Furthermore, no correlation was observed between PNI and age, menopausal status, or estrogen receptor (ER) status [ ]. 3.3. limited number of PNI-positive cases, establishing PNI as an independent prognostic factor was not feasible [ ]. In Duraker’s study, a relatively high frequency of PNI (25.73%) was reported in invasive breast carcinomas (IBCs), with an even higher prevalence (up to 68.7%) observed in more aggressive pT4 tumors [ ]. Despite this, the analysis found no significant association between PNI and disease-free survival, LRR, or distant metastasis. Furthermore, no correlation was observed between PNI and age, menopausal status, or estrogen receptor (ER) status [ ]. 3.3. Perineural Invasion Across Breast Cancer Subtypes The incidence and distribution patterns of PNI across breast cancer subtypes demonstrate significant variability in current medical literature, with comprehensive subtype-specific analyses remaining limited [ , , ] ( ). Certain breast cancer subtypes appear to have a higher propensity for PNI. Duraker et al. (2006) reported a higher frequency of PNI with ductal and mixed-type carcinomas, suggesting a correlation between PNI and aggressive histological patterns, with PNI observed in 25.7% of IBC cases [ ]. Additionally, hormone receptor-positive tumors, particularly those expressing ER and/or progesterone receptor (PR), exhibited higher rates of PNI [ ]. Hosoya et al. (2023) showed that invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST) showed a PNI incidence of 14.1%, while invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) had a slightly lower rate at 13.3%, with no statistically significant difference between them. Notably higher rates were observed in mixed carcinomas and invasive micropapillary carcinomas, with incidences of 33.3% and 50%, respectively. Metaplastic carcinoma demonstrated the highest PNI incidence, observed in 100% of cases evaluated. In terms of molecular subtypes, HER2-positive tumors had a PNI incidence of 14.3%, whereas triple-negative breast cancers (TNBC) exhibited the lowest rate among subtypes, at 7.1%. These findings highlight the variability of PNI prevalence across different histologic and molecular breast cancer subtypes, suggesting that tumor biology may influence PNI [ ]. 4. Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Perineural Invasion 4.1. Tumor Microenvironment Extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening is a well-documented factor that drives malignancy and progression of multiple tumors, including pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and breast cancer [ , ]. Increased ECM stiffness has been shown to promote several malignant behaviors of cancer cells, such as enhanced proliferation, metabolic reprogramming, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), metastasis, and resistance to chemotherapy [ , , , ]. Recent studies demonstrate that a stiffened ECM significantly enhances the invasive capabilities of breast cancer cells [ ]. Additionally, ECM stiffness alters the secretory profile of breast cancer cells, increasing nerve growth factor (NGF) expression, further facilitating interactions between cancer cells and nerve structures, ultimately promoting PNI [ ]. Recent research by Han et al. (2024) explored the relationship between tumor microenvironment (TME) and PNI in breast cancer [ ]. Authors demonstrated that a stiff ECM facilitates PNI via integrin β1-mediated signaling pathways. They found that PNI-positive tumors exhibit increased activation of integrin β1, focal adhesion kinase (FAK), and Yes-associated protein (YAP), features associated with aggressive breast cancer behaviors, thereby supporting the clinical observations of poorer outcomes in PNI-positive cases [ ]. In other words, integrin β1 mediates mechanotransduction from ECM stiffness, activating FAK and YAP to promote PNI. Moreover, the type of nerve involved is of relevance, with sympathetic nerves primarily promoting tumor growth, and parasympathetic and sensory nerves exerting inhibitory effects on breast cancer progression [ ]. Integrins, a family of heterodimeric cell-adhesion molecules, play a critical role in cellular interaction with the ECM [ , ]. They establish a direct mechanical link between the cell and its surrounding microenvironment by binding extracellular ligands and the intracellular cytoskeleton [ , ]. Among these, integrin β1 has been identified as the primary receptor responding to ECM stiffness in breast cancer. The increase in ECM rigidity enhances integrin-mediated mechanotransduction, intensifying tumor malignancy. Clinically, human breast tumors are characterized as exhibiting a fibrotic and stiffened microenvironment, and breast cancer cells within these tumors demonstrate increased integrin activity, focal adhesion formation, and integrin signal transduction. Furthermore, data derived from clinical samples support the experimental findings, indicating a strong correlation between breast tumor stiffness and the frequency of PNI [ ]. Previous studies have established that tumor cells can activate downstream signaling cascades through ECM-binding receptors, including integrins, epithelial discoid protein domain receptors DDR1/2, mechanically sensitive channels PIEZO1/2, and the hyaluronic acid receptor CD44 [ , , ]. These receptors play key roles in converting mechanical signals from the ECM into intracellular pathways, affecting tumor cell behavior and disease progression. Matrix crosslinking and increased stiffness enhance integrin signaling, fostering tumor progression and invasiveness [ ]. Given these findings, targeting integrin-mediated mechanotransduction and associated signaling pathways presents a potential therapeutic opportunity to mitigate breast cancer progression and PNI [ , , , , ]. Conclusively, recent evidence suggests that ECM stiffness not only promotes tumor cell invasion and innervation but may also modulate immune cell

mechanically sensitive channels PIEZO1/2, and the hyaluronic acid receptor CD44 [ , , ]. These receptors play key roles in converting mechanical signals from the ECM into intracellular pathways, affecting tumor cell behavior and disease progression. Matrix crosslinking and increased stiffness enhance integrin signaling, fostering tumor progression and invasiveness [ ]. Given these findings, targeting integrin-mediated mechanotransduction and associated signaling pathways presents a potential therapeutic opportunity to mitigate breast cancer progression and PNI [ , , , , ]. Conclusively, recent evidence suggests that ECM stiffness not only promotes tumor cell invasion and innervation but may also modulate immune cell dynamics within the TME. A stiffened ECM has been shown to impair immune cell infiltration, particularly affecting T-cell trafficking and activation, potentially altering the immunological landscape required for tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) development. The resulting immunosuppressive milieu may hinder TLS formation or function, thus diminishing local antitumor immunity and permitting enhanced perineural spread. Additionally, mechanosensitive pathways activated by ECM rigidity, including the YAP/TAZ and FAK axes, may indirectly suppress chemokine gradients and stromal interactions essential for TLS maturation. 4.2. Tertiary Lymphoid Structures Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) are ectopic lymphoid formations that arise in response to chronic inflammation and contribute to local antitumor immunity. Their presence and interaction with stromal blood vessels influence tumor behavior, including PNI and LVI [ , , , ]. TLS absence in HER2-positive and TNBC correlates with increased PNI, suggesting a protective role against perineural spread. HER2+/TLS- tumors exhibit a significant increase in PNI, and TNBC/TLS- tumors show the higher risk of recurrence and invasion [ ]. These findings suggest that TLSs may play a protective role in limiting tumor progression and invasion. The influence of TLSs on tumor invasion is closely related to the TME, as their interaction with stromal blood vessels varies among breast cancer subtypes, affecting immune cell recruitment, vascularization, and metastatic potential [ ]. The interwoven connection between immune and stromal cells within TLSs is critical for their antitumor functions [ ]. Despite their association with higher tumor grades and LVI, TLSs also correlate with improved disease-free survival in HER2+ breast cancers, suggesting their dual role in tumor aggressiveness and immune surveillance [ ]. The prognostic significance of TLSs is further supported by their association with improved disease-free and overall breast cancer survival rates [ ]. For instance, one study found that TLSs are associated particularly with early-stage tumors and high tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. TLSs’ presence suggests a strong antitumor immune environment, reinforcing their potential as prognostic indicators in breast cancer [ ]. The interplay between ECM stiffness and TLS formation suggests a complex crosstalk between stromal mechanics and immune regulation in breast cancer. It is plausible that in tumors with highly fibrotic and rigid ECMs—such as in triple-negative and HER2-positive subtypes, as previously discussed—the physical properties of the stroma may limit immune cell recruitment or positioning, thereby impairing TLS assembly. This could explain the observed correlation between TLS absence and increased PNI in these subtypes. Moreover, the absence of TLSs may further permit unchecked neurotrophic signaling and tumor–nerve interactions, creating a permissive environment for neural infiltration. Thus, the convergence of biomechanical and immunological dysregulation may jointly facilitate perineural invasion in aggressive breast tumors. 4.3. Molecular Pathways Cancer innervation refers to the recruitment of nerves by tumors into the TME and the induction of nerve branches within the TME, which in turn affects cancer development [ , ]. Tumor innervation is considered a critical factor in cancer progression, as nerves regulate various biological processes within the TME, including cellular proliferation, immune evasion, and metastatic potential. Regarding the origin of these nerves, several studies have reported that tumors can recruit or modify peripheral nerves to support their growth [ , ]. This suggests an intricate interaction between cancer cells and the nervous system, enabling tumors to utilize neural signaling for their advantage. Specifically, tumor cells can induce axonal sprouting and neurogenesis, further incorporating nerve fibers into the TME [ ]. Pathological specimens reveal a higher density of nerve fibers in breast cancer tissue compared to normal breast tissue or benign breast tumor tissue, with a positive correlation between nerve density and tumor aggressiveness [ , ]. This association emphasizes the potential role that nerve infiltration may have in facilitating tumor progression [ ]. The presence of these nerve fibers may serve as a prognostic indicator of patient outcomes. Breast cancer cells can promote the intratumoral infiltration of nerve fibers, which further intensifies with the malignant progression of the disease. Several studies show that breast cancer cells secrete various cytokines, including neurotrophins and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), to promote the growth and branching of nerve fibers [ , , ]. Therefore, tumor-induced nerve growth is an active process driven by tumor-derived factors. The interaction between breast cancer cells and nerve fibers highlights a critical

infiltration may have in facilitating tumor progression [ ]. The presence of these nerve fibers may serve as a prognostic indicator of patient outcomes. Breast cancer cells can promote the intratumoral infiltration of nerve fibers, which further intensifies with the malignant progression of the disease. Several studies show that breast cancer cells secrete various cytokines, including neurotrophins and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), to promote the growth and branching of nerve fibers [ , , ]. Therefore, tumor-induced nerve growth is an active process driven by tumor-derived factors. The interaction between breast cancer cells and nerve fibers highlights a critical path in breast cancer pathology that may provide novel targets for therapeutic intervention. 5. Histological Features of Perineural and Intraneural Invasion in Breast Pathology Perineural and intraneural involvement in DCIS and IBC demonstrate significant histopathological findings ( ). In DCIS, tumor cells are present in the surrounding nerve sheath without invasion into the nerve itself. It has been shown that PNI in the context of DCIS often occurs in a background of complex sclerosing/radial scars and sclerosing adenosis, as mentioned previously, which can be a key histopathologic indicator of DCIS [ ]. By definition, DCIS is non-invasive; intraneural invasion is exclusive to invasive carcinomas. Therefore, compared to PNI, intraneural invasion involving DCIS is not possible, emphasizing intraneural invasion as a characteristic of IBC. Histological analysis often demonstrates displacement of epithelial glands into the perineural space closely mimicking true invasion and further complicating accurate pathological assessment through misinterpretation as invasive carcinoma. This emphasizes the need for increased awareness among pathologists regarding the potential for PNI in ADH and DCIS. Careful histopathological evaluation, along with correlation with clinical and radiologic findings, is essential to avoid misdiagnosis. In rare challenging cases, the use of immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis can be instrumental to help differentiate between DCIS and IBC and ensure accurate pathological diagnosis [ ]. In DCIS, the myoepithelial layer remains intact, whereas in invasive carcinoma, it is disrupted or lost [ ]. So IHC markers like p63 or calponin may be used to confirm myoepithelial integrity in DCIS, distinguishing it from invasive carcinoma. While IBC can demonstrate features of PNI similar to DCIS, the key defining feature in intraneural invasion includes the presence of tumor cells within the nerve fascicle [ ]. Specifically, infiltration into the endoneurium and axonal degeneration secondary to tumor cell invasion are key features. Histologically, PNI is identified based on standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections, where tumor cells are seen tracking along, wrapping around, or infiltrating nerves. There are no IHC stains currently validated or routinely used to predict PNI in any type of cancer, including breast cancer. While certain IHC markers (e.g., S100 and neurofilament proteins) may help highlight nerve fibers in challenging cases (for morphologic confirmation when nerves are hard to distinguish) [ , ], they are not used to predict PNI. In terms of predictive biomarkers, as discussed previously, studies have identified molecular markers (e.g., neurotrophins, MMPs, RET, etc.) associated with PNI, but none are currently used clinically in routine pathology. 6. Reporting Perineural Invasion in Breast Cancer Given the emerging research on PNI as a potential indicator of aggressive tumor behavior, standardizing PNI reporting especially in breast cancer could improve risk stratification. The College of American Pathologists (CAP) includes the assessment of PNI within its standardized guidelines for evaluating certain malignancies, such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, prostate, gastric, colorectal, gallbladder and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma [ , , , , , , ]. However, unlike other malignancies, the CAP protocol for breast cancer does not mandate PNI reporting, reflecting its uncertain prognostic value [ ]. This may reflect the inconsistencies in its detection and interpretation but equally highlights the need for additional research to bridge the gaps. Nonetheless, accurate documentation and incorporation of PNI in pathology reports will undoubtedly contribute to awareness of it and support clinicians in optimizing risk assessment. 7. Imaging Modalities for Perineural Invasion Detection in Breast Cancer Imaging modalities play a vital role in PNI diagnosis, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and computed tomography (CT). For detecting PNI in breast cancer, especially with suspected brachial plexus involvement, MRI remains the gold standard due to its superior soft tissue contrast and ability to visualize neural structures. These characteristics enhance MRI sensitivity for detecting PNI in breast cancer subtypes where perineural spread is suspected. Doran et al. (2024) described key MRI features indicative of PNI, including T2 signal expansion, abnormal enhancement, and loss of normal fat planes surrounding nerve pathways [ ]. In head and neck tumors, MRI can detect perineural tumor spread with a sensitivity of 95%, though its accuracy decreases to 63% when mapping the full extent of the spread [ ]. PET using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) serves as an adjunct imaging technique to MRI, detecting abnormal

soft tissue contrast and ability to visualize neural structures. These characteristics enhance MRI sensitivity for detecting PNI in breast cancer subtypes where perineural spread is suspected. Doran et al. (2024) described key MRI features indicative of PNI, including T2 signal expansion, abnormal enhancement, and loss of normal fat planes surrounding nerve pathways [ ]. In head and neck tumors, MRI can detect perineural tumor spread with a sensitivity of 95%, though its accuracy decreases to 63% when mapping the full extent of the spread [ ]. PET using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) serves as an adjunct imaging technique to MRI, detecting abnormal FDG accumulation along nerve pathways in a linear distribution. This pattern is highly suggestive of PNI, and when combined with MRI, enhances the accuracy of PNI detection [ ]. A CT scan is a secondary modality utilized for detecting PNI due to its decreased sensitivity compared to MRI. Tu et al. (2023) reported common CT findings, including abnormal soft-tissue attenuation extending along neural structures. However, CT’s low contrast resolution limits its effectiveness in accurately delineating nerve involvement [ ]. While imaging provides vital diagnostic and pathologic insight, limitations exist. PNI can mimic other conditions, including radiation-induced neuritis or chemotherapy-associated neuropathy [ ]. PNI may present with minimal abnormalities on MRI, such as intermediate T2 signal expansion or subtle abnormal enhancement extending along nerve pathways. These features create difficulty in detection without high-resolution imaging and careful interpretation [ ]. Post-therapy changes further complicate PNI detection, as prior surgical interventions or radiation therapy may distort anatomic structures, obscuring the presence of nerve invasion. This is particularly relevant in treatment-related fibrosis and scarring, common with breast cancer, which can mimic or mask perineural tumor spread [ ]. Technical limitations also pose additional challenges. High-resolution thin-cut contrast-enhanced MRI is optimal for detecting PNI, but specialized imaging may not be available in all clinical settings. Emerging techniques, including tractography and contrast-enhanced PET/MRI, hold promise for improving PNI detection but remain under investigation and are not yet widely accessible [ ]. 8. Clinical Manifestations of Perineural Spread in Breast Cancer In breast diseases, the clinical utility of imaging modalities is exemplified in case reports demonstrating their role in diagnosing perineural tumor spread. 8.1. Brachial Plexopathy from Perineural Spread The perineural spread of breast cancer to the brachial plexus is a rare but increasingly recognized phenomenon. Anatomical studies and clinical reports provide insight into pathways and manifestations. The pathways through which breast cancer metastasizes to the brachial plexus remain uncertain. However, proposed mechanisms describe PNI via longitudinal extension of neoplastic cells within the brachial plexus, occurring in both anterograde and retrograde directions. This allows for tumor spread to the nerves of the arm, cervical roots, spinal canal, spinal fluid, and contralateral brachial plexus [ ]. Anatomical studies suggest the intercostobrachial nerve is the most likely route, given its proximity to the breast and established communication with the brachial plexus. Established communications include the medial cord, medial and posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerves, and the T2 ventral ramus [ ]. Other potential, less common routes include the lateral and medial pectoral nerves, arising from the lateral and medial cords, and supraclavicular nerves, which may communicate with the brachial plexus via the suprascapular nerve and C5 root [ ]. Murthy et al. (2020) further support this hypothesis, suggesting that malignant cells invade small nerves with connections to the brachial plexus, such as the intercostobrachial, pectoral, and supraclavicular nerves, before spreading intraneurally to parent nerves and entering the brachial plexus [ ]. Given that most breast cancers originate in the upper outer quadrant, the intercostobrachial nerve is considered the most probable pathway for perineural spread [ ]. Loukas et al. (2006) described extrathoracic communication with the brachial plexus involving T2 and the intercostobrachial nerve. It was suggested that extrathoracic communications arise via the intercostobrachial nerve and medial cord and intrathoracically through the ventral ramus of T2, serving as conduits for perineural tumor spread [ ]. This theory was demonstrated in a case report involving a 51-year-old woman with a history of ER-positive IDC of the breast who developed progressive left brachial plexopathy more than 20 years following treatment [ ]. Her symptoms evolved from numbness and pain in the medial arm to weakness, Horner’s syndrome, and contralateral involvement, suggestive of bilateral PNI [ ]. MRI revealed diffuse thickening and nodular enhancement of the left brachial plexus, extending into the intradural C7 and C8 roots. PET/CT showed increased metabolic activity in the left brachial plexus. A fascicular biopsy of the left lower trunk confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma within the nerve, with strong ER positivity and HER2/neu amplification [ ]. Retrospective studies have further documented perineural spread of breast cancer to the brachial plexus. A study by Jack et al. (2022) reviewed 19 patients with biopsy-confirmed perineural spread [ ]. Im et al. (2024)

to weakness, Horner’s syndrome, and contralateral involvement, suggestive of bilateral PNI [ ]. MRI revealed diffuse thickening and nodular enhancement of the left brachial plexus, extending into the intradural C7 and C8 roots. PET/CT showed increased metabolic activity in the left brachial plexus. A fascicular biopsy of the left lower trunk confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma within the nerve, with strong ER positivity and HER2/neu amplification [ ]. Retrospective studies have further documented perineural spread of breast cancer to the brachial plexus. A study by Jack et al. (2022) reviewed 19 patients with biopsy-confirmed perineural spread [ ]. Im et al. (2024) described seven patients with brachial plexopathy secondary to perineural tumor spread, identifying IDC (3), metaplastic carcinoma (1), lung adenocarcinoma (2), and papillary thyroid carcinoma (1) as primary malignancies. Initial presentation involved progressive unilateral pain or paresthesia, followed by motor weakness, with lower trunk plexopathy being the most common electrodiagnostic finding [ ]. 8.2. Intradural Extramedullary Metastasis via Perineural Invasion Rare cases of intradural extramedullary metastasis via PNI illustrate the potential for breast carcinoma to metastasize to the spinal cord and nerve root ganglia. Schulz et al. (2009) reported a case of breast cancer metastasis to the L2 nerve root ganglion, involving intradural tumor spread. A 46-year-old female presented with severe right-sided radicular pain and moderate weakness of hip flexion and knee extension. MRI revealed an L2 nerve root lesion, followed by histologic examination confirming breast cancer metastasis via immunostaining [ ]. Jayakumar et al. (2020) described a woman in her late sixties with breast cancer and pre-existing infiltrative disease of the left brachial plexus. Spinal MRI revealed an intramedullary spinal cord metastasis at C6-C7. This case highlights intramedullary metastases with the potential for PNI extending beyond brachial plexus lesions into the spinal cord [ ]. Similarly, Mackel et al. (2020) reported a 66-year-old woman with a history of node-positive ER/PR-positive infiltrating ductal carcinoma, who developed bilateral buttock and leg pain, twelve years later. MRI of the total spine revealed a bilobed, intradural, intramedullary–extramedullary, homogenously enhancing lesion involving the conus medullaris and cauda equina. The lesions confirmed suspicion of intradural metastasis via PNI, secondary to prior breast carcinoma. This case further emphasizes the delayed and unpredictable nature of perineural metastatic spread in breast cancer, as well as the devastating consequences associated with extension to the spinal cord and nerve roots [ ]. 8.3. Optic Nerve Sheath Metastasis Optic nerve sheath metastasis, though rare, presents with vision loss and perineural enhancement on MRI. A large study by Yousef et al. (2024) analyzed 9902 breast cancer patients, reporting that 0.5% developed ocular or periocular metastasis, which accounted for 2.4% of all metastatic cases. Further breakdown displayed optic nerve involvement in 11% of those cases, with 44% of patients exhibiting bilateral disease. The time of ocular metastasis varied, with 49% occurring after breast cancer diagnosis, 24% occurring concurrently, and 5% appearing before primary tumor diagnosis. The most common sites of ocular metastasis included the orbit (47%), choroid (40%), and iris (2%) [ ]. Gasperini et al. (2007) reported a 36-year-old woman with bilateral optic neuropathy and central nervous system metastasis from breast carcinoma. Brain and orbital MRI revealed diffuse meningeal enhancement, perineural enhancement of both optic nerves, and enhancement of the right optic nerve head, consistent with metastatic disease [ ]. Similarly, Verma et al. (2019) described a 68-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer and bone metastases who presented with blurring in her left eye two decades after mastectomy. Examination revealed an isolated peripapillary mass, with MRI confirming optic disc metastasis secondary to breast carcinoma [ ]. In another case, Biswas et al. (2007) reported a 39-year-old woman with a known history of breast cancer who developed bilateral painless vision loss. Examination revealed subretinal lesions, retinal detachment, and later left proptosis with ocular movement restriction, indicating extraocular metastatic spread. Histopathology confirmed lobular adenocarcinoma, highlighting the potential for optic nerve and retinal involvement in metastatic breast cancer [ ]. 9. Prognostic Significance of PNI in Breast Cancer Given the wide range of PNI frequencies reported in breast cancer, its prognostic relevance remains unclear. Nevertheless, Liebig et al. (2009) highlighted an important consideration in that PNI is frequently reported jointly with LVI as one pathologic feature in breast cancer, clouding its value as an independent prognostic marker [ ]. For instance, in two separate retrospective studies, McCready et al. (1996 and 2000) evaluated PNI in conjunction with LVI in IBC [ , ]. Findings from the two studies suggested an association between these combined features and increased risks of local recurrence and distant metastasis [ , ] ( ). 9.1. Perineural Invasion and Locoregional Recurrence PNI has been studied in many different types of cancers, but there is still debate over its significance in breast cancer and whether it directly increases the risk of

pathologic feature in breast cancer, clouding its value as an independent prognostic marker [ ]. For instance, in two separate retrospective studies, McCready et al. (1996 and 2000) evaluated PNI in conjunction with LVI in IBC [ , ]. Findings from the two studies suggested an association between these combined features and increased risks of local recurrence and distant metastasis [ , ] ( ). 9.1. Perineural Invasion and Locoregional Recurrence PNI has been studied in many different types of cancers, but there is still debate over its significance in breast cancer and whether it directly increases the risk of LRR or if it is just a marker of more aggressive tumors [ , , , , ]. Narayan et al. (2021) found a higher 7-year LRR rate in PNI-positive cases (7.1% vs. 4.7%) in a cohort of 8864 IBC patients. After controlling for key clinical and pathological variables, the risk of LRR remained notably higher among patients with PNI (hazard ratio 1.46, p = 0.034), conferring an increased risk of recurrence, comparable in magnitude to LVI and ER/PR-negative receptor status. These findings reflect the possible prognostic impact of PNI in breast cancer [ ]. 9.2. Perineural Invasion Versus Lymphovascular Invasion Several studies have examined the relationship between PNI and LVI in breast cancer, with differing conclusions on whether PNI independently affects prognosis. Narayan et al. (2021) [ ] found that tumors with PNI were more likely to also have LVI, but PNI predicted worse outcomes, whereas LVI showed an association but had weaker hazard ratio and lower statistical confidence. Hosoya et al. (2023) confirmed a strong association between PNI and LVI and found that PNI independently predicted recurrence even when adjusting for LVI [ ]. On the other hand, Duraker et al. (2006) observed a strong correlation between PNI and LVI but concluded that PNI was not an independent prognostic factor, and that LVI contributed more toward prognosis and survival whereas PNI was not statistically significant [ ]. Therefore, although all three studies show a relationship between PNI and LVI, they ultimately have differing conclusions in terms of the role that PNI has on prognosis. While Narayan et al. (2021) and Hosoya et al. (2023) both support PNI as an independent prognostic factor even after LVI is adjusted for, Duraker et al. (2006) found it non-significant after adjusting for LVI [ , , ]. These conflicting results may stem from several factors. First, the definition and histologic criteria used to diagnose PNI may vary across studies, potentially affecting consistency in reporting. Second, differences in sample size and patient cohorts—particularly in terms of tumor subtype distribution, stage at diagnosis, and treatment modalities—could influence statistical power and outcomes. Additionally, variations in how LVI is assessed and controlled for in multivariate models may impact the apparent independent contribution of PNI. That being said, there is a need for standardized diagnostic criteria and large-scale prospective studies to determine the true prognostic value of PNI in breast cancer. 10. Therapeutic Implications and Future Directions 10.1. Current Treatment Approaches Breast cancer that presents with PNI has become an increasingly important feature when it comes to assessing tumor biology and patient prognostic factors with the aim of establishing effective therapeutic measures. The interaction of malignancies with the peripheral nervous system has been shown to be a crucial component in the progression of such neoplasms [ ]. Furthermore, breast lesions such as ADH and DCIS of the breast, which may exhibit PNI, indicate the possibility of early involvement of the nervous system and its structures in tumor development [ , , ]. Currently, the mainstay of treatment of breast cancer remains hormonal therapy, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and surgical intervention [ , ]. Radiation may reduce LRR risk in PNI-positive cases, similar to its use in head and neck cancers [ ]. While there is a strong association between PNI and cancer outcomes in other malignancies such as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, prompting the use of radiation therapy to improve local control [ , ], a lack of enough resources has yet to indicate such an association in breast cancer [ ]. Radiation therapy is indicated in breast cancer treatment after surgery and sometimes before surgery (neoadjuvant therapy) to reduce the risk of recurrence, particularly in cases with high-risk pathological features, such as lymph node involvement, large tumors (larger than 5 cm) which carry a higher risk of recurrence, positive or close surgical margins, and cancers with extensive LVI [ , ]. Current breast cancer therapies do not adjust for PNI status. Patients with TNBC may benefit from intensified chemotherapy regimens, such as anthracycline and taxane-based therapies, due to the aggressive nature of TNBC [ ]. For HER2-positive subtypes, the addition of targeted therapies like trastuzumab is beneficial, despite the PNI status [ ]. Hormone receptor-positive subtypes

therapy) to reduce the risk of recurrence, particularly in cases with high-risk pathological features, such as lymph node involvement, large tumors (larger than 5 cm) which carry a higher risk of recurrence, positive or close surgical margins, and cancers with extensive LVI [ , ]. Current breast cancer therapies do not adjust for PNI status. Patients with TNBC may benefit from intensified chemotherapy regimens, such as anthracycline and taxane-based therapies, due to the aggressive nature of TNBC [ ]. For HER2-positive subtypes, the addition of targeted therapies like trastuzumab is beneficial, despite the PNI status [ ]. Hormone receptor-positive subtypes may require a combination of endocrine therapy and chemotherapy to address the potential for LRR. 10.2. Emerging Targets for Therapy Current breast cancer therapies do not adjust for PNI status, but emerging data suggest targeted therapies could benefit PNI-positive cases. In fact, growing research regarding therapy for malignancies that are positive for PNI has led to several novel targets that may impact the process which drives PNI. 10.2.1. Integrin Signaling and ECM Stiffness Within this category of potential therapeutic methods, the role of the ECM and the role of integrins in the spread and invasion of PNI-positive tumors has been assessed [ ]. Inhibiting integrin β1 or NGF signaling could disrupt PNI mechanisms, offering new therapeutic possibilities. It has been demonstrated by Han et al. (2024) that integrin signaling through B1-FAK-YAP is further promoted by a stiffened microenvironment within tumors [ ]. The evidence highlighted indicates that possibly targeting integrin B1 could disrupt this cascade pathway and, in turn, reduce tumor invasion into neural structures [ ]. Additionally, integrin B4 is another component that has shown expression not only in vascular and lymphatic structures, but also in peripheral nerves, which supports current research in using it as a staining marker compared to the more conventional H&E [ ]. Research into this molecule can potentially reveal further possibilities in the development of therapeutic measures, in addition to detection methods currently being studied. 10.2.2. Neurotrophic Factor Blockade Adding on to other studied methods involving integrin signaling, the effective blockade of neurotrophic signaling has become a promising strategy in the treatment of PNI-positive breast cancer [ ]. Nerve growth factor (NGF) has been reported to be a target for such therapy due to the associated overexpression of NGF in breast cancer cells when compared to other tissues such as breast epithelium [ ]. This further indicates that an increase in NGF may be associated with further growth in breast cancer cells, and it has been discovered that effectively diminishing or neutralizing NGF contributed to reduced ability of malignant cell proliferation [ ]. This indicates that if NGF reduction reduced malignant cell proliferation, then inhibiting NGF may provide improved outcomes in inhibiting tumor growth [ ]. Additionally, further studies regarding neurotrophic factor blockades have indicated that anti-NGF antibodies can significantly reduce the neurotrophic effect of NGF and thus inhibit nerve fiber growth, which is a crucial component in PNI-positive breast cancers [ ]. 10.3. Need for Further Research Understanding the molecular pathways for targeted interventions is also essential, as PNI is not considered a passive process anymore, but active biological crosstalk between nerves and malignant cells [ ]. A key pathway being assessed within the neurotrophin receptor system is NGF-TrkA signaling which indicates that this pathway is a chief contributor for PNI [ ]. This pathway is being increasingly researched due to higher TrkA expression being observed in IBCs [ ], opening the possibility for this pathway being studied for the development of effective therapy [ ]. Additionally, another pathway that would be crucial to further understanding PNI-positive breast cancer is the MAPK/ERK pathway. This is due to studies indicating that the MAPK/ERK pathways are involved in the signaling that contributes to malignant spread of cancer cells [ , ], possibly by contributing to their ability to affect the ECM around nerves. 11. Conclusions Perineural invasion in breast pathology holds important clinicopathological implications. Its association with aggressive tumor behavior, potential locoregional recurrence, and possible poor prognosis highlights the need for improved recognition and reporting. Advances in molecular profiling have begun to elucidate the complex tumor–neural interactions that facilitate PNI, suggesting potential targets for therapeutic intervention. However, current knowledge remains limited due to the lack of standardized diagnostic criteria. Addressing these gaps through future research could refine risk stratification models and guide personalized treatment strategies. Recognizing the significance of PNI in breast cancer may ultimately contribute to better clinical management and patient outcomes. Therefore, future research should standardize PNI definitions, explore its molecular basis, and evaluate targeted therapies to improve outcomes in PNI-positive breast cancer.

chunks.content: Introduction Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS) comprises a heterogeneous group of hereditary connective tissue disorders characterized by joint hypermobility, skin fragility, and abnormalities in collagen synthesis and structure. Although its clinical manifestations are predominantly musculoskeletal and cutaneous, recent years have revealed a broader spectrum of neurological and radiological complications, whose frequency remains low but carries significant diagnostic implications [ , ]. Among these manifestations, involvement of the central and peripheral nervous system in patients with EDS is uncommon and poorly documented. Optic neuritis, typically associated with inflammatory or demyelinating processes, has rarely been described in the context of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, raising questions about potential mechanisms of tissue vulnerability and predisposition to inflammatory phenomena. Similarly, schwannomatosis, characterized by the presence of multiple schwannomas without vestibular involvement represents a rare entity that shares genetic and clinical features with neurofibromatosis type 2, but with a distinct profile regarding prognosis and management [ ]. The co-occurrence between bilateral optic neuritis and a nerve sheath tumor in a patient with classical‑like Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (clEDS) constitutes an exceptional finding from a radiological perspective. This case provides educational value by highlighting the importance of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a diagnostic tool for simultaneously identifying inflammatory processes of the optic nerve and neuroaxis tumor lesions [ ]. The presentation herein aims to contribute to the existing literature through a detailed description of unusual radiological findings in a patient with EDS, emphasizing the rarity of this co-occurrence and its relevance for clinical and academic practice in radiology. Case presentation We present the case of a 26-year-old female patient with no personal history of chronic comorbidities and a family history of lymphoma in her paternal grandfather. She presented a 2-month history of fluctuating amaurosis in the right eye, accompanied by migraine-like headache with aura, arthralgia in the shoulders and knees, alopecia, and paresthesia in the lower limbs. On initial physical examination, the patient was conscious, oriented, afebrile, with blood pressure of 110/80 mmHg, heart rate of seventy beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 99%. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed optic disc blurring, while neurological assessment showed preserved muscle strength, normal reflexes, and absence of meningeal signs or focal deficits. Hyperchromatic café-au-lait macules were observed on the upper limbs, a finding that raised suspicion of phacomatosis. Laboratory studies revealed abnormal values of anti-Ro, anti-La antibodies, borderline levels of anti-Sm, and anti-β2 glycoprotein antibodies, along with low complement C3 and C4 levels and proteinuria of 127 mg/24 h ( ). The remaining hematologic and biochemical parameters were within normal limits, including hemoglobin of 13.8 g/dL and preserved renal function. These findings suggested the possibility of early or indeterminate connective tissue disease. Radiological assessment was the cornerstone of diagnosis. Orbital MRI demonstrated thickening and signal intensity changes in both optic nerves, with post-contrast enhancement, consistent with active bilateral optic neuritis, more pronounced on the right side ( ). Brain MRI revealed a lesion within Meckel’s cave with partial extension into the ipsilateral lateral pontine cistern, suggestive of a trigeminal nerve sheath tumor ( ). Enhancement along the cisternal segment of the trigeminal nerve and expansion of Meckel’s cave further increased suspicion of a neural origin tumor. Cervical MRI revealed intramedullary nodular lesions at C5 and C7 ( A). Thoracic MRI demonstrated multiple solid lesions located intradural-extramedullary and intramedullary ( B). Finally, lumbar and sacral MRI identified multiple intradural-extramedullary nodules arising from the filum terminale and cauda equina ( C). Overall, the radiological findings suggested multiple nerve sheath tumors in the intradural‑extramedullary compartment, with additional intramedullary nodular lesions of indeterminate etiology. Additional complementary studies included transesophageal echocardiography, which showed prolapse of the anterior mitral leaflet and an aneurysmal interatrial septum without interatrial communication ( A), and abdominal ultrasound revealing a simple cyst in the left kidney without other abnormalities ( B). Although incidental, these findings were documented as part of a comprehensive evaluation. The patient received immunosuppressive therapy with mycophenolate mofetil and deflazacort, along with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and supportive measures. Rheumatology considered initiating rituximab in the context of an indeterminate connective tissue disease. During hospitalization, the patient showed favorable clinical evolution without new neurological deficits and was discharged after 5 days, with scheduled follow-up in ophthalmology, neurology, neurosurgery, and genetics. During outpatient follow-up, a genetic profile was performed, revealing TNXB variants consistent with clEDS, OMIM 606408 . This finding correlated clinically with joint hypermobility, mitral valve prolapse, arthralgia, and slender habitus, leading to the formal syndromic diagnosis and continuation of a multidisciplinary approach involving rheumatology, ophthalmology, neurology, neurosurgery, and genetics. Genetic counseling, cardiovascular and joint surveillance, and imaging follow-up were recommended given the coexistence of bilateral optic neuritis and spinal space-occupying lesions compatible with schwannomatosis, with plans to expand genetic studies for phacomatosis as clinically indicated. Monitoring of immunological parameters and mild proteinuria (127 mg/24 h) continued, with no evidence of renal impairment,

a genetic profile was performed, revealing TNXB variants consistent with clEDS, OMIM 606408 . This finding correlated clinically with joint hypermobility, mitral valve prolapse, arthralgia, and slender habitus, leading to the formal syndromic diagnosis and continuation of a multidisciplinary approach involving rheumatology, ophthalmology, neurology, neurosurgery, and genetics. Genetic counseling, cardiovascular and joint surveillance, and imaging follow-up were recommended given the coexistence of bilateral optic neuritis and spinal space-occupying lesions compatible with schwannomatosis, with plans to expand genetic studies for phacomatosis as clinically indicated. Monitoring of immunological parameters and mild proteinuria (127 mg/24 h) continued, with no evidence of renal impairment, and medical management was adjusted according to clinical and radiological activity. The final diagnosis integrated clinical, radiological, and genetic findings: active bilateral optic neuritis with right-sided predominance; left trigeminal nerve tumor; multiple spinal nerve sheath tumors; clEDS associated with TNXB gene variants, with mitral valve prolapse; indeterminate connective tissue disease with hypocomplementemia and borderline serologies (anti-Ro/La/Sm and anti-β2GPI); and Gilbert’s syndrome. Discussion Optic neuritis is an inflammatory optic neuropathy that typically presents with acute or subacute visual loss [ , , ]. Bilateral involvement is less common and warrants consideration of alternative etiologies beyond classical multiple sclerosis, particularly neuromyelitis Optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) [ , , ]. In our patient, orbital MRI demonstrated bilateral optic nerve thickening and contrast enhancement consistent with active inflammation. Antibody testing for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG was not available, limiting etiologic clarification. From a radiological perspective, brain and orbital MRI is the study of choice for evaluating optic neuritis [ ]. Brain MRI is used to identify periventricular demyelinating lesions, typically oval and larger than 3 mm, most associated with multiple sclerosis or neuromyelitis Optica [ ]. Enhancement and thickening of the optic nerve on contrast-enhanced MRI (gadolinium) confirms active inflammation [ ]. The American College of Radiology (ACR) recommends contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits as the most appropriate initial study when optic neuritis is suspected, both to confirm the diagnosis and to rule out other etiologies and assess the risk of multiple sclerosis [ ]. In our patient, bilateral optic neuritis was identified with right-sided predominance as an uncommon and clinically relevant finding, although optic neuritis is well documented in the literature [ ]. Comprehensive neuroaxis MRI revealed multiple intradural-extramedullary and intramedullary nodular lesions involving cranial and spinal segments [ ]. These findings were radiologically compatible with multiple nerve sheath tumors [ ]. However, according to updated 2022 consensus criteria, definitive classification of schwannomatosis requires molecular testing for SMARCB1, LZTR1, or NF2 variants [ ]. In the absence of genetic confirmation, the diagnosis remains presumptive. Café-au-lait macules prompted evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), but the patient did not meet NIH diagnostic criteria, as no cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic pathway gliomas were present. [ ] Systemic causes of bilateral optic neuritis such as sarcoidosis should also be considered; however, our patient demonstrated no clinical, radiologic, or laboratory features suggestive of granulomatous disease. According to the 2017 International Classification of the Ehlers–Danlos syndromes, classic EDS is primarily associated with COL5A1 and COL5A2 variants while TNXB variants are associated with clEDS [ ]. Neurological involvement is not considered a defining feature of this subtype. Therefore, rather than suggesting a shared pathophysiological mechanism, the present findings are more appropriately interpreted as a rare co-occurrence of independent pathological processes. From a radiologic perspective, this case underscores the value of complete neuroaxis MRI in patients presenting with atypical optic neuritis and concurrent neural lesions. Careful integration of imaging, clinical findings, and genetic data is essential to avoid overinterpretation and to guide multidisciplinary management. This case report has several limitations. Histopathological confirmation of the nerve sheath tumors was not obtained. Molecular testing for SMARCB1, LZTR1, and NF2 variants was not available, precluding definitive classification according to updated schwannomatosis criteria. Antibody testing for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG was not performed, limiting etiologic clarification of bilateral optic neuritis. Although a TNXB variant was identified, full molecular characterization and segregation analysis were not available. Finally, the relatively short follow-up period restricts conclusions regarding long-term progression and sustained treatment response. Conclusion/Teaching points The coexistence of bilateral optic neuritis and multiple nerve sheath tumors in a patient with genetically characterized classical‑like EDS (TNXB variant) represents a rare and diagnostically challenging presentation. Comprehensive neuroaxis imaging plays a central role in identifying concurrent inflammatory and tumoral processes, while cautious interpretation and multidisciplinary evaluation are essential to ensure appropriate management. Patient consent Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this case report and any accompanying images. All personal identifiers have been removed or anonymized to protect the patient’s privacy and confidentiality.

documents.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria staging of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

chunks.content: Introduction Pancreatic cancer (PC) is among the most aggressive abdominal malignancies. Although its incidence is lower than that of colorectal and gastric cancers, its mortality consistently ranks among the highest [ ]. Epidemiological evidence indicates a sustained rise in PC incidence over the past two decades, and by 2040 it is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide [ ]. At present, surgical resection remains the only treatment with curative potential. However, most patients present at diagnosis with locally advanced disease or distant metastases, and fewer than 20% are eligible for resection [ ]. Accordingly, precise preoperative assessment of tumor resectability, vascular involvement, and distant metastasis has become a key determinant of prognosis and a cornerstone for guiding individualized therapeutic strategies. Imaging plays an indispensable role in the early detection and preoperative staging of PC, a priority repeatedly emphasized across major international guidelines. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network recommends multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) as the first-line modality for preoperative assessment [ ]; the European Society for Medical Oncology highlights magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)—particularly magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRI-MRCP)—for its unique advantages in delineating the pancreatobiliary ducts and detecting small lesions [ ]; and the American College of Radiology underscores the central role of endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) in early lesion detection and histologic tissue acquisition [ ]. Collectively, these positions underscore the complementary and integrative value of MDCT, MRI, and EUS within the diagnostic pathway. Specifically, MDCT, by virtue of superior spatial resolution and vascular reconstruction, is widely used for initial preoperative screening and staging; MRI, with excellent soft-tissue contrast and high-resolution depiction of the pancreatobiliary ducts, outperforms computed tomography (CT) for evaluating ductal involvement and detecting small-volume lesions; and EUS, leveraging ultrahigh near-field resolution, is indispensable for identifying lesions < 2 cm and for tissue acquisition. In recent years, emerging techniques—including contrast-enhanced EUS (EUS-CE) [ ], manganese dipyridoxyl diphosphate–enhanced MRI (MRI-MnDPDP) [ ], ^18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography combined with multidetector computed tomography dynamic perfusion contrast-enhancement (PETCT-18F-FDG+MDCT-DPCE) [ ], and the pancreatic multiphase contrast-enhanced MDCT protocol (CT-MDCE-Panc) [ ]—have expanded diagnostic boundaries, demonstrating substantial potential to improve diagnostic sensitivity and specificity and reflecting a broader shift from purely morphologic assessment toward functional and molecular imaging. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of these modalities in routine practice remains debated. EUS offers high sensitivity, but specificity can be affected by operator experience and lesion location. MDCT is indispensable for assessing vascular invasion and distant metastasis, yet its ability to detect early, small-volume lesions is relatively constrained. MRI provides superior delineation of local anatomy and pancreatobiliary ductal structures, but its clinical deployment is often restricted by availability and cost [ – ]. Within this complex clinical landscape, optimizing the integration and selection of imaging modalities has become a central challenge in the management of PC. Despite the central role of imaging in the management of PC, substantial differences persist among modalities in sensitivity, specificity, and clinical applicability, and no consensus has been reached on an optimal choice. Prior systematic reviews have largely been confined to pairwise comparisons, limiting the integration of multimodal evidence and precluding an overall ranking of diagnostic performance, which in turn hampers evidence translation into clinical practice. Against this background, and within a graded reference standard framework, a Bayesian network meta-analysis (Bayesian NMA) was undertaken to synthesize direct and indirect comparative evidence, enabling systematic comparison and ranking of multiple imaging techniques so as to provide a more robust and generalizable evidence base for preoperative evaluation and clinical decision-making in PC. Materials and methods The study adhered to the latest international standards for systematic reviews and meta-analyses and their extensions, including the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [ ], the PRISMA extension for Diagnostic Test Accuracy (PRISMA-DTA) [ ], and the PRISMA extension for Network Meta-analyses (PRISMA-NMA) [ ]. The protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420251133046). Inclusion criteria Study population Eligible participants were patients with PC undergoing preoperative evaluation. Diagnosis and staging were defined according to the ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pancreatic Cancer (2023) [ ], with reference to the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma and their interpretive publications [ ], and the ACR Appropriateness Criteria® for Staging of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma [ ]. To ensure uniformity, studies were included if verification of the original articles unambiguously confirmed that enrolled patients met the above guideline-based criteria for PC. No restrictions were imposed on sex, age, or race. Imaging modalities included EUS, MRI, CT, and transabdominal ultrasound (TA-US), encompassing both conventional protocols and contrast-enhanced techniques. ACR Appropriateness Criteria® for Staging of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma [ ]. To ensure uniformity, studies were included if verification of the original articles unambiguously confirmed that enrolled patients met the above guideline-based criteria for PC. No restrictions were imposed on sex, age, or race. Interventions Eligible studies were required to use imaging examinations as the primary diagnostic approach, with objectives focused on evaluating the preoperative diagnostic performance for PC. Imaging modalities included EUS, MRI, CT, and transabdominal ultrasound (TA-US), encompassing both conventional protocols and contrast-enhanced techniques. Multimodal combined imaging strategies were also considered; however, standalone positron emission tomography (PET) was not eligible. Studies could evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of a single modality or conduct parallel or combined comparisons across multiple modalities. Any study involving the above techniques and reporting extractable diagnostic performance data met the inclusion criteria. Outcomes Eligible studies were required to report at least one imaging diagnostic performance metric, including sensitivity (SEN), specificity (SPE), area under the curve (AUC), positive likelihood ratio (PLR), negative likelihood ratio (NLR), and diagnostic odds ratio (DOR). These metrics could be provided directly by the original articles or derived by constructing 2 × 2 contingency tables (true positive, TP; false positive, FP; false negative, FN; true negative, TN). Study design Eligible studies were prospective diagnostic accuracy studies conducted at single or multiple centers, with consecutive or random enrollment and extractable raw diagnostic data (2 × 2 contingency tables) for network comparison. We did not restrict eligibility to randomized controlled trials; instead, we applied prespecified design-based criteria and assessed risk of bias and applicability using QUADAS-2. Reference standard (gold standard) Level-1 (highest level): Histopathological confirmation based on resected surgical specimens, including pancreaticoduodenectomy, distal pancreatectomy, or central pancreatectomy. This standard applied to resectable or borderline-resectable cases, with postoperative pathology confirming pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), and with the interval between imaging and surgery minimized. Level-2 (intermediate level): Positive histopathological or cytological findings obtained via invasive sampling, including endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA), aspiration cytology, or brush cytology collected through endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). This standard applied to unresectable cases or patients requiring a definitive diagnosis prior to systemic therapy, with explicit documentation of the sampling site and results unequivocally indicative of PDAC. Level-3 (lowest level): In the absence of tissue confirmation, a composite reference standard determined by multidisciplinary consensus, integrating characteristic imaging progression, evidence of distant metastasis, and follow-up outcomes. The minimum follow-up duration was 6 months; follow-up of ≥ 12 months conferred higher diagnostic reliability. This standard applied to patients in whom pathologic evidence could not be obtained due to high-risk factors or refusal of invasive procedures. In the primary analyses, Level-1 and Level-2 standards were prioritized as reference criteria; Level-3 studies were included only when necessary to maintain network connectivity. Exclusion criteria Studies were excluded if: (i) they were not prospective diagnostic study—such as retrospective studies, observational studies, case series, case reports, reviews, or existing systematic reviews/meta-analyses; (ii) the study population did not meet the prespecified criteria, including postoperative patients, healthy controls, animal experiments, or cohorts not clearly defined as preoperative individuals with clinically or imaging-based high suspicion of PC; (iii) the imaging modality fell outside the prespecified scope—i.e., did not use EUS, MRI, CT, or transabdominal ultrasound (TA-US) as the principal diagnostic tool. Studies of standalone PET were excluded; multimodal protocols were eligible if they included at least one of the aforementioned modalities; (iv) the intervention did not align with the study objective, such as studies limited to therapeutic procedures, optimization of image-guided biopsy trajectories, sampling methodology research, or imaging applications unrelated to the diagnosis of PC; (v) serious design deficiencies precluded extraction or derivation of diagnostic-performance data, such as absence of a parallel comparator, missing key outcomes, or evidently duplicated datasets; (vi) the prespecified reference standards were not used (Level-1, Level-2, or Level-3 meeting the minimum requirements). Search strategy A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was conducted to identify clinical studies evaluating EUS, MRI, and CT for preoperative diagnosis in PC. The strategy combined subject headings and free-text terms, including “pancreatic cancer,” “pancreatic neoplasms,” “pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC),” “endoscopic ultrasound,” “magnetic resonance imaging,” “computed tomography,” “diagnosis,” “preoperative evaluation,” and “imaging examination.” The time frame spanned database inception to July 12, 2025. In PubMed, filters were set to Clinical Trial, Humans, and publication years 2000–2025; equivalent restrictions were applied to the other databases. The finalized PubMed search string is presented in Table , and complete strategies for the remaining databases are provided in the Appendix. Study selection and data extraction All retrieved records were independently screened by two reviewers. Titles and abstracts were first assessed against the prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria; studies deemed potentially eligible then underwent full-text review to determine final inclusion. Any discrepancies were adjudicated by a third reviewer. For all included studies,

The finalized PubMed search string is presented in Table , and complete strategies for the remaining databases are provided in the Appendix. Study selection and data extraction All retrieved records were independently screened by two reviewers. Titles and abstracts were first assessed against the prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria; studies deemed potentially eligible then underwent full-text review to determine final inclusion. Any discrepancies were adjudicated by a third reviewer. For all included studies, data were extracted using a predesigned, standardized Excel spreadsheet, capturing article title, first author, year of publication, country/region, sample size, patient age, sex distribution, imaging modality, comparator(s), and reference standard. Diagnostic performance data (TP, FP, FN, TN) were taken directly from the original publications and cross-checked to ensure accuracy and internal consistency. Risk of bias assessment Methodological quality was evaluated using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool [ ], assessing risk of bias and applicability concerns across four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. Two reviewers conducted the assessments independently with cross-verification; disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. All procedures were implemented in RevMan 5.4 (Cochrane Collaboration, London, UK), and risk-of-bias plots and summary tables were generated for visualization to support the objectivity and consistency of the conclusions. Statistical analysis All analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.3) within a JAGS environment, using a Bayesian bivariate random-effects framework (Reitsma model) to synthesize diagnostic performance across imaging modalities. Weakly informative priors were specified, and posterior distributions were obtained via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The sampling scheme comprised 4 chains (adaptation 20,000; iterations 60,000; thinning interval = 4). Convergence was assessed by inspection of trace plots and the Gelman–Rubin diagnostic; potential scale reduction factors were approximately 1 (≤1.05), indicating stable and reliable posterior estimates. Effect measures included SEN, SPE, DOR, and Youden’s index, each reported with 95% credible intervals (CrI). Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the posterior variances of the study-level random effects on the logit scale (τ 2 _SEN = sd_se 2 ; τ 2 _SPE = sd_sp 2 ), together with their covariance (ρ·sd_se·sd_sp) and correlation (ρ), all summarized by posterior medians and 95% CrI. At the network level, comparative ranking was conducted using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), cumulative ranking probability curves, and a league heatmap, with robustness additionally examined through relative sensitivity (RSEN) and relative specificity (RSP) models. Local inconsistency was evaluated by node-splitting to compare direct and indirect evidence, while transitivity was appraised empirically with attention to study design, grading of the reference standard (Level-1 to Level-3), and balance in index–reference test pairing and flow/timing. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the dependence of SUCRA rankings on individual studies. Overall diagnostic performance was synthesized using SROC curves derived via the Reitsma approach, and publication bias was explored with funnel plots and Egger’s regression test. Finally, key comparisons were graded with the GRADE framework across five domains—risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias—to support the evidentiary reliability and generalizability of the conclusions for clinical application. Results Literature search Systematic searches of PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were conducted, with limits set to clinical studies in humans and publication years 2000–2025. The search yielded 1440 records; 519 remained after deduplication. Title and abstract screening excluded 489 records, leaving 30 studies for full-text assessment. A further 20 articles were excluded for not meeting the inclusion criteria, and 10 prospective diagnostic studies were ultimately included for quantitative synthesis and analysis. The study selection flow is shown in Fig. . Study characteristics A total of 10 prospective diagnostic studies were included, encompassing single-arm and multi-arm designs and comprising 623 patients; all studies conducted analyses at the patient level. Most investigations adopted Level-1 as the primary reference standard; where surgery was not feasible, Level-2 and, when necessary, Level-3 standards were used as supplements. Eight imaging interventions were represented: MRI-MRCP ( n = 2) [ , ]; ERCP-IDUS ( n = 3) [ – ]; EUS-B ( n = 4) [ – ]; CT-MDCE-Panc ( n = 4) [ , , , ]; EUS-CE ( n = 2) [ , ]; TA-US ( n = 2) [ , ]; MRI-MnDPDP ( n = 1) [ ]; and PETCT-18F-FDG+MDCT-DPCE ( n = 1) [ ]. All studies were published between 2000 and 2012, in English, and were conducted across multiple countries, including Germany, Italy, and France. The baseline characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table . Quality assessment Risk of bias was evaluated in the 10 included studies [ – ] using QUADAS-2. In Patient Selection, two studies [ , ] employed

CT-MDCE-Panc ( n = 4) [ , , , ]; EUS-CE ( n = 2) [ , ]; TA-US ( n = 2) [ , ]; MRI-MnDPDP ( n = 1) [ ]; and PETCT-18F-FDG+MDCT-DPCE ( n = 1) [ ]. All studies were published between 2000 and 2012, in English, and were conducted across multiple countries, including Germany, Italy, and France. The baseline characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table . Quality assessment Risk of bias was evaluated in the 10 included studies [ – ] using QUADAS-2. In Patient Selection, two studies [ , ] employed prospective consecutive or serial enrollment and were rated as low risk of bias; six studies [ – , , , ] did not adequately describe the enrollment pathway and were judged as unclear risk; two studies [ , ] showed selective inclusion or single-source recruitment and were rated as high risk. In the Index Test domain, four studies [ , , , ] explicitly stated that index test interpretation was performed independently and blinded to the reference standard and were rated as low risk; five studies [ , , , , ] did not clearly report blinding or independent interpretation and were judged as unclear risk; one study [ ] was rated as high risk because index test results may have been influenced by knowledge of the reference standard. For the Reference Standard, five studies [ , , , , ] used surgical pathology as the reference standard capable of correctly classifying the target condition and were rated as low risk; the remaining five studies [ , , , , ] did not clearly report whether interpretation of the reference standard was independent of the index test and were judged as unclear risk. In Flow and Timing, five studies [ , , , , ] ensured an appropriate interval between the index test and the reference standard and included all enrolled participants in the analysis, and thus were rated as low risk; three studies [ , , ] had insufficient follow-up information or incomplete outcome data and were judged as unclear risk; two studies [ , ] were rated as high risk because some participants were not included in the final analysis or the test–reference interval was inappropriate. Regarding applicability concerns, all studies were judged to be at low concern across patient characteristics, clinical setting, index tests, and reference standards. Overall, methodological quality was moderate: most studies performed well in patient selection, reference standard specification, and study flow, whereas potential bias clustered in the adequacy of enrollment, implementation of blinding/independent interpretation, and completeness of outcome data. The distribution of risk-of-bias judgments and the summary assessments are presented in Fig. . Evidence network The network of evidence is shown in Fig. . Blue nodes denote imaging interventions, with node size proportional to the volume of evidence; edge thickness and the accompanying numeric labels indicate the number of direct pairwise comparisons between modalities. As illustrated in Fig. a, MRI-MRCP, CT-MDCE-Panc, and EUS-B occupy central positions with larger evidence volumes and multiple direct contrasts, whereas MRI-MnDPDP and PETCT-18F-FDG+MDCT-DPCE appear as smaller nodes with limited direct evidence. Figure b overlays orange nodes representing the graded reference standards (L1, L2, L3, and their combinations), which are displayed solely for visualization and were not included in the comparative analyses. Overall, the topology indicates that central nodes contributed the majority of direct evidence, while peripheral nodes relied predominantly on indirect comparisons to maintain network connectivity. Accordingly, several nodes can be considered ‘open’ in the sense that they are sparsely connected and informed by few (or single) studies, which increases uncertainty for comparisons involving these modalities. Consistency assessment To examine agreement between direct and indirect evidence, node-splitting was performed for all modality pairs with head-to-head comparisons. Six contrasts were evaluated: ERCP-IDUS vs EUS-B, ERCP-IDUS vs EUS-CE, ERCP-IDUS vs TA-US, CT-MDCE-Panc vs EUS-B, CT-MDCE-Panc vs TA-US, and ERCP-IDUS vs MRI-MRCP. Except for ERCP-IDUS vs EUS-B ( p = 0.04) and ERCP-IDUS vs EUS-CE ( p = 0.045), all tests yielded p values > 0.05, indicating no statistically significant inconsistency. Given the multiplicity inherent to node-splitting, pBayes signals were interpreted as exploratory and no formal multiplicity correction was applied. Results of the global consistency assessment are presented alongside the node-splitting outputs in the Supplement for cross-reference. Overall, the findings support the plausibility of the consistency assumption, and the consistency model was deemed appropriate for this diagnostic Bayesian NMA. Detailed results are shown in Fig. . Transitivity assumption All included studies were prospective diagnostic studies, thereby avoiding the selection bias inherent to retrospective designs. The reference framework centered on L1 surgical histopathology, supplemented when necessary by L2 biopsy/cytology and L3 follow-up–based composite standards, yielding L1+L2, L1+L3, and L1+L2+L3 tiers to maintain uniform diagnostic verification. Baseline characteristics were highly homogeneous across cohorts
