Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.1.2) and SPSS (version 22.0). Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables are presented as frequencies (percentages). Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons between benign and malignant nodules were performed using Student’s t-test, Mann–Whitney U test, χ² test, or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Multicollinearity was evaluated using the variance inflation factor (VIF). A VIF > 10 indicated severe multicollinearity ( ). Predictors included in the final model did not exhibit severe multicollinearity ( ). Candidate variables were initially screened using univariable analyses (P < 0.05), after which final predictors were selected based on statistical significance together with clinical and radiologic plausibility to preserve interpretability. It is important to clarify that while AI software was employed for the automated and objective extraction of quantitative imaging features, the predictive model itself is a conventional multivariable logistic regression, not an end-to-end deep learning classifier. Categorical variables were modeled in full to maintain clinical relevance ( ). The final model was constructed by simultaneously entering all selected predictors. For interpretability, selected continuous variables were scaled to clinically meaningful units before inclusion: minimum and maximum CT attenuation (per 100 HU), nodule volume (per 1000 mm³), and nodule area (per 500 mm²). Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Discrimination was quantified using AUC; calibration was evaluated using calibration plots and mean absolute error. The full model was benchmarked against prespecified clinical-only, imaging baseline, and guideline-like imaging models in the same cohort using AUC (95% CI) and DeLong’s test. Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) to estimate optimism ( ). Variable selection was conducted once in the full cohort prior to bootstrapping, rather than being repeated within each bootstrap sample. We acknowledge that this approach may lead to an underestimation of model optimism, which is a limitation of our validation strategy. No external validation dataset was available. Clinical utility was evaluated using decision curve analysis (DCA) across clinically relevant high-risk thresholds to determine the net benefit of applying the model in clinical decision-making ( , ). A nomogram was constructed from the final multivariable logistic regression model. The full prediction formula is provided in . All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Study population and baseline characteristics The final analysis included 951 patients who underwent surgical resection of solid or part-solid PNs measuring ≤ 3 cm. The cohort comprised 741 (77.9%) malignant and 210 (22.1%) benign lesions. This malignancy prevalence reflects the preselected surgical cohort and should not be interpreted as the malignancy prevalence of incidentally detected PNs. presents the baseline clinicopathological and radiological characteristics of the cohort, stratified by pathological outcome. Several key variables differed significantly between benign and malignant nodules. Patients with malignant nodules were more often female (60.9% vs. 47.1%; P < 0.001) and asymptomatic at the time of detection (77.1% vs. 66.2%; P = 0.001). Malignant nodules were also more likely to have a shorter interval from detection to surgery (< 2 years: 87.2% vs. 74.8%; P < 0.001), a mixed radiographic appearance (59.9% vs. 27.1%; P < 0.001), a consolidation-to-tumor ratio (CTR) ≤ 0.5 (43.2% vs. 18.1%; P < 0.001), and the presence of suspicious radiologic features (78.4% vs. 41.0%; P < 0.001). Furthermore, malignant nodules exhibited significantly lower minimum CT attenuation (median −607 HU vs. −452 HU; P < 0.001) and a lower SII (median 432.0 vs. 480.7; P = 0.013). Predictor selection and final prediction model Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify independent predictors of malignancy ( ). The final multivariable model was constructed by jointly considering statistical significance and clinical/radiological relevance. An evaluation of multicollinearity among candidate predictors is provided in . The complete prediction formula for calculating the linear predictor and individual malignancy probability is provided in . The model identified female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.81, P = 0.002) and suspicious radiologic features (aOR = 8.43, P < 0.001) as strong positive predictors of malignancy. Nodule size > 2–3 cm (vs. ≤ 1 cm) was also a significant positive predictor (aOR = 3.31, P = 0.001). Factors associated with a lower likelihood of malignancy included the presence of symptoms at detection (aOR = 0.53, P = 0.003), time to surgery ≥ 2 years (aOR = 0.55, P = 0.014), SN appearance (vs. mixed; aOR = 0.54, P = 0.035), CTR > 0.5 (aOR = 0.33, P < 0.001), and higher minimum (aOR = 0.82 per 100 HU, P = 0.001) and maximum CT attenuation values (aOR = 0.95 per 100 HU, P = 0.028). The full set of coefficients and 95% confidence intervals is provided in . The complete prediction formula for computing

Factors associated with a lower likelihood of malignancy included the presence of symptoms at detection (aOR = 0.53, P = 0.003), time to surgery ≥ 2 years (aOR = 0.55, P = 0.014), SN appearance (vs. mixed; aOR = 0.54, P = 0.035), CTR > 0.5 (aOR = 0.33, P < 0.001), and higher minimum (aOR = 0.82 per 100 HU, P = 0.001) and maximum CT attenuation values (aOR = 0.95 per 100 HU, P = 0.028). The full set of coefficients and 95% confidence intervals is provided in . The complete prediction formula for computing the linear predictor and individual malignancy probability is provided in . Although the SII was significantly associated with malignancy in univariable analysis ( ), along with other inflammatory markers (NLR, PLR, and MLR), it did not remain independently associated after multivariable adjustment and was therefore excluded from the final parsimonious model ( ). Model performance and validation The overall performance of the final model is presented in . The model demonstrated excellent goodness of fit (likelihood ratio chi-square = 277.02, P < 0.0001) and accounted for a substantial proportion of variance (R² = 0.388). A Brier score of 0.117 indicates good overall predictive accuracy. The model demonstrated strong discriminatory ability, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.836 (95% CI: 0.804–0.869) for the entire cohort ( ). The model also exhibited excellent calibration. The calibration plot demonstrated close agreement between predicted malignancy probabilities and observed outcomes across the full range of risk ( ). Based on 1000 bootstrap repetitions, the bias-corrected curve closely followed the ideal reference line, indicating minimal overfitting. Quantitatively, the model showed a low mean absolute error of 0.015, with a bootstrap-corrected calibration slope of 0.98 and an intercept of 0.02, indicating excellent agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes with minimal systematic over- or under-estimation. Internal benchmarking against baseline models In internal benchmarking analyses ( ), the full clinico-quantitative imaging model achieved the highest discrimination (AUC = 0.838), outperforming the clinical-only model (AUC = 0.666; P < 0.001) and the guideline-like imaging model (AUC = 0.733; P < 0.001). The imaging baseline model showed discrimination close to that of the full model (AUC = 0.822), but the full model remained statistically superior ( P = 0.017). Clinical utility and risk stratification DCA indicated that the model provided greater clinical benefit than strategies of treating all patients or treating none across a broad range of clinically relevant threshold probabilities (approximately 0.10–0.45) ( ). The model successfully stratified patients into three distinct model-defined predicted-risk strata with clearly different malignancy rates ( , ). Risk strata were defined by quartiles of predicted malignancy probability for descriptive purposes rather than predefined clinical thresholds. The observed malignancy rate was 43.3% in the lower predicted-risk stratum (lowest 25% of predicted probabilities, n = 238), 86.7% in the intermediate predicted-risk stratum (middle 50%, n = 475), and 95.0% in the higher predicted-risk stratum (highest 25%, n = 238). Because this cohort comprised patients selected for surgical evaluation, even the lower predicted-risk stratum retained a substantial malignancy prevalence. These findings highlight the practical value of the nomogram in guiding preoperative clinical decision-making. Subgroup analysis Subgroup analyses demonstrated that the model maintained strong and consistent discriminatory performance across key patient and nodule characteristics ( ). The AUC remained high across subgroups defined by nodule size (≤ 2 cm: AUC = 0.846; > 2 cm: AUC = 0.761), nodule type (solid: AUC = 0.826; mixed: AUC = 0.765), CTR (≤ 0.5: AUC = 0.711; > 0.5: AUC = 0.856), sex, symptom status, and time to surgery, indicating broad applicability of the model. Clinical implementation To support clinical implementation, we developed a user-friendly, point-based nomogram incorporating all significant predictors from the final model ( ). This visual tool enables clinicians to rapidly estimate the probability of malignancy for an individual patient. In addition, the model has been made available as an interactive web-based calculator at ( https://ruanyingding.shinyapps.io/myshinyapp/ ). Discussion In this large cohort of surgically resected patients, we developed and internally validated an AI-assisted clinico–quantitative imaging nomogram, which demonstrated strong discrimination (AUC = 0.836), excellent calibration, and greater net clinical benefit than strategies of treating all or no patients across a wide range of clinically relevant thresholds (0.10–0.45). It also effectively stratified patients into risk groups, with a monotonic increase in observed malignancy from 43.3% in the lower predicted-risk stratum to 95.0% in the higher predicted-risk stratum. Although systemic inflammatory indices were assessed, none remained independently associated with malignancy after multivariable adjustment. Consequently, the final model included a streamlined set of clinically and radiologically relevant predictors. Notably, the observed malignancy rate remained substantial even in the lower predicted-risk stratum (43.3%), reflecting the malignancy-enriched nature of a surgically selected cohort (77.9% overall malignancy prevalence). It also effectively stratified patients into risk groups, with a monotonic increase in observed malignancy from 43.3% in the lower predicted-risk stratum to 95.0% in the higher predicted-risk stratum. Although systemic inflammatory indices were assessed, none remained independently associated with malignancy after multivariable adjustment. Consequently, the final model included a streamlined set of clinically and radiologically relevant predictors. Notably, the observed malignancy rate remained substantial even in the lower predicted-risk stratum (43.3%), reflecting the malignancy-enriched nature of a surgically selected cohort (77.9% overall malignancy prevalence). This highlights the spectrum effect, where prediction tools developed in higher-prevalence clinical settings may yield miscalibrated absolute risks if applied directly to unselected screening or incidental populations ( ). In particular, absolute predicted probabilities may differ when the model is applied to populations with substantially different malignancy prevalence. Consequently, our model is most appropriately applied to preoperative risk stratification in patients already deemed candidates for surgical evaluation, rather than for initial triage in screening programs. The lower predicted-risk stratum in our cohort should not be interpreted as a “rule-out” category to defer diagnostic workup. Broader clinical application will require external validation and recalibration in lower-pretest-probability cohorts, with careful attention to calibration and decision thresholds ( , ). To contextualize our findings, current PN management frameworks such as the Fleischner Society recommendations and Lung-RADS remain indispensable ( , ). However, these frameworks rely largely on visual assessment of size and density and may be limited in diagnostically challenging indeterminate nodules ( ). AI-based analysis of CT volumes has been shown to improve malignancy discrimination compared with visual assessment alone ( ). Building on this rationale, our study translates automated AI-derived quantitative imaging measurements into a transparent, multifactorial prediction model that integrates key imaging metrics with essential clinical variables. In this framework, AI was used to improve the objectivity and reproducibility of quantitative imaging measurements, while prediction remained based on a transparent statistical modeling framework. We also evaluated systemic inflammatory and metabolic host factors as candidate predictors. In our cohort, these host factors showed associations in univariable analyses but did not provide independent predictive value in the final multivariable model. The final prediction model identified several strong and clinically interpretable independent predictors of malignancy, emphasizing the benefit of integrating multidimensional data. In particular, AI-derived imaging features, including the CTR and minimum and maximum CT attenuation, were significant contributors. The pronounced inverse relationship between higher minimum CT attenuation and malignancy (aOR = 0.82 per 100 HU, P = 0.001) is consistent with the established understanding that benign lesions, such as granulomas or intrapulmonary lymph nodes, often exhibit higher density due to fibrosis or calcification, whereas malignant nodules tend to have lower attenuation because of ground-glass components or necrotic regions ( , ). The automated extraction of these imaging features highlights the important role of AI in improving the objectivity, reproducibility, and quantitative rigor of radiographic assessment, surpassing the limitations of subjective visual interpretation ( , ). Emerging evidence further demonstrates that combining AI-derived texture-based radiomics features or deep-learning imaging features with other data sources, such as circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) fragmentomics, can create multimodal models with enhanced diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility for indeterminate PNs, as demonstrated in a recent large multicenter study ( ). In future iterations, our nomogram could potentially be adapted to incorporate ctDNA or other biomarkers, further improving its predictive power and clinical applicability. In this study, several non-imaging predictors also provided valuable insights. Female sex was associated with a higher risk of malignancy (aOR = 1.81, P = 0.002). Conversely, symptomatic presentation at detection was associated with a lower risk of malignancy (aOR = 0.53, P = 0.003). This counterintuitive finding may reflect the specific clinical context of our surgical cohort, where symptomatic patients might undergo more aggressive workup leading to the resection of benign inflammatory or infectious lesions that mimic malignancy, whereas asymptomatic nodules detected incidentally and proceeding to surgery are often those with highly suspicious imaging features despite lacking symptoms. In addition, a longer interval from nodule detection to surgery (≥ 2 years) was independently associated with a lower probability of malignancy (aOR = 0.55, P = 0.014), consistent with the established concept that long-term nodule stability supports benignity ( ). However, it is also important to recognize that the time interval variable may partly reflect clinical decision-making processes and physician confidence in nodule stability, rather than solely representing a biological characteristic of the nodule itself. Given differences across clinical settings and case mix, external validation and recalibration in unselected cohorts are warranted. In addition to local radiological features, we assessed systemic inflammatory markers, including the SII. At baseline, malignant nodules exhibited lower SII values (median 432.0 vs. 480.7; P = 0.013), and SII was associated with malignancy in

with the established concept that long-term nodule stability supports benignity ( ). However, it is also important to recognize that the time interval variable may partly reflect clinical decision-making processes and physician confidence in nodule stability, rather than solely representing a biological characteristic of the nodule itself. Given differences across clinical settings and case mix, external validation and recalibration in unselected cohorts are warranted. In addition to local radiological features, we assessed systemic inflammatory markers, including the SII. At baseline, malignant nodules exhibited lower SII values (median 432.0 vs. 480.7; P = 0.013), and SII was associated with malignancy in univariable analysis. This finding also suggests that further studies should evaluate model transportability across different healthcare systems and patient populations. Accordingly, future iterations of our nomogram may incorporate tumor-proximal immune or molecular biomarkers to improve biological interpretability and discrimination. This study has several important strengths. First, the final model combines AI-derived quantitative imaging features with key clinical variables. Although systemic inflammatory markers were systematically assessed as potential predictors, they did not retain independent significance after multivariable adjustment, resulting in a biologically informed yet streamlined model. Second, the use of a fully automated feature quantification platform (InferRead CT Lung) improves objectivity, enhances reproducibility, and reduces operator-dependent bias. Third, we provide an open-access, web-based nomogram to support immediate clinical implementation. Finally, the model underwent optimism-corrected bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) and DCA, demonstrating strong predictive performance and greater standardized net benefit than treat-all or treat-none strategies across clinically relevant thresholds (0.10–0.45). Complete logistic regression coefficients and odds ratios are reported to ensure transparency. This study also has some limitations. The single-center, retrospective design may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability, highlighting the need for external validation in prospective, multicenter cohorts ( , ). Notably, despite the excellent calibration performance observed (slope = 0.98, intercept = 0.02), a key methodological limitation remains that predictor selection was performed once in the full cohort prior to bootstrap validation, rather than being embedded within the resampling process; this approach may still lead to a slight underestimation of model optimism. In addition, the malignancy-enriched surgical cohort may yield miscalibrated absolute risks if the model is applied to unselected nodules, underscoring the need for external validation and potential recalibration. Relatedly, the relatively high malignancy prevalence even in the lower predicted-risk stratum in our cohort indicates that the model’s absolute risks and “low-risk” interpretation may not generalize to low-prevalence populations without recalibration ( , ). We were unable to uniformly capture CT-defined nodule location (central vs. peripheral) across the study period, which may introduce residual confounding related to histology and patient demographics. Because the model was developed using a Chinese patient population, its performance in other ethnic and geographic settings requires evaluation and potential recalibration ( ). The model does not include molecular biomarkers; incorporating liquid biopsy or genomic data could improve predictive accuracy and biological interpretability ( ). In addition, imaging predictors were limited to AI-extracted quantitative metrics rather than high-dimensional texture-based radiomics; future work could evaluate whether adding higher-dimensional radiomic or deep-learning features further improves performance. Head-to-head comparison with established models was not feasible due to unavailable predictors; we benchmarked against predefined baseline models. Moreover, comparisons with penalized or non-linear machine-learning approaches were not performed and should be assessed in future studies with external validation ( ). Finally, because the model relies on a proprietary commercial AI platform, cross-software reproducibility requires further validation. This study introduces a practical tool for preoperative risk stratification of indeterminate PNs ≤ 3 cm—an AI-assisted clinico–quantitative imaging nomogram that leverages AI for automated feature extraction within an interpretable logistic regression framework. By combining automated imaging quantification with clinical data, the model may support individualized decision-making primarily in surgically selected, malignancy-enriched cohorts. Its applicability to screening or incidental nodule populations requires further validation and recalibration. Future work should prioritize external validation, ideally in multicenter settings, and recalibration as needed in independent, unselected nodule cohorts. Integration of molecular biomarkers may further improve performance.

Introduction The Tomosynthesis Mammography Imaging Screening Trial (TMIST) EA 1151, sponsored by ECOG ACRIN is being conducted to assess the effectiveness for breast cancer screening of digital breast tomosynthesis (TM) compared to digital mammography (DM) in an anticipated population of 128,905 women. Participants are randomized 1:1 into trial arms in which they are screened using conventional 2D mammography or where they receive tomosynthesis with additional 2D views or synthetic 2D depending on the preference of the site radiologist. TMIST is funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI). This report describes the quality control (QC) methodology used in TMIST and summarizes selected test results over the initial 5-y period from October, 2017 to December, 2022. It is important that all equipment is operated within appropriate parameters with regard to image quality and dose for the findings of the study to be valid and capture the true capacities of the two technology types. In the Digital Mammography Screening Trial (DMIST), , the QC tests for digital systems closely emulated those designed originally for testing Screen Film systems, and tests varied among manufacturers. In TMIST, there was an opportunity to take advantage of more sophisticated digital tools to assess stability and performance. Direct digital image transmission to a central Physics QC core (PQCC) also allowed automated analysis to be performed for many of the tests. Tomosynthesis systems are fairly mature and have been in the marketplace long enough for most of the initial problems to be worked out, however when the protocol was written, there was no consensus on what tests would be included in an optimal QC testing program. The American College of Radiology (ACR) has an approved comprehensive “alternative standard quality assurance” program for digital mammography and tomosynthesis. However, when TMIST commenced operation, this program was used by very few facilities; most still used the manufacturer specified QC program. Similarly, in principle, EUREF or EFOMP protocols – , could have been used to obtain data that could be compared across systems, but these are not commonly used in the U.S., would require different equipment and would have increased the workload for the site technologists or physicists. The TMIST QC program was designed specifically to allow measurement on systems from multiple vendors, located at many sites, with differing levels of medical physics support. It is complementary to existing federal requirements in the US, and requires that all systems are maintained and perform QC to meet applicable accreditation standards. In TMIST, a simple set of weekly and monthly tests was implemented to limit the additional workload on the technologist. Physicist reports (Mammography Equipment Evaluation) were used to ensure that performance of the equipment was at an acceptable level. Data on tube output and half-value layer (HVL) were gleaned from these reports and used to estimate subject radiation exposures. A set of physics tests to be performed annually by the QC technologist and analysed by the PQCC team was developed to consistently evaluate all tomosynthesis units involved in the trial. As in our development of the QC program for the earlier DMIST Trial, , the testing protocol and initial pass/fail criteria were established at the outset of the trial and designed so that, as much as possible, tests could be applied generically among the different tomosynthesis systems. Wherever appropriate, the design of the tests was based on the IAEA Quality Control Program for Digital Mammography. Limits were set to be consistent with equipment design to allow for expected day-to-day variability of test results, but sufficiently restrictive to identify systems with substandard imaging performance. The initial limits were established based on preliminary measurements with some of the equipment, however, with further experience it became necessary to adjust some tests (e.g., to accommodate file formats) during the trial. We aimed to closely adhere to the established protocol in order to enable consistent monitoring of performance across different types of equipment over a period of time. An important objective was to identify specific tests that could effectively identify issues with image quality or anticipate equipment failure. This information would be valuable in developing a well-structured quality control program for digital mammography and tomosynthesis. In this report, the unique QC tests for the weekly and monthly QC are described along with objectives and pass/fail criteria for the tests. Initially, it was planned that both “FOR PROCESSING” (raw) and “FOR PRESENTATION” images would be submitted, but because of technical constraints at some sites, the program was modified, to make submission of FOR PROCESSING images optional. This resulted in the loss of the ability to perform “linear systems” analysis on all images. Tests of subject contrast and resolution were carried out and tracked. The annual QC portion which tests automatic exposure control response vs thickness, resolution, noise levels and geometric accuracy will be described in a future paper. The

This resulted in the loss of the ability to perform “linear systems” analysis on all images. Tests of subject contrast and resolution were carried out and tracked. The annual QC portion which tests automatic exposure control response vs thickness, resolution, noise levels and geometric accuracy will be described in a future paper. The Physics QC protocol and additional detailed test results are available through a direct link in the online article’s section. 2. Methods 2.1. Data Collection and overall QC program structure All images in TMIST, including QC and study subject mammograms (both DBT projections and reconstructed volumes) for the study are collected by the ACR using its “Transfer of Images and Data” (TRIAD) software package. This software runs on a computer at each screening facility. The overall schematic of data flow as well as analysis and reporting operations is illustrated in . QC images are transferred from ACR to the PQCC using secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) to the “QC core” cloud servers (Amazon Web Services (AWS)), which automatically determine the image type and perform appropriate analysis. Results from each test are stored in a database, and available for review by personnel at the screening sites on a secure password-protected web application ( tmistqc.org ). Website access requires user registration and approval. Users are restricted to view data only from the clinical site(s) for which they are approved. After associating a given set of subject images with an assigned study subject ID, TRIAD then removes any Protected Health Information (PHI) from the DICOM header and transmits these images to ACR for future reader studies and secondary uses. Each de-identified subject image header is also sent to the PQCC without the clinical image pixel data so that technical factors can be tracked and evaluated. Results for the analysis of header data will be presented in a companion paper (MS#22-2140). Please note that in several places in this report, for the readers’ convenience, we have reproduced some text and wording of the test criteria verbatim from the online TMIST Quality Control Manual, specifically developed for the program. 2.2. Site Initiation and Credentialing Requirements To ensure that all image files required for clinical imaging were appropriately sent through TRIAD , submission of a credentialing phantom was required. For this purpose, either the Mammographic Accreditation Phantom (MAP) or the new digital mammography phantom (DMP) as specified in the American College of Radiology (ACR) Mammography Accreditation Program and mandated by the Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA) could be used. Most sites already had, and were familiar with at least one of these phantoms. To complete the credentialing process, sites had to be able to transfer images of all required types via the TRIAD software (provided by ECOG/ACRIN). These include 2D mammograms, reconstructed tomosynthesis volumes, and synthetic 2D images (if used by the center). Depending on the site preferences, images are either transferred from the mammography unit directly to the TRIAD server or first sent to the local or research PACS and then moved to the TRIAD server. To verify that a site was providing at least a minimally acceptable level of image quality, their ACR (MAP or DMP) phantom was imaged both in DM and TM modes for each machine intended to be used for participant imaging in the trial. For each unit or new detector, phantom images were subjectively reviewed. Minimum scoring requirements were set based on ACR published standards ( e.g ., 4 specks, 3 masses and 3 fibers perceivable in the MAP phantom or 3 specks, 2 masses and 2 fibers in the DMAP phantom), as well as the requirement that images be free from obvious artifacts such as “dead” lines, hot or dead pixels, electromagnetic field (EMF) ripple or streaking. From the image headers of the credentialing images, the unique detector ID and station serial number were extracted to identify each machine enrolled in the program. As part of QC oversight, we requested that sites forward us all service reports and physicist’s reports for credentialed units. Service information was collected in our database so that it could be cross referenced with QC shifts and failures. 2.3. Description of the TMIST QC program The QC tests, frequencies, and objectives of the tests are summarized in . Only the weekly tests will be discussed in this report. Phantoms used in the tests, software analysis tools and results will be described in a later section. Description of the TMIST QC program The QC tests, frequencies, and objectives of the tests are summarized in . Only the weekly tests will be discussed in this report. Phantoms used in the tests, software analysis tools and results will be described in a later section. A governing philosophy for the QC approach used in TMIST is to assess the image quality in “patient imaging mode” as would be used in the clinic and viewed by the radiologist. In other words, “FOR PRESENTATION” mammograms, reconstructed tomosynthesis planes and, if used by the radiologists, synthetic mammograms and optional “slab” views are evaluated in the tests. By choosing these images for evaluation, the QC captures the effects of the entire imaging chain – including non-linear reconstruction and image processing that may change behavior depending on underlying imaging conditions or changes to the system software. The technologists are asked to use the same compression paddles, compression force, grid and fully automatic exposure control (AEC) settings for the QC testing as would normally be used to image patients. It was emphasized that for consistency of operation, the same AEC setting, reconstruction mode and large paddle be used for the tests every time they are performed. Some sites were asked to use a semi-manual technique such as “AutoTime”, because we found that slight compression thickness variations could change AEC operation enough (usually kilovoltage (kV) changed) that the test results became inconsistent and outside control limits. Every test in the program has a baseline value established for each parameter based on up to five repeated measurements. Baselines were established at the beginning of QC accrual or whenever we were able to determine that a change in equipment or operating conditions had taken place. To meet the mammographic standard of practice for all digital mammography (DM) and tomosynthesis mammogram (TM) units used to image TMIST subjects, the mammography technologist and the site Qualified Medical Physicist (QMP) perform the standard QC tests required to maintain accreditation in the facility jurisdiction. Each report from the QMP is collected when they perform their testing, including the Annual Mammographic Equipment Evaluation (MEE) and any post-service MEE. In addition, all TMIST sites are provided with identical TMIST test phantoms (described in a later section) to harmonize the quality control across sites and vendors. Facilities used pre-existing uniform thickness PMMA phantoms (2.5 cm for GE, 4 cm for Hologic and Siemens) for flat-field tests. Using those phantoms, the technologists take a limited number of QC exposures. Image sets for each of the QC tests are sent to the TRIAD server and uploaded as “Site Qualification” images. To minimize the number of test images that must be acquired, several tests are performed within a single image acquisition. Additional testing was also performed on the synthetic 2D mammogram of the TMISTQC phantom (weekly) and a tomosynthesis acquisition of a uniform plastic block (monthly). There were varying (and initially low) rates of use of synthetic 2D images at sites, so we did not have adequate experience to include the data for analysis. Monthly uniform QC tests are not reported here because the detection of artifacts was qualitative, performed by individual site technologists, and information recording was often inconsistent. The images received from ACR are analyzed by automated software at the PQCC, and results are available for viewing on the tmistqc.org website by site personnel using a password-protected login. The technologist then reviews the charts to ensure that the values from test images are within control limits (kV, mAs, SDNR, slice heights, etc .). Alerts for test results which fall outside variance limits are automatically emailed to all users registered for that site. The site technologist is also required to examine a webpage ( tmistqc.org ) containing several small processed version images (thumbnails) and regions of interest (ROIs) for consistency with previous tests. These processed thumbnails are described in detail below for the weekly 2D SDNR, and the ROIs are described in detail for the TMIST 3D tests. The technologist is required to record the presence of artifacts and/or concerns about image quality using the comment feature, and digitally sign the charts by clicking on “Pass” or “Fail”, as appropriate. As described in the following sections, each test in the QC program has a specified threshold value for “achievable” (high quality) and “acceptable” (minimum standard) results. The facility was not allowed to continue to image TMIST subjects with equipment not meeting the acceptable standard of operation because of potential concerns regarding the diagnostic value of the procedure and/or its safety. If one of those reasons is determined to be responsible for an out-of-limit warning, the variance is documented, but is not displayed on the QC chart nor used in computing failure statistics. Automated Processing of Images As shown in , all images are transferred from the central ACR image repository via secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) to the TMIST QC file portal. An automated service excludes non-relevant DICOM files (such as screen-captures, dose reports and CAD reports) that may be included in the examination package. Such extraneous files are expected, because it is more effective and reliable to send the entire study content, rather than depending on each site to select only the relevant file types. Relevant files are pushed via DICOM protocols to a “watchdog” service that analyzes each incoming image to identify the phantom type (TMISTQC, uniform monthly (no disk), 2D SDNR (uniform with disk), MAP or annual phantoms). This identification is performed based on automatically detected structures in each image (e.g. shape: semicircular vs uniform vs small block) and by additional aluminum spheres (BBs) at expected locations (e.g. a binary-coded serial number is located in the corner of each TMISTQC phantom consisting of BBs and spaces). Further identification is based on a priori knowledge of the approximate locations of inserts in the phantom. For example, the sphere, 4 speck groups, and a single BB appear in predefined, otherwise uniform regions in the 2D image or volume, and simple thresholds identify the precise locations of the inserts. The speck groups are located at 10.5, 20.5 and 30.5 mm heights to evaluate slice height reporting accuracy. Images that cannot be identified by automatic means are flagged for review by a physicist who can redirect the image for the correct analysis by the watchdog service. Reporting and Display of Results The testing and display software was inspired by “Gladys” , , which was an early version of a centralized software for remote collecting and monitoring of mammography system performance. In the TMISTQC software, the results of each test, as well as DICOM tags for the image such as detector ID, time of acquisition, detector temperature and technical factors are captured in a database. Key results are published on the TMISTQC.org website and reviewed by the site technologist. Examples of time-charts of test results displayed at TMISTQC.org are shown in . For a system to be operating within acceptable limits, all plotted parameters are required to be within the control limits (red lines) indicated on the chart. Any out of range points are colored red. Marginal limits are also shown (orange lines) and marginal points are colored orange. For any CRITICAL or NONCOMPLIANT variances, alert emails are sent both to the site and the PQCC physicists. Alerts are also sent if the test results are submitted late or if the site technologist has not reviewed the tests in a timely manner. Details on the time frames used to determine when alert emails were sent are included in the in . Sites with excellent performance indicators for more than 12 months are given “gold status” and the frequency of the “weekly” tests is reduced to monthly. 2.4. Compression Thickness Accuracy & Compression Settings The TMISTQC phantom is known to be exactly 40 mm thick. Compression thickness errors can contribute to changes in AEC operating points and can potentially change the number of reconstructed planes in the TM volume, potentially causing tissue to be missed from the reconstructed image volume. So, it is important that the readout be accurate. When phantom thickness is reported to be higher (>47 mm) or lower (<35 mm) than the expected thickness, an alert is sent to have the image checked manually, and the PQCC requests that the system calibration be corrected. During the study we became aware that on System D the thickness readout could vary, depending on the compression setting chosen (“FAST” or “NORMAL”), resulting in changes to the kV, mAs and estimated dose. From that point forward, the compression setting tag (private tag 0x0019, 0x1025) was added to the list of tags extracted from the headers and stored in the database for troubleshooting. For all units where both paddle settings had been used for weekly TM QC image acquisition, the average reported thickness, kV, exposure and estimated dose were calculated for both settings. The absolute percent differences in exposure and reported dose were calculated, as well as the absolute difference in thickness (mm) and kV. Test Limits and Definitions of Variances At the outset of the trial, test parameters and limits were either estimated from previous experience in the DMIST QC program or from other protocols such as the European Reference Frame (EUREF) tomosynthesis QC protocol recommendations. Test limits are provided in . When a critical variance was detected, PQCC emailed the site, often requesting that the test be redone because there was an error in the positioning or compression of the phantom; or because the choice of technique factors was inappropriate or inconsistent. The technologist was instructed to report on the website if they had found an artifact on the image submitted for each test; and to describe any corrective actions on the website, if any chart parameters were found to be out of limits. Most frequently, they reported an error in performing the QC, such as not compressing appropriately or not selecting the correct operating mode. When an operator error occurred, the technologist was instructed to repeat the test exposure using the correct protocol and request that PQCC not display the erroneous point on the graph (nor use it in compiling failure statistics). Correspondingly, if PQCC staff observed a finding outside the limit, and an acceptable explanation for it, they would enter comments for a marginal or failing point on the graph, and set the point to not display, and not contribute to the data for analysis. Other causes of variances include performance degradation, but also may be a result of intentional changes in operation, triggered either by the PQCC or the site itself. The following are conditions that could cause variances from an indication of stability without necessarily impacting image quality: use of a different compression plate, variable compression pressure (among technologists), a different image size or slice thickness, dependence of automatic kV selection on compression thickness readout, different positioning of phantoms, use of different reconstruction algorithms or reconstruction parameter settings, recalibration of equipment (flat-fielding or software updates), improper performance of the test (phantom upside down or no compression). Correlation of QC failures with equipment service and clinical image quality When we became aware that service was performed on a system, this information was collected in a table in our QC database. To study the correlation of QC failures with equipment service, we cross referenced the dates of failing or marginal QC with the dates of service. We calculated the odds-ratios for service to the equipment following failing/marginal vs passing QC for the time period until the subsequent passing QC. In addition, the clinical image headers from the study subjects were automatically checked by the QC software against the QC status (Passing, Marginal, Failing, Overdue) of the mammography equipment at the time of image acquisition. Since the actual pixel data of the clinical images was not forwarded to our QC servers to protect patient privacy, any exams done while the QC for the equipment was failing were flagged for qualitative review by the ECOG/ACRIN clinical image QC core. 3. Manufacturer 2 has two tomosynthesis acquisition modes, normal and high-definition (HD). The normal mode bins detector pixels together in x and y directions, such that four pixels in the detector form 1 pixel in the projection image, while HD mode does not employ binning. In addition, on later versions of the reconstruction software, the HD mode projections can be reconstructed in 1 mm slices or 6 mm slabs. 9.9% of the TMIST 3D QC for system D was done in HD mode, and a further 6.7% was done on the 6mm slabs. The original analysis software was designed with thresholds set to find changes only at specific spatial frequencies (1, 2 & 4 cy/mm). A change in paddle size affects the collimation, which in turn may affect the scatter conditions and the noise. The alternate paddles and compression settings can report a slightly different thickness and can dramatically affect the AEC operation. Discussion The automated QC system performed well, but because the QC images were not submitted directly from the acquisition workstations, and manual intervention by imaging staff was required to identify the appropriate images and push them to TRIAD, we did not achieve our desired instantaneous feedback of results to the mammographic technologist. Sites that used USB keys or DVDs to transfer images (“sneaker net”) had even longer delays between QC imaging and posting results to the website. In addition, there were a few rare problems related to uptime reliability caused at the following points of failure: a) TRIAD connectivity at the sites, b) TRIAD upgrades causing temporary outages, c) intermittent failures of the SFTP transfer of data to the QC core, d) software image analysis tools that failed without warning, and did not automatically restart (these were ultimately resolved) and e) connectivity problems with the Amazon Cloud data repository. We believe that the large standard deviation and large range of values seen in are due mainly to the wide variation of system designs, and therefore that harmonized QC testing employing universal threshold values would not be useful. In the case of the height of the calcification groups, Slice 0 was initially assumed to be the bottom of the volume. Some vendors “pad” the volume on the bottom by 3–5 mm to avoid missing tissue and some do not. This explains the wide range in the reporting of a measurement that should be both accurate and reproducible. On the other hand, when the test results are examined on the basis of machine type as in , it is seen that the ranges and standard deviations of all parameters are much tighter. There was also a large variation in the test results for the DM weekly test ( ). Some of the difference between systems can be attributed to differences in the vendor-supplied uniform blocks and their positioning for the measurement. Most of the sites with equipment from manufacturer 1 used the vendor-supplied 2.5 cm thickness of PMMA, while manufacturer 2 sites used the supplied 4.0 cm thick PMMA and manufacturer 3 sites used the supplied 4.0 cm thick block of PMMA that mounts at the tube port. Differences also were expected because “FOR PRESENTATION” images were analyzed, and thus image signal levels did not linearly track with x-ray fluence. We expected the signal and contrast values to differ among sites, but within a site, tests performed by the same staff using the same phantoms would yield consistent values of SDNR and dose, allowing reliable tracking at each site. As seen by the ratio of marginal results to failures described in and , the relatively low incidence of actionable problems detected by the TMIST QC program may be due to the dedication and initiative of the technologists who often detected problems during their testing and corrected them promptly, thus avoiding an actual recorded failure. As well, mammography equipment design has matured and computer control of components has resulted in quite tight control of electronic parameters such as kV and mAs which were problematic at the time of development of MQSA requirements. Since the intent of the QC program was to detect changes in equipment behavior and image quality before

described in and , the relatively low incidence of actionable problems detected by the TMIST QC program may be due to the dedication and initiative of the technologists who often detected problems during their testing and corrected them promptly, thus avoiding an actual recorded failure. As well, mammography equipment design has matured and computer control of components has resulted in quite tight control of electronic parameters such as kV and mAs which were problematic at the time of development of MQSA requirements. Since the intent of the QC program was to detect changes in equipment behavior and image quality before the clinical image quality was affected, tight “achievable” and “acceptable” test tolerances were used, and sites participating in the study were instructed not to image TMIST subjects on equipment with failing QC. This approach was, overall, successful, as there were very few (3) exams done on underperforming equipment. In light of the low number of exams done on “failing” equipment, it is not surprising that there are very few examples of clinical images such that it was not possible to correlate failing QC with changes in clinical image quality. On the other hand, as seen in , the odds ratios appear to suggest that there is a correlation between observations of marginal or failing QC tests and the need for equipment service. It is extremely important to be able to detect any mis-reporting of compression thickness by the acquisition unit, as the AEC uses this measurement to set the kV and target/filter combination before exposure. Such errors also cause the calculation of dose to be inaccurate. During the weekly QC, some sites were inconsistent in the paddle setting used (“FAST” vs “NORMAL” compression) and due to differences in the thickness calibration, the calculated dose was different by up to 39%. On occasion, the change in reported thickness resulted in a change in the kV selected by the exposure control system, which caused the mAs to change as well. We have learned that certain aspects of the test procedures require further refinement to be useful in a practical QC program. For example, our observation of a relatively high frequency of marginal test results probably indicated that the initial limits set in the protocol were unrealistic. A tolerance exceeding the baseline value by 10%, in retrospect, was often too restrictive. For example, there are a large number of marginal results for the NPS values in . Noise measurements are highly dependent on image processing filters. They are also affected by software changes and the fact that tomosynthesis reconstruction is a non-linear operation. In our tests, it is likely that the region of interest used for NPS determination was too small to allow a stable measurement. It may be possible to improve this metric so that it becomes a reliable constancy test, by using more sub-regions, employing a wider acceptable range (e.g 20%) or a combination of the two. Furthermore, we found that our monitoring at fixed spatial frequencies (1, 2 & 4 cy/mm) was generally insensitive to EMF ripple artifact or grid-lines in the image. More effective analyses of the NPS test results, perhaps with automatic peak detection could be used to better detect and analyze these phenomena. As expected, slice sensitivity profiles (resolution in the z direction) differ among machine types due to variability of the range of projection angles and differences in artifact-reduction image processing. While the wider acquisition angle and more projections used by systems E and F might suggest one to expect superior resolution in the z direction, seen with smaller FWHM values for the ASF-z, this was not the case. This suggests that the reconstruction software and image processing are having a large impact on the characteristics of final 3D volumes. Measurements on the reconstructed volume show that for System D in both the x and y directions the FWHM is almost the same for both binned (140 μm) and un-binned (70 μm) reconstructions. The ASF test was not designed to fully characterize the resolution ( point-spread-function), but rather to monitor changes in reconstructed shape of an object of known shape and providing substantial SNR. Measurements of FWHM-x and z were assumed to be sensitive to changes in the reconstruction conditions such as geometry, scan motion or reconstruction software. , and demonstrate some large changes in behavior following baseline “resets”, suggesting image quality can be quite different before and after hardware or software changes. The notable exception is the “technique change” where the site changed the acquisition settings to deal with unstable test behavior (e.g. from “AutoFilter” to “AutoTime”) without a real change in image quality. Note that in many cases, multiple changes to the system may have occurred at the same time (e.g. equipment change and software upgrade) that could explain the sometimes dramatic change in

in the reconstruction conditions such as geometry, scan motion or reconstruction software. , and demonstrate some large changes in behavior following baseline “resets”, suggesting image quality can be quite different before and after hardware or software changes. The notable exception is the “technique change” where the site changed the acquisition settings to deal with unstable test behavior (e.g. from “AutoFilter” to “AutoTime”) without a real change in image quality. Note that in many cases, multiple changes to the system may have occurred at the same time (e.g. equipment change and software upgrade) that could explain the sometimes dramatic change in test results. Nevertheless, special care should be given to evaluating image quality after such system changes, especially if the dose increases significantly or if the image quality (e.g. SDNR) is reduced. Site engagement in a QC program is essential for its success. From our experience it is most effective and responsive when the Mammography QC technologist takes ownership of the program and the program is not seen to be punitive. We believe this is seen in the consistent performance noted in the Gold status sites. On the other hand, there were some sites which had problems in performing and reviewing the tests. For example, we noted that “Pass” was assigned to a test result even when there was a clear chart failure and /or clear presence of artifacts in the thumbnail images. Although support material (videos, “cheat sheets”, manuals, and presentations) were provided, we believe that additional training on reviewing the website results would be beneficial. COVID-19 had a serious impact on the TMIST study, with many sites stopping screening for long periods (> 3 months), staff illness and burnout. A number of the sites put accrual on hold for extended periods, and a few ceased new recruitment of subjects to the trial. Large gaps in QC data points were seen, and when the sites returned to the TMIST QC program, it was often necessary to set new baselines, because system values drifted at some sites or unreported service interventions occurred during the downtime. 5. Conclusions The QC test results demonstrated that, overall, the tomosynthesis mammography equipment used in TMIST operates in a consistent and repeatable manner for all machine types. The tests were useful in verifying that the systems were operating correctly. It is encouraging that changing trends could be seen in certain parameters such as tube output (mAs) drifting preceding a tube failure. This suggests that detecting trends may serve as an early warning for incipient system failure, although further study is required to reliably detect these trends. Because the Automatic Exposure Control and display software can compensate for changes in equipment performance, subjective assessment of severity of artifacts, variability of system signal levels and noise characteristics are unreliable. Similarly, gradual degradation of performance, such as spatial resolution is difficult to detect subjectively. This motivates the use of quantitative tests like ASF and SDNR, which are easy to perform on a digital system and are not observer dependent. Our experience was that SDNR and other metrics frequently changed whenever there was a software or image processing algorithm change. There was added value in having the responsible site QC technologists review both the images and the web charts to encourage them to take ownership of the process, but the effectiveness of this is highly dependent on the motivation and diligence of each individual. Compression thickness errors are potentially a large source of variation in image quality and dose. We saw up to a 39 % difference in reported dose on the phantom when sites switched between the FAST and NORMAL paddle settings, because of differences in thickness readout. These differences in reported thickness can result in changes in the AEC behavior, such as a choosing a lower or higher kV. The change in beam quality could lead to changes in contrast and noise and deposited dose. As shown in our paper on compression thickness errors, there is also a clinical implication due to the exclusion of tissue from the reconstructed volume if the thickness is under-reported. A comprehensive evaluation of the compression thickness accuracy, or the effect of using a different compression paddle is not performed by most physicists during their surveys, so it is recommended that this test be included in any Mammographic Equipment Evaluation. Our charts provided much more data than would be needed in a regular QC program, and in future work we will present a suggested minimal set of tests. Further investigation of the long-term failure characteristics of digital mammography systems is advisable, and continued tracking of QC at TMIST sites will generate adequate statistics to enable the detection of trends. Since many changes in noise characteristics occur when software is upgraded or image processing filters are changed, it will be necessary to capture information

during their surveys, so it is recommended that this test be included in any Mammographic Equipment Evaluation. Our charts provided much more data than would be needed in a regular QC program, and in future work we will present a suggested minimal set of tests. Further investigation of the long-term failure characteristics of digital mammography systems is advisable, and continued tracking of QC at TMIST sites will generate adequate statistics to enable the detection of trends. Since many changes in noise characteristics occur when software is upgraded or image processing filters are changed, it will be necessary to capture information about such changes, available from “private tags” in the DICOM header to isolate the effect of trending changes caused by software upgrades and other minor system adjustments. Automated QC is effective and timely if it can be accomplished without the need for manual upload of images as was required in this clinical trial. Cloud based solutions which can meet the requirements for security of PHI are available. There is the opportunity to improve efficiency, reducing both labor costs and variability through automation of many of the routine QC tests, thereby allowing technologists to focus on imaging patients. It is worth mentioning that there are special challenges in creating and operating a physics QC program embedded within a large multisite clinical trial. The clinical environment of an imaging facility focusses on managing a demanding workload of imaging procedures (some within and others outside the study) and the time and effort required to carry out nonstandard QC activities and data submission is often viewed as extra labor and distraction from the primary mission. This is especially true when the equipment generally appears to be functioning well and reliably and failures are uncommon. For this reason there is a necessary tension between operating a comprehensive QC program and the cooperation of the participating sites in the study. In practice this drove several changes in the QC protocol over time, changes that attempted to relieve some of the labor burden of the QC procedures while attempting to ensure consistent imaging performance. In our program, these changes included: making the submission of DICOM FOR PROCESSING images optional and reducing required frequency of additional dedicated TMIST tests for systems that are demonstrating consistent performance. Finally, based on our experience in TMIST, we believe that it is reasonable to streamline QC for both tomosynthesis and digital mammography considerably. chunks.content: Introduction Computed tomography (CT) using iodine-containing contrast media is a routine and highly informative diagnostic imaging technique. Most of the administered iodinated contrast media is excreted from the kidneys. However, post-contrast acute kidney injury (PC-AKI), one of the most serious adverse reactions to contrast media [ , ], may occurred in some patients, particularly in patients with kidney disease [ – ]. PC-AKI often presents within 2 to 5 days after administration of contrast media, with an increase in the serum creatinine (sCr) level by 0.5 mg/dL or more (or 25% elevation or more) [ , ]. The risk factors for PC-AKI may be procedure-related or patient-related [ ]. And patient-related risk factors include aging, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), acute renal failure, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and congestive heart failure [ , , , ]. In patients with eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , further deterioration of renal function may occur after contrast-enhanced CT scans [ ]. A propensity score matching study concluded that the likelihood of PC-AKI increased by 51% in adult patients with pre-CT eGFR ≤ 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 [ ] . Japanese guidelines recommend that patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 should not receive iodinated contrast media without appropriate precautions (e.g. using physiological saline intravenously) [ ]. The European Society for Urogenital Radiology (ESUR) classifies three levels of renal dysfunction: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; the last two levels are risk factors for PC-AKI [ , ]. For patients with acute disease, patients with acute deterioration of chronic disease, or hospitalized patients, ESUR recommends evaluating renal function within 7 days before contrast media administration [ , ]. In contrast, ESUR recommends that all other patients need to evaluate renal function within 3 months before contrast media administration [ , ]. The American College of Radiology (ACR) also proposes that individual patient’s condition and associated risk factor(s) should be taken into consideration before using contrast media [ ]. Therefore, in order to identify patients at high risk of PC-AKI, the measurement of eGFR, a hematologic marker of renal function, is suggested to be implemented before the administration of contrast media [ , , , , ]. However, few studies have evaluated renal function over time, and the timing of eGFR test prior to contrast-enhanced CT has not been standardized. The purpose of this retrospective observational study was to identify patient-related risk factors for impaired renal function at 6 months and 1 year. Thus, we retrospectively reviewed the variation in eGFR over time in outpatients, and selected outpatients whose eGFR values were decreased from ≥ 30 to < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 at 6 months or 1 year after the initial eGFR evaluation. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were then performed to evaluate the associations between comorbidities and eGFR decline, thereby identifying independent risk factors for eGFR decline. The anticipated results of this study may provide insight into the timing of eGFR test prior to contrast-enhanced CT for patients with various comorbidities. Materials and Methods Study population This retrospective observational study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of our hospital (IRB approval number: 20–196). The requirement for signed informed consent was waived because of the retrospective nature of this study. Outpatients who visited our hospital and underwent eGFR assessment, with or without contrast-enhanced CT, from April 2017 through March 2019 were initially included. Because the assessment of renal function differs between children and adults, outpatients younger than 18 years were excluded from the study. Regarding the selection of diseases of interest, we referred to guidelines for the use of contrast media [ ] and chose diseases that are generally considered to cause renal dysfunction [ , , – ] or whose treatments are associated with renal dysfunction [ ]. However, since most included outpatients had multiple comorbidities, all comorbidities found in included outpatients were documented in this study. The baseline disease characteristics of all included outpatient were extracted from medical records. And all included patients were outpatients at the baseline, 6-month follow-up, and 1-year follow-up. Kidney function evaluation Outpatients’ diagnostic and renal function data were extracted from the clinical data warehouse of our hospital. Renal function was assessed based on the eGFR that was calculated using an equation specific for Japanese [ ]. According to the classification of CKD [ , ], outpatients were divided into three groups based on the initial eGFR: ≥ 60, between 30 and 59, and < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Outpatients with an initial eGFR of < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were excluded, because they already had impaired renal function and needed appropriate precaution for contrast-enhanced CT [ , , ]. In this study, decline

renal function data were extracted from the clinical data warehouse of our hospital. Renal function was assessed based on the eGFR that was calculated using an equation specific for Japanese [ ]. According to the classification of CKD [ , ], outpatients were divided into three groups based on the initial eGFR: ≥ 60, between 30 and 59, and < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Outpatients with an initial eGFR of < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were excluded, because they already had impaired renal function and needed appropriate precaution for contrast-enhanced CT [ , , ]. In this study, decline in renal function was defined as when eGFR dropped to below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 at 6 months or 1 year after the initial evaluation. Statistical analysis Age is presented as mean and standard deviation; the rest variables are presented as count and percentage. The differences between two initial eGFR groups were examined with the Fisher’s exact test, except for the difference in age that was examined with the independent two samples test. The association between initial eGFR value and eGFR decline (below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) was evaluated by univariable logistic regression analysis. Subsequently, univariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the associations between comorbidity and eGFR decline within the initial eGFR group at 6 months and 1 year. The comorbidities with P values less than 0.1 identified in univariable logistic regression models were chosen to be entered into the multivariable analysis with backward selection. All statistical hypothesis tests were two-side, and the significance level was set as 0.05. The statistical analyses were performed using the IBM SPSS Statistics 25.0 (IBM Corporation, Armonk, NY, USA). Results Patient selection A total of 117,019 outpatients aged 18 years and older who underwent renal function test between April 2017 and March 2019 were initially selected for this retrospective study. The flowchart of outpatient selection is shown in Fig. . Of them, 19,020 outpatients who had no confirmed disease diagnosis and 1,009 outpatients who had initial eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m 2 were excluded. As a result, 96,990 outpatients were included. After excluding 66,395 outpatients who did not have eGFR test at 6-month follow-up, the remaining 30,595 outpatients who had eGFR test at 6 months were subjected to the final analysis. In addition, after excluding 69,292 outpatients who did not have eGFR test at 1-year follow-up, the remaining 27,698 outpatients who had eGFR test at 1 year were independently analyzed in this retrospective study (Fig. ). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics Among 30,595 outpatients with 6-month follow-up data, 5,686 outpatients had initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and 24,909 outpatients had initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (Table ). Outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were significantly older than those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (P < 0.001). There were significantly more males in the initial eGFR between 30 and 59 group compared with the initial eGFR ≥ 60 group (P < 0.001). Outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had significant higher percentages of CKD, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension, acquired absence of kidney, glomerular diseases, gout or hyperuricemia, ischemic heart diseases, arrhythmia, heart failure, arteriosclerosis obliterans, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cerebral infarction, gastric ulcer, IgG4-related disease, hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, migraine, asthma, malignant neoplasm of colon, and malignant neoplasms of urinary tract, than those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (all p ≤ 0.03) (Table ). Among 27,698 outpatients with 1-year follow-up data, 4,954 outpatients had initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , and 22,744 outpatients had initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (Table ). Outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were significantly older than those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (P < 0.001). There were significantly more males in the initial eGFR between 30 and 59 group compared with the initial eGFR ≥ 60 group (P < 0.001). Outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had significant higher percentages of CKD, DM, hypertension, acquired absence of kidney, glomerular diseases, gout or hyperuricemia, ischemic heart diseases, arrhythmia, heart failure, arteriosclerosis obliterans, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cerebral infarction, gastric ulcer, IgG4-related disease, hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, migraine, asthma, malignant neoplasm of colon, and malignant neoplasms of urinary tract, than those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (all p ≤ 0.011) (Table ). Association between initial eGFR and eGFR decline In outpatients with 6-month follow-up data, 3.4% of outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had eGFR decline, defined as eGFR decreasing to below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , at 6 months. In contrast, only 0.02% of outpatients with initial eGFR ≥

arrhythmia, heart failure, arteriosclerosis obliterans, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cerebral infarction, gastric ulcer, IgG4-related disease, hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism, migraine, asthma, malignant neoplasm of colon, and malignant neoplasms of urinary tract, than those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (all p ≤ 0.011) (Table ). Association between initial eGFR and eGFR decline In outpatients with 6-month follow-up data, 3.4% of outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had eGFR decline, defined as eGFR decreasing to below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , at 6 months. In contrast, only 0.02% of outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had eGFR decline at 6 months (Table ). Univariable logistic regression analysis revealed that outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were 175.94 times more likely to have eGFR decline at 6 months, compared to those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (P < 0.001) (Table ). In outpatients with 1-year follow-up data, 5.1% of outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had eGFR decline at 1 year. In contrast, only 0.06% of outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had eGFR decline at 1 year (Table ). Univariable logistic regression analysis indicated that outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were 94.10 times more likely to have eGFR decline at 1 year, compared to those with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (P < 0.001) (Table ). Associations between comorbidities and eGFR decline in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> Univariable logistic regression analysis revealed that in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , CKD, DM, hypertension, glomerular diseases, gout or hyperuricemia, arrhythmia, and heart failure were significantly associated with eGFR decline at 6-month follow-up (all p ≤ 0.011) (Table ). Moreover, in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , CKD, DM, hypertension, glomerular diseases, gout or hyperuricemia, arrhythmia, heart failure, cerebral infarction, migraine, and malignant neoplasm of urinary tract were significantly associated with eGFR decline at 1-year follow-up (all p ≤ 0.024) (Table ). Associations between comorbidities and eGFR decline in outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> Univariable logistic regression analysis disclosed that in outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , CKD and heart failure were significantly associated with eGFR decline at 6-month follow-up (both p ≤ 0.036) (Supplementary Table 1). Furthermore, in outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , hypertension, gout or hyperuricemia, ischemic heart diseases, arrhythmia, heart failure, and myasthenia gravis were significantly associated with eGFR decline at 1-year follow-up (all p ≤ 0.045) (Supplementary Table 2). Independent risk factors for eGFR decline identified by multivariable logistic regression analysis To investigate whether the comorbidities had independent and significant influence on the risk of eGFR declined to below 30, four multivariable logistic regression models were conducted. The comorbidities with P values less than 0.1 in Tables , and Supplementary Tables 1, 2 were entered into the process of model selection for the corresponding multivariable logistic regression analysis. Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , CKD, hypertension, and heart failure were significant risk factors for eGFR decline at 6-month follow-up (all p ≤ 0.034) (Table ). However, more comorbidities, including CKD, hypertension, glomerular diseases, gout or hyperuricemia, heart failure, migraine, and malignant neoplasm of urinary tract, were significant risk factors for eGFR decline at 1-year follow-up in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (all p ≤ 0.014) (Table ). On the other hand, multivariable logistic regression analysis disclosed that in outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , only CKD was significant risk factor for eGFR decline at 6-month follow-up (P < 0.001) (Table ). Moreover, hypertension and heart failure significant risk factors for eGFR decline at 1-year follow-up in outpatients with initial eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (both p ≤ 0.010) (Table ). Associations between contrast administration and eGFR decline in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> As revealed in Table , outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were at significantly increased risk of eGFR decline at 6 months and 1 year (OR = 175.94 and 94.10, respectively). So, the associations between contrast administration and eGFR decline, regardless of comorbidities, were assessed in outpatients with initial eGFR between 30 and 59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Logistic regression analysis revealed that contrast administration was not significantly associated with eGFR decline in outpatients receiving eGFR test at 6 months (OR = 1.03, P = 0.886) (Supplementary Table 3). And contrast administration was also not significantly associated with
